The aightle88 beggar, resting in the friendly ahadow of St. Peter's, his ahrunken

Though philosophers may widely differ as to that which lies at the goal of our

How beautiful, how true! We are but wanderera on a shell-lined shore, wait·

To relieve the distressed, to sympathize with the afflicted, and to protect the
innocent, is the great object we have in view; and to this end we meet and perfect
our organizations in order that we may have the benefit of an united effort in this
great and noble work.
If a pebble oast into the sea producee changes whose influence is felt upon the
farther shore, if a spoken word is indelibly written upon the viewless pages of the
air, may we not reasonably hope that the influenoe of a kind and generous act may
be as widely felt. The diamond wu once a rude, uncouth and shapeless fragment
of carbon, hidden away in gloomy gorges, where suns never shone and moonbeams
never strayed; but, by the action of time, tbe influence of the elements, and the
lapidary's skill, it became a sparkling gem, coveted and prized by the nobility of
earth. May we not draw from it a parallel, which in its soope shall extend from
the sodden sands of time to the boundless realms of immortality. Words of love
and kindred acts-though in themselves of little worth, and perhaps forgotten,
hidden and lost amid the rubbish of time- may, hy and by, in the great laboratory
of eternity, be crystallized into gems of unfading beauty to deck the jewels we spall
wear in the Great Temple above-diadems for our brows when we enter those

The traveler in the south of Spain, leaving the beautiful vale where the Guadal·
quiver flow~. and traversing barren hills and sterile wutes, tlnde himself at nightfall
beneath the towering heights of Granada. As he lies down to rest he listens to the
musio of murmuring watere. He falls aeleep to its lullaby; it ministers to him in his
dreams, and greets his ear as the first glad voice of the morning. It is the sound of
the irrigating rivulet, brought into existence by the Moorish inhabitants of Granada
more than ti ve hundred years ago. That unhappy people have long 1lnoe been driven
from the shores of Spain ; their temples have been demoliehPd, and the palaces of
their Kings have crumbled into dust; but this simple work of their hands ha.11
remained to oomfort and cheer the'weary traveler through the succeeding ages. Ro
the generous acts and kind offices which we perform und~r the guidance of the
"ub!ime principles of our ancient and honorable Fraternity, will live to feed the
streams of moral fertility which shall oontinue to flow for the benefit of mankind,
when the places we oc~upy shall be vaoa.nt and our names even shall be obliterated
from the tablets of earth.
Our ancient brethren, who wrought with tools and builded material edifices,
have left us a bright example. As they erected temples, so let us build characters.
With our mystic trowels let us spread the cement of brotlerly love and affection
while we live, and, dying, leave behind us a mausoleum of hearts to succeeding
generations.

1'reasurer NATHAN WESTON SPAULDING. prooeeded to the performance of their duty,
r.nd reported, in substance, that the Lodge was in such a state of discord that they
deemed it unwise to return the charter. Desiring, if possible, to restore harmony
and save the Lodge, I determined to visit the brethren and make a la11t effort to
11ffect a reconciliation. I therefore informed the acting Master of my intended
vi1it and requested him to call the brethren together. At the appointed time I
went to Santa Clara and found the major part of the brethren assembled at the
J,odge-room. Upon thorough investigation I diacovered that offenses had been
oommitted which the Lodie had not sufficient vitality to punish, and that the
r11toration of the charter would cause the well·dispoeed members immediately to
dimit, and would also remove the ban of suspension from those who had evidently
been guilty of un-masonic conduct. New difficulties here arose. While I waa
111tisfied that the charter ought to be revoked, and understood that the resolution
of this Grand Body empowered me to exercise such authority as the exigenciea
required, I felt then, and am still of the opinion, that the revocation ef a charter
11 a sovereign act, or the exercise of a power which resides in the Grand Lodge alone,
and which ought not to be delegated. I further saw that an appeal, notice of which
had been given prior to the arrest of the charter, could not be entertained by the
Grand Lodge when the body from whose decision it had been taken waa not in
existence. I therefore ordered the charter continued in arrest until this Annual
Communication, and cited the acting Master to appear before you and show cause,
if any, why the Lodge should not be declared extinct. I recommend the revoca·
tion of the charter, and ask your careful attention to the t>ffenses committed, in t he
hope that in your wisdom some measures may be adopted whereby suitable pun·
ishment may be meted out to the offenders who have caused discord and confusion
in a once useful and honored subordinate of our J urisdiotion.
In December last I received information that 01,ay Lodge, No. 101, located at
Dutch Flat, in Placer County, had voted to invite the members of another fraternal
organization to an installation banquet, and proposed to defray the expenses of the
feast out of the funds of the Lodge. Feeling it to be my duty to inform the Lodge
that such action would be a direct violation of an edict of the Grand Lodge, I addressed a communication to the Master, in which I informetl him that it had been
repeatedly· decided, in language so plain as to preclude the possibility of misconstrue·
tion, that any Lodge that should appropriate its funds, or allow them to be approprl·
ated, for such a purpose, would bejfalse to its trust and 'should be held strictly to BC·
count for its action. I then stated, in the kindest manner possible, that the brethren
should find some other source from which to pay the expenses of the propo!ed ban·
quet. The Master, whose term of office was about to expire, promptly replied that
he would do all in his power to have my instructions carried into effect. In a few
days, however, I received a letter from the Secretary, propounding certain questions, one of which led me to believe that there was a disposition to evade the
proper interpretation of the edict to which reference had been made. I promptly

replied, stating in substance, that no funds of the Lodge could be used to pay for
banquets or for refreshments of any kind. Time passed on, and no satisfactory
information having been received as to the action which the Lodge had taken in
the matter, I went to Dutch Flat without announcing my visit, called upon the
Secret~ry, and requested him to accompany me to the LodQ,"e-room. I made known
the object of my visit and asked him to show me his books. Upon examination
and inquiry I ascertained that the brethren had paid, by contribution, the per capita
quota of the expense represented by the number of visitors present, and that
the share of the outlay indicated by the number ()f members in attendance was then,
by private t1nderstanding, paid by the Senior Warden; and, further that, at a sub·
sequent meeting, the Senior Warden was reported to be in distress, whereupon a
motion was carried to relieve his distresses by donating to him a sum of money
exactly equal to that which he had advanced for the banquet.
When I had ascertained the nature and extent of this proceeding I sent for the
recently installed Master, and on bis arrival interrogated him in regard to the matter
in question. He promptly replied that the expenses of the banquet had been paid
by private oontribution. I called his attention to the fact that the Secretary had
just shown by the records that a part of the expenses had been paid by a charitable
donation to the Senior Warden. His answer, somewhat confusedly given, was that
the Secretary had no right to make any such statement. I then put the question:
"Did you or did you not know, when, as Master of the Lodge, you entertained the
motion to donate a certain sum of money to the Senior Warden, that it was not for
charity but for the purpose of defraying a part of the expenses of your installation
banquet?" After making several attempts at evasion, and after the question had
been several times repeated, he finally admitted that he knew that the money was
to be given for another purpose under the sacred name of charity. Other members
of the Lodge had now arrived, and among them was the former Secretary, with
whom I had corresponded, and who was also a Past Master and the same brother
who had reported the Senior Warden to be in distress and madethe motion to relieve
him. These brethren informed me that it had long been their custom to prepare a
banquet on the oocasion of the installation of officers, and to furnish refreshments
whenever the Lodge had work; and that the expenses had invariably been paid
from the Treasury; also that one of their installation banquets had cost the round
sum of six hundred dollare, and that no objection had ever been made. One of
·these brethren very ourtly informed me of the result of a further Interference with
their festivitiea in the following langua'!e: "If we are to be deprived of our little
eats and drinks in this manner, we will reduce the dues to nothing and run the
Lodge out of the accumulated fund." All present, except the brother who made
the motion, seemed to think that the action of the Lodge was justifiable under the
circumstances. This brother, however, frankly admitted that the Lodge took this
method of concealing the payment of the expenses of the banquet; or to use his
own words: "It was done to whip the devil round the· stump."
On my return to Sacramento I issued an order for the arrest of the charter, and
also another order exempting from the effect of this arrest all members of the
Lodge excepting those who were present at the meeting when this action took
place, and a certain other brother who was present at a previous meeting when
my first Jetter was presented to the Lodge, and who, in a somewhat defiant manner, declared that neither the Grand Lodge nor the Grand Master had any right
to interfere with the, disposition of its funds; that the Lodge had earned its money,
and had a. pP.rfect right to dispose of it at its own discretion. These orders were
duly executed, and the Master was summoned to appear at this session of the Grand
Lodll0 to answer to the charges of willfully violating an edict of this Grand Body
and fraudulently disbursing the funds of his Lodge.

HINKS departed this life, under circumstances which appeal to our deepest sorrow.

vehicle was everturned, and Bro. HINES, in falling, sustained injuries which ~oon

I now close the account of my stewardship, and surrender the trust which you
have reposed in me. In the discharge of all my official duties, I have endeavored,
by precept and example, to inculcate and cherish the sublime prlnciples of Free·
masonry, and if I have erred, I hope it may have been on the side of charity. In
retiring from the high po'sition with which you have honored me, I desire to return
to the brethren of the Jurisdiction the offerings of a grateful heart for the confi.
dence they have reposed in me, and for their many evidences of brotherly love and
esteem. M:y thanks are also due to the Inspectors of the Districts for kind atten·
tions and hearty co-operation. I am also mindful of my obligations to some of the
Past Grand,Masters for valued counsels kindly given. I also tender thanks to my
associates, the present Grand Officers, for the assistance and support which they have
always cheerfully given; and I desire especially to mention the Grand Secretary, with
whom I have been so intimately associated during the year of my administration.
No member of this Grand Lodge can know and approlciate the ability, the efficiency
and the worth of that Grand Officer, until he has been assoCiated with him in the
relation of Grand Master. For the valuable assistance which he has so promptly,
so cheerfully, and so courteously given me, I now tender to him my sincere and
heartfelt thanks.
Brethren, let us now give our attention to the purposes for which we have
assembled. Let all our deliberations be characterized by the true spirit 0f brotherly love; let our social relations be kindly and fraternal; let sincerity and plain
dealing distinguish us; and· let justice be the guide of all our actions. And when
we shall go from this Temple to our usual vocations, let us carry with us the beautiful lessons of Freemasonry, and earnestly endeavor to put in practice its sublime
principles in the every day walks of life. Then, as the signs in the Western sky
admonish us that life's sun is near its setting, we shall lay aside our working tooli
and quit ~arth's field of labor-wearv, it may be, with the burdens we have borne,
but buoyant with the hope that we shall receive at last our Supreme Grand
Master's kind WELL DONE.

Lodge, as follows :To the M. ·• W. •• Grand Lodge of Calif<Yrnia :The undersigned presents his thirty-second Annual Report to the Grand Lodge,
with an expression of his regret that lack of health has prevented him from mak·
ing it as full as he could have wished, and as it has been sometimes heretofore, but
with the hope that no business of importance will be found to have been neglected.
The Proceedings at the last Annual Oommunication were printed aud diatdbuted, or reserved for binding, as has been cuRtomary in the past.
Many more books have been added to the library of the Grand Lodge durin1r
the year, some by purchase, but moat by exchanges with other Grand Lodges and
with collectors; and it is with sorrow that the writer is oompelled to say that the
expectation of beinir enabled by thia time to have a new catalogue of our books prepared,·as suggested in his last report, haa been disappointed. Thia has been caused
partly by the reason above given, but principally by the fact that he has thus far
been unable to procure manv still missing numbers of the Proceedings of other
Masonic Grand Bodies, which he desired to fill up the hiati in and complete the
imperfect seriea ot the transactions of several of those bodie&, before the preparation of another catalogue was commenced. Much correspondence has been had
upon the subject, and with partial success. It will be oontinued, but probably with
little further result, unless some of the older Grand Bodies publish, (as several of
them have done or are doing,) those of their early proceedings which are out of
print or were never printed.
Handsomely bound and pr11perly inscribed copies of the Proceedings at our last
Communication, which contain the action of the Grand Lodge relati •e to the death
and burial of our late greatly beloved and much lamented Bro. LEONIDAS E.
PRATT,· Past Grand Master, were, in due season, prepared and transmitted, on
behalf of the Grand Lodge, to the widow and the two sons of the deceased.
The old editions of the pamphlets known as the "Reccrrd-Book of EzampleLodge,
a suggestive formula for the use of Secretaries in opening and keeping their Record·
Books," and the "Form for Records of Trials and of Transcripts thereof," which
were prepared by the undersigned many years ago, having been nearly exhausted,
and sundry changes havinir occurred in the laws and usages of our .Turisdiction, since
they were written, which made them incorrect and to some extent misleading, new
ones- revised, corrected, and somewhat enlarged-have been prepared. Oopiea of
these, printed and published in the (now) uniform style and octavo form of all our
publications, were transmitted to all the L odges, Grand and Past Grand· Officers,
and lnspectera of Districts of our Jurisdiction, in July last; and, if there be no
objection, will also be sent to the several Grand Lodges with which we are in correspondence.

Of the proposed amendments to the by-laws of Lodges which have been received
during the year, the approval of the Grand Master in seventeen cases has been
filed in this office. Of these, seven-being from Lodges Nos. 5, 59, 88, 158, 184,
279, and Calla.yomi, U. D.-proposed changes in the time for stated meetinflS;
three-being from Lodges Nos. 121, 144, and 234-proposed to reduce the fees for
degrees ; one-being from Lodge No. 127-proposed to increase those fees ; twobeing from Lodges Noe. 45 and 60, proposed to reduce the monthly dues; twobeing from Lodges Noe. 13 and 274, proposed to increase those dues; lme-being
from Lodge No. 270, proposed to abolish the fee for affiliation; and one-being from
Lodge No. 21, proposed to reduce that fee.
A proposed amendment to the by-laws, relative to duties of the Treasurer and Secretary, from Lodge No. 21, was disapproved by the Grand Master for ·the reason
that the change would not be in conformity with the Uniform Code of By-Laws of
Lodges : and for the same reason a proposed amendment as to the times of payment
of dues, from Lodge No. 79, was by him disapproved. A proposed amendment to
the by-laws, relative to the reduction of dues of members, from Lodge No. 246, was
disapproved by the Grand Master for the reason that the rate of dues proposed was
thought to be too low for the Lodge to maintain a healthy and useful . existence.
For a like reason two similar proposed amendments from Lodge No. 259, were
not approved by that officer ; and a proposed amendment of the same character
from Lodge No. 271, was not approved, as it did not appear that it had received the .
necesaary vote required by the law.
As directed by our law, all the feregoing are submitted to the Grand Lodge for
" final action, as will alrio be the Books of By-Laws of the eight Lodges now existing
under dispensation.

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :To the M. ~ W. '. (kand Lodge of Calif<YT"Tlia:-

In making my report to this Grand Body, I regret that I cannot present it more
full and complete. F or many years it has been my ambition t o submit reports to
the Grand Lodge which should embody concise accounts of the working condition
of each and every Lodge in the Jurisdiction. Thie year I think that I have failed
in lloCCOmplishing that object, but this failure has been through no fault of mine. ,,
I have used every e~ort.to persu~de the ~nspec~ors o~ the. various Dil!tric~s t:<> for·
ward their reports m time, and, to their credit be 1t said, the large maJor1ty of
them have done so; but there are always a few wh<1 either send no report at all, or
forward it at so late a date as to render it practically worthless in the preparation
of my own report to the Grand Lodge.
I have received reports from the Inspectors of thirty-one of the thirty-sevel) Districts, viz: From the let, 3d, 4th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, 13th, 1ilth, 16th,

1887.]

Grand Lodge of California.

41

17th, 18th, 19th, 20th, 21st, 22d, 23d, 24th, 25th, 26th, 27th, 28th, 29th, 30th, 31st,
lllld, 33d, 34th, 35th, a.nd 37th; leaving the 2d, 5th, 6th, 12th, 14th, a.nd 36th Districts unheard from. There may be some reasonable uxcuse for the failure of the
In1pectors of these Districts to report, but I very much fear that carelessness or
Indifference would be in most cases the only truthful plea.
Inspector JOHN M. MELENDY, of the First District, reports the five Lodges
therein to be in a sound and healthy condition financially, although very little
work has been done during the year, except in Arcata Lodge, No. 106, which has
been tolera.bly prosperous in that re~pect. The Lodges are in good working order;
their officers are fairly proficient in the work; and no element of discord mars the
b1rmony and good feeling which prevails. The Lodge meetings are well attended,
and there is no lack of interest or zeal in the cause of Masonry, althoul!'h the
Increase in membership has been but small.
Inspector GEORGE H . KNIGHT, of the Third District, reports that, owing to the
exigencies of business, he had been able to visit but one of the four Lodges under
his supervision, that being Adin Lodge, No. 250. This Lodge, he says, is in a
flourishing condition, has conferred four degrees during the year, and has a present
membership of forty-six. It is free from debt, owns its hall, and has $311 in its
treasury. The officers are proficient and the work is done in accordance with the
requirements of t.he Grand Lodge. By correspondence with the Master of North
Kast Lodge, No, 266, he learns that that Lodge is in a prosperous condition, having
conferred twelve degrees durinir the year. Its membership num!>ers forty-eight,
and it has $479 in its. treasury. The officers are well-informed and the work is well
done. Surprile Vallel/ Lodge, No. 285, ·owns its hall and is free from debt. It has
conferred no dflKrees for several years, but the utmost harmony prevails among its
members. He had not been able to hear directly from the officers of AUuras Lodge,
No. 248, as his lettjlrs of inquiry were unanswered; but incidentally he learned
that the Lodge had done considerable work during the year, and, from his know!·
edge ef the officers, he is satisfied that the work was well done.
Inspector EDWARD A. REID, of the Fourth District, reports that, by reason of
Ill-health, he had been unable to visit all the nine Lodges comprised within his
District; but, from oorrespondenoe and interviews with their officers and members,
he is satistied that the work done during the pa.st year has been up to the approved

Of these cases, eight were widows an.d daughters of Masons, two of the ladies
belnir over eighty years of age. One of these old ladies died shortly after comins
under the care of the Board; the other still Ii ves, and will be fed, clothed, and
oared for by the Hoard until she, too, passes into the shadow before the threshold
11f the Hereafter. In addition, the Board has buried five brethren, one of them
l.lting embalmed and shipped East at the request and expense of the Lodge of which
the deceased was a mem~er, said Lodge being at Sullivan, Illinois. The other four
wore found by the way·side, sick, weary, and dying, with only strength remaining
to make an appeal for help. They were nursed, tenderly cared for, and burled,
pauing away with the full oonsciousneBB that their brethren of the mystic tie would
11tend, even into the portals of the iirave, that charity which we are taught is be·
rand and eternal.
Had it not been that the funds of the Board were handled with the most rigid
IOOnomy, and that such a large balance was carried over from the last year, end- •
lug September 30th, 1886, these funds would have been now exhausted. As it
11, the expenditures have been $228 41 in excess ef the reeelpts from all sources.

held in the city of Montgomery, commencing on the sixth day of December, 1886,

The Grand Master's Address is a well written document, being a model both a1
to quality and quantity. He states that when the Grand Lodge of Alabama was
organized, in 1821, it was composed of seven subordinate Lodges, there. being only
eleven Lodges in the State, with a me~bership of one hundred and thirty. Now
there were two hundred an<l fifty Lodges and twelve thousand active ~ember1.
During the sixty.five years since 1821, thirty.two Grand Masters ~ad presided over
the Craft twenty.three of whom had laid S11ide their working tools and entered
up&n thelr lasting refreshment. The present Grand Seo~etary had held hie office
for twenty.nine years, and had been present at every session.
The Grand Master was pleased to repor,f; that the pa.et twelve months had been
undisturbed by any calamity, save an unprecedented overflow in April la.et, which
resulted in great destruction of property.
Some of the Lodges had "experienced refreshing revivala ; " others had not
been thus blessed ; but still, in almost every county, Masonry was "making steady
progress and gaining a hold in the affeotions and. admiration .of _th~ people." Here
is some good counsel which may well be heeded in other Jur1sd1ct1ons also:A Mason la judged by the company he keeps. That member who seeks and
kee the company of the low, the vulgar, the obecen~, the blasphemer, the drunk·
ard1the blackleg the libertine, the slanderer, will brinl{ reproach _upon ~he Orde~
he has espoused. ' In Masonry, as in all social life, evil com'l!unicat10ns w1 .corrup
good morals. * * * What affects a part, affects the entire body Mason~c.
He had laid thret! corner.,tonea : one for . the monument to be erected on the
capitol grounds in Mpnt.gom~ry to the memory of t~e. Co~federa~e dead ; one for

gate to Bro. WILLIAM YATES TITCO.MBE, the Representative of the Grand Lodge

This Communication WIM! called by Grand Master GREEN to consider the difli·
culties which had arisen between himself, as representing the Grand Lodge, and
Hiram Lodge, No. 1, of l'.liew Haven. As nearly aR we can giither the facts of the
case from these proceedings, they are substantially as follows :...1..
Hiram Lodge, No. 1, is the oldest Lodge in the Jurisdiction, its charter ante·
dating, by a number of years, the formation of the Grand Lodge, It is a large,
wealthy, and, if we may judge from what we read, somewhat a self-willed Lodge.
Some years ago the Grand Lodge of Conneotiout adopted a uniform system of
work, which it required all its subordinates to.practice. This work differed In
some particulars, and especially in the third degree, from that which Hiram Lodge
had always followed. Alleging that the Grand Lodge had altered the Ancient
LandD>arks, which is especially prohibited in the "Old Charges," Hiram Lodge
refused· point blank to change its own work and adopt that of the Grand Lodge.
Remonstrances from several Grand Masters were of no avail. At length the
matter was brought before tbe Granii Lodge, which, after due consideration, per·
emptorily required the recusant Lodge to adopt the prescribed' work ; and, in the
event of continued refusal, authorized and directed the Grand Master to depose
the officers of the Lodge, $d order the election of others who would comply. In
the discharge of this duty 'he Grand Master met with constant and almost in1ult.
ing refusals of the Lodge to comply, or observe his edict for a change in its officers.
We must say that the oorrelponden11e, published in these proceedings, lacks very
much of a Masonic or conciliatory spirit. The J:;.odge almost unanimously stood
by its rebellious officers, and adopted a series of resolutions denouncing the Grand
Master and Grand Lodge alike. This was the fe~her that broke the camel's back,
and so the Grand Master called this Special Communication of the Grand Lodge,
and laid th ti whvle mii.tter before that Body.

Relations with all Masonio Bodies were friendly, "with one exception." That
exception we soon ascertained to be the Grand Lodge of England, and the difficulty
with that Grand Body arose In this manner: Our readers are already familiar
with the fact that trouble bas all along existed between the Grand J,odges of Quebec
and England, because the latter has upheld the course of 1everal Lodges in Mon.
treal, which still act under their charter& from the Grand Lodge of Enlj'land, and
refuse to acknowledge the authority or jul'lSdiotlon of the Grand Lodge of Quebec.
Thie last Body has uniformly held to the American doctrine of exclusive Masonic
Jurisdiction, but that never bas been, and is not now, the policy or Ma1onic
doctrine of the Grand Lodges of England, Scotland and Ireland. These .claim
jurisdiction over all.their chartered Lodges, in the colonies of the Empire as well
as at home, and if any of tha Lodges prefer not to join with a local Grand Lodge,
they are upheld by the Parent Body. 'l'he difficulties growing out of this position
lire apparent, but, we believe, have been satisfactorily settled in all disputed cases,
except that of Quebec. The Grand Lodge of that Province, after much and prolonged, though fruitl\ll'B, negotiation, at length issued its Edict of non.intercourse
with the recusant Ll>dgee, a~d, as a matter of course, with the Grand Lodge of
England. And bavirl1t done ~hie, an appeal has been made to other Grand Bodiea,
and particularly to those in the United States, to stand by Quebec in this doctrine
of Exclusive J uri~diction. The Grand Lodge of Illinois responded favorably to
this appeal, and at its last Annual Communication adopted this resolution :Reaolved, That th~ Grand Lodge of Illinois regards all Lodges in the Province
of Quebec, holding allegiance to any Grand Lodge other than the recognized Grand
Lodge of that Province, as illegal and irregular, and that all Lodges and brethren

The seventy-llfth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of J.Jouisiana

thirteenth day of July, 1886, called to lay the corner-stone of the "Hall of the

And still another was held in the same city, on the twenty-fifth day of Novem~

The pamphlet before us is graced with a fine steel portrait of Grand Master
HORNOR, accompanied with a brief biographical notice, from all which it is very
patent that he is a man and Mason eminently worthy of these honors.
At the Annual Communication the Grand Master delivered an Address which.
although somewhat longer than is usual for such documents, is well worthy of the
space it occupies. He begins with sad, but appropriate references to the many
dead of the year, and the Joss sustained thereby by the Fraternity. The list
included Past Grand Master J All!ES L. LOBDELL; Past Grand Master WrLLIAlll R,
WHITAKER, who died in Wisconsin, and, by request of Grand Master HORNOR,
was buried in Boston by the Grand Lodge of Massaohusetts; Pa•t Deputy Grand
Master SAMUEL 0. SCRUGGS; and also several prominent l:'ast Masters of subordl•
nate Lodges.
A considerable portion of this Address is devoted to the connection of the
''Temple property and the finances of the Grand Lodge." The formerhali been, and
is, an elephant of uncomfortable dimensions, that has long troubled the wisest men
of the Craft. Up to date there had been spent upon the new Masonic Temple the
sum of $128,000, most of it raised by heavy taxation upon the Fraternity; and ye&
the Grand Master says he " cannot see that we have any nearer prospect now of
completing the building, than when the foundations were laid." He is of the
opinion that the Grand Lodge had carried this burden lonll' enough, and he suggestli
that the whole property be sold, and the Fraternity thus be ridden of the burden,
The Grand Lodge concurred in this recommendation, and ordered the Directors to
place the property on the market.
In relation to the difficulties between the Grand Lodges of Quebec and England,
the Grand Master endorses the former to the fullest extent, and recommends non·
intercourse with the latter until justice is done to Quebec. After a lonQ' discussion
of a resolution to that effect, its consideration was postponed until the next Annual
Communication, and the Grand Master was requested to correspond with the two
Grand Bodies, "and endeavor to heal the differences now existing between these
Grand Lodges, and to report the result thereof at the next Annual Communio1o
tion."
From personal observation and correspondence, the Grand Master believed that
a better feeling existed among the s~bordinate Lodges-more enthusiasm was
exhibited, and more interest taken in the work and meetings, all hetokening
"a revival of our Jong Jost prosperity."
The Grand Master, alluding to the opinion of many of the Craft, that the
multitude of other secret societies is injuring Masonry, does not so believe. Most
of these are merely life-insurance companies, carrying within them the seeds of
their own dissolution. Masonry can neither adopt their theories or practices, as
they would be subversive of her fundamental dogmas. Much can be said on both
sides of this question, but we have neither space nor inclination to take part in the
discussion.
Upon the recommendation of the Committee on Correspondence, the Grand
Lodge formally recognized the Grand Lodges of South Auotralia and of the Federal
District of Mexico.
"Louisiana Relief Lodge, No. 1," the counterpart of our Masonic Board of
Relief of Sa.n Francisco, made a good report of its work during the year. Among
those helped was one from California t1> the amount of fifteen dollars.

But whilst all around changes have been perpetually going on in form and sub1tanoe, tenets and miesion, Masonry has not changed. It has grown from a small

oentury of time save here; for the truth ia perfection at all tim.e8 and amid all chan(IU.
Builded upon the immutable foundation of Truth, Love and Justice, it has seen

brother whose birthday we observe with grateful affection. Not only great in
those qualities which distinguished him as soldier and statesman .. ~ut equally faithful in the duties of domestic life and as a private citizen of the Jtepubli2J he is to
us a noble example of those virtues which Masonry seeks to inculcate. Too generous for bigotry in any form, too modest for self-seeking, too ll'reat for rivalry, he
entered the Lodge-room a Fellow Craftsman and a brother, desiring only to ad·
vance the interests of this beloved Institution, and to manifest in his daily life the
value of its life-giving principles.

whom he had spent his strength were unable to supply.
A noble eulogy, showing the good man and Mason. And so for nearly ninety
years did be bless the world, until be was called home to everlasting refreshment.

Dispensations had been granted for nine new Lodges. Several pages of the
Address are devoted to the details of the arrest of the chartera of several Lodgea.
Two or three were for refusing to discipline brethren who were engaged in the
"saloon business" or selling intoxicating drinka aa a beverage. It appears that
this is forbidden by the State laws, and hence has been declared by the Grand
Lodge to be a Masonic crime. In these particular cases the brethren;admitted in

open Lodge that they were so engaged, and yet the Lodge voted that they were
not guilty. This the Grand Master considered to be a very grave offence, and
the charters were arrested. He closes what he has to say in relation to one of the
offending Lodges, with this exhortation to, the brethren of the Grand Lodge and
elsewhere: "If y<>u love Freemasonry, punish those who violate her laws and
trample her sacred precepts beneath their feet." The action of the Grand Master
was endorsed by the Grand Lodge.
'
In this Jurisdiction the Grand Master has the right to order a new trial in all
cases where, in his opinion, due and proper justice has not been done. In one case
a brother, who was a county officer, had embezzled money to the amount of thou·
sands. His Lodge tried him therefor and found him guilty, but only sentenced
him to suspension for one year. Deeming this punishment wholly inadequate, the
Grand Master ordered a new trial, which resulted in the expulsion of the offending
brother.
The Grand Master closes this interesting Address with these timely thoughts,
suggested by the immovable Pyramid upon the shifting, sandy plains of Eygpt :~
So, brethren, out upon the plains of this active, restless, changeful, daniteroUI
age, there arises, amidst this unrest, doubt, perplexity and Agnosticism, like the
!!'reat Pyramid, the Masonic Order, built upon the idea of a Supreme Ruler, begin•
mg and ending in the Great Architect of the Universe, coming up out of the deep
unknown past, hoary with age, yet new and frelilh with thought and principle ; conservative, yet progressive; old, yet always young with truth; formal, yet vitald•
profound, yet simple ; symbolic, yet clear; silent, yet speaking with power, in an
through all the avenues of thought and feeling-permanent, changeless, abidinir
forever. Against its foundations the waves of Atheism are broken and dashed
back into a sea of confusion, like the waves of the Levant when they strike the
immovable granite of Gibraltar.
Amidst this wild storm of cban!(e. when every ship upon life's sea. is hard
pressed, when every little batteau, with its precious freight, is swinging up and
down upon the wavelets which roll beneath it,-ah ! when amidst all this pressure
upon the weary, anxious, toil-worn hurried human heart and brain, a morbid desire
for excitement usurps the place of duty, when liberty is fast driftml!' into licenset
when sober reflection is about to cease, when character is becommg weak ana
plastic, when love of money roots out the love of truth, when dissipation becomes
the alternative to labor, when this fever of modern life is praying upon modern
integrity, then, as if built for the hour, as if J>redestined for the times, and foreor·
dained to cope with these evils, the Masonic Temple rises in its stately beauty and
grandeur, bright, calm and serene, reflecting the iridescent rays of her Great Light,
buttressed upon the existence of the "one true and living God,'' and girded with
the iron girders of truth to the eternal principles of right. These waves of saoreligious change fall harmless at its base ; these storms of mutability roar around its
columns without effect; the mutterings of Agnosticism die away in its corridors,
without a r•sotmding echo in its halls. The :!l.ood-tide of these new, false, destruc·
tive ideas, doctrines and teachings, is stayed against this barrier. Masonry is
indeed one of the grea.t conservative forces of our times ; not only moulding the
character and lives of her members, but exerting a world-wide influence promotive
of the welfare of millions of our race who never saw its "Ught."
And thus has Masonry stood, powerful and conservative, checking the wildest
passions of men in the darkest hours of the most fearful revolutions of the past;
thus Masonry stands to·day, holding, or helping to hold, in check the evil tenden·
cies of our times; making men more thoughtful, earnest and true; binding them
with her beautiful symbolic cords to that which is changeless; projecting their lives
out of the basis of an immortality; teaching, at all tiwes, benevolence and charity,
fraternity and fidelity.

1t length in the proceedings. We would like to copy many paragraphs from this

SOLOMON was the founder of Mas_onry. We copy it without comment:The next subject to which I turn is that of the traditions of Masonry. It has
always been a subj~ct of earnest inquiry whether the statements made to our candidates in Blue Lodge Masonry, in relation to King SOLOMON and other worthies
of the period, are true ; that is, whether they were, in reality, the founders and
patrons of our Order. 'l'hese traditions beinl{ held in all parts of the world, and
among nations widely separated, there is a strong presumption of their truth, even
11 the fact that every nation has some traditions relative to the Flood is a presumption of the truth of the Bible statements in regard to the Flood. But the Masonic
visitor to Jerusalem and .:>ther parts of Oriental countries, if he will qualify himself
lo converse with well-informed natives, and to read their books in the languages
•poken there, will find corroborative evidence, of the most direct and satisfactory
uharacter, that the Blue Lodge traditions cherished in this country are well
founded. For my part, I have no more doubt that King SOLOMON conceived the
plan of Freemasonry and established It in Jerusalem, than I have that MOSES was
the founder of J udr.ism, or that ALEXANDER the Great was the founder of the
Grecian Empire. In visiting localities named in the Masonic Lectures, such as
'l'yre, Gebal, Lebo.non, Joppa, Jerusalem and other places, there is abundant food
for confirmation, both in the ancient monuments remaining there, and the myths
preserved by the people. This is particularly true of Jerusalem, where, although
the 'l'emple of SOLOMON has long since disappeared from the eye of man, thefoun·
dations of the Temple abide there-grand, massive and indestructible as the prinolples of Freemasonry themselves. And it were well for Freemasonry in this
country if our learned and enterprising brethren would but qualify themselves in
the study of the languages indigenous there, and make visits there and secure
these precious proofs of our antiquity as o.n Order, upon which so much depends,
and return and teach them to the rest.

MONTANA.

The twenty-second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Montana
was held in the city of Helena, commencing on the sixth day of October, 1886,-the
M.·. w.·. JOSEPH A. HYDE, Grand Master, presiding, and the B.'. w.·. CORNELIUS
HEDGES being Grand Secretary. Twenty.five Lodges were repr!lsented.,
.
We have, as a frontispiece to the proceedings before Ul!, 11 beautiful steel engraving of the Grand Master, and there is also, further on, one ot Past Grand Master
HUGH DUNOAN. Our brethren in Montana are accustomed thus to honor those
who are called upon to preside over the Craft.
The Grand Secretary, probably because he is the most important officer of the
two, takes precedence of the Grand Master, so far as their Annual Reports are
concerned. From one of the paragraphs in the Report of the officer first namtld,
it is quite evident that Bro. ABELL'B medicine for promptness in returns and payment
of dues, is either not administered or fails of the pesired effect. Bro. HEDG11i8
complains that "there is no perceptible improvement in the matter of making
returns." Only fifteen Lodge elections had been reported at all, and up to the eve
ef the meeting of the Grand Lodge, only sixteen returns had been received, and
only ten of those Lodges had paid their dues. We do not wonder at the discouragement of Bro. HEDGES, nor that the Grand Lodge is only able to pay him the
· pitiful sum of five hundred dollars per annum for his valuable services. As a
remedy worth trying, he suggests that, as the Secretaries of subordinate Lodges
are paid for their services, it might be well to fine each delinquent Lodge five
dollars, and then the Secretary would be made to make his report in time or pay
the fine out of his own pocket. A good suggestion.
Two· dispensations had been granted during th~ year for the formation c1f new
Lodges. We have also this item of interesting information, which we would be
glad to republish as true also of California:During the past year, a member of one of our subordinate Lodges, well endowed
with this world's goods, and still better endowed with the loftiest J?rinoiples of
Masonic charity, has signified by a will that he bas executed, his intention to make
the Grand Lodge of Montana his chief legatee, for the purpose of endowing a
Masonic Home and Asylum for aged and distressed Master Masons, their widows

'ad orphans. • • * The name of thia generous and noble-hearted brot,lier when

ind tranquillity seem to prevail in all the Lodges. There is not a ripple upon the

The Grand Lodge, on the report of a speoia.l committee, voted a donation of one
hundred dollars for the relief of suffering Masons in Charleston. Fifty dollars for
the relief of sufferers by fire at Galveston, Texas, had been previously forwarded
by the Grand Master. 'rhe Grand Lodge approved his action.
We infer from a resolution adopted by the Grand Lodge, tha'•the ubiquitous
reporter and interviewer had been prowling around the Grand Lodge, for it was
declared that any publication of its proceedings, except in the regular form and
way, was "uncalled for, unmuonlo, and detrimental to the best interests of the
Craft; and the practice is hereby strictly forbidden."
Upon the report of the Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence upon the so-called
Louisiana Resolutions, it was'resolved that, while the Grand Lodge only recognized
the three degrees of Entered Apprentice, Fellow-Craft, and Master Mason, it would
"not assume to pass upon the ola.ims of any other organiiation11, whether claiming
to be Masonic or otherwis~, or dictate to the members of its Lodges what other
a1eociations or organizations they may connect tbemulves with, so long as its
rightful and exclusive control of Blue Lodge Masonry ia not infringed or interfered
with, or the allegiance of its members perverted." A very sensible resolution.
The new Masonic Temple, recently erected 11t Helena, was dedicated during this
Communication,
When we say that the Report on Foreign Correspondence is airain from the pen
of the worthy Grand Secretary, sufficient evidence is offered that it is one of the best
received. Bro. HEDGES alw&ya knows what to say, how to say it, and stops when
he gets through; and who can do better than that T His report, covering one hun·
dred and forty pages of the appendix, needs no apology, even if it was commenced

aotice is. taken of the California proceedings for 1881'S, Grand Officers HINllls, ABELL
and SHAEFl"EB coming in for their full and merited share. Bro. HEDGES thinks

all dues," it " would indicate the return of the age of miracles."

On the twenty.fourth day of June, 1886, the oldest Lodge in the Jurisdiction, St.

The Grand Master devotes considerable space to the case of one PBEBOOTT, out of
which had arisen disputed questions as to jurisdiction and property between the
Grand Lodges of New Hampshire and Vermont. The Committee on Masonio Jurle·
prudence also directs attention to the eanie, both holding that Vermont is wrong. It
appears that PBESOOl'T, who was an express messenger on one of the railroads, was
rejected In the Lodge of his residence, and then crossed the Connecticut River and
was received in a Vermont Lodge. As our brethren in New Hampshire present the
question, it would seem that they were right, but we shall see, by and by, what the
Vermonters have to say. The case involves that vexed, and apparently never-to·be·
settled question of "Perpetual Jurisdiction."

future, and yet had been expelled for that single offense, the committee approved the
finding of the Lodge, bot changed the sentence to one of suspension.

Is not the following pleasing incident worthy of mention here also? We
think so.:Here let me with pride revert to an instance of the practicality of Masonic work
and teaching that has occurred during the past year. On the second of March, m

under water, with the sea breaking in wild waves fifteen feet over her, and in a
short time she WILi! a fantastic iceberg, with half-frozen men clinging to her rigl!'ing.
A brother of Marin~ra' Lodge, of Barnegat, was casually attracted t o the peouliar
position of the boat. He watched it for a moment, when behold I a signal ! An
mstant later it was repeated-and again. It was the Masonic si11nal of distress I
Onr seafaring brethren called for help-and not in vain. He who saw their significant appeal aelayed not, but flew to the nearest life-savinl!' station for nesistance.
Meanwhile the orew, six in all, seeking safety, had floated a boat, and we're out
upon the angry waters, while their vessel fast went to pieces. They were unable
t o row to shore, and drifted helplessly toward the open sea. But soon strong men
with willing hands and all useful appliances, were able .t o compau their relief, and
brought th.,10 safe to shore, exh11.u11ted and badly frozeu, but with bleaai.nga for the

Grand Master J. WIMBURN I.AURIE was absent in England at the time of the
Annual Oolnmunlcatlon. He forwarded a short Address in writing, but, not being
received in time, it was not read In Grand Lodge, bat Is published In the proceeding-.
It appears that when last elected to his high office, he was absent as a General of the
forces sent to quell the RIEL rebellion in the North-west. He returned his cordial
thanks for the great compliment thus paid him. He did not return from the seat of
war until July, and early In the autumn was compelled by urgent business to leave
for Europe. So that, as a matter of fact, the Deputy had been the acting Grand
Master for the most of the year, and we have his Address also before as. Of the real
Masonic work of brotherly love and relief performed by the Grand Master while in
Europe, we have this Interesting account from his own pen:1 had been but a few days in England when the Servo-Bulgarian war hroke out·
and the accounts transmitted through the British Minister, resident in Belgrade'
deMcribed the arrival from tae battle.field of large numbers of wounded for whom
no hospital provision had been made. 'l'he Briti~h Red Cross Society at o~ce decided
~o sen~ assistance; and, as I had lately had considerable experience In such work, I
1mmed1ately volunteered to proceed to the seat of war, and was appointed Commissioner to S~rvia, where for two months I took charge of a couple of hospitals, and
trust that m some degree I was able to alleviate suffering, and assist In restoring to
their families and their country many who would otherwise have perished • and I
feel sure yon will be gratified that your Grand Master was privileged to he e~gaged
in such eminently Masonic work, although not carried on directly under the auspfoes
of the Craft.
It was with particular pleasure that 1 found myself associated in such good work
with th~ energetical.ly benevolent of other .European nations-Austrian, Germiw;
Roumaman, Hnngar1an, and later on, Rnssrnn; and I would specially mention a
s~olet:v, t~~ Knights of Ma.lfa, drawn from the highest classes, socially, In the Austrian Empire, men of the highest nobility, who have devoted themselves to this work
and titted up an ambulance railway train at their own cost, and who pass from one
seat of war to another, giving reilef to the suffering, clearing out the overcrowded
ambulanres, and transferring the patients from the immediate surroundings of war
to less disturbed districts where they can be better cared for. These were·not
Masonic Bodies, but they were influenced by the same spirit; and our object Is not
solely ~o swell t.he number of our initia~es, bot ra~her to foster the spirit with which
we claim to be imbued, and to spread 1t world-wide; and we hail as co-workers all
who have the same aims as ourselves, even if they have not become brethren of the
mystic tie.

The Address of Deputy Grand Master Ross is of considerable length, but entirely
confined to the business of the Jurisdiction. He had vi~ited the Lodges In Cape
Breton Island, and gives an interesting account of Masonic affairs as he found' them
in that out of the way place. This island is noted for its coal mines. After visiting
"Syrian Youth Lodge'\ at " Little Glace Bay," the Grand Master says that ou his
way back to Sydney the aame night, he "overtook a number of men with lanterns,
who, the driver said, w~re members who had walked three or four miles from the
neigh boring mines especially to attend the Grand Master's visitation, and who carried
lanterns to lighten their way through the inky darkness of the night." From this It
is quite evident that there are some live Masons in Cape Breton. At the invitation of
another Lodge in that island, the Worshipful Master and a Past Master rode thirteen
miles in a heavy rain storm to be present at the meeting. Good pluck, that!

" A member of the Lodge at P. had been a resident of R. F., and so re~ided at
the time of his death. He was lo comfortable circumstances pecunlarily, and hie
family were able to pay the expenses aooruiog from his sickness. He was lJuried
with Masonic honors. After his death, the Lodge at R. F. present ed a bill for money
paid out for nursing, which the family refused to pay, claiming that it was the duty
of the Lodge to provide him with nurses, etc. The bill was then presented to tqe
Lodge at P ., whioh refused to pay, on the ground that the nursing should have been
voluntarily performed by meml>ers of the Lodge, and referred the matter to me for
my opinion. I replied as follows: The family, if, as you say, it is responsible, should
pay the bill. It Is an error to suppose that a well-to·do person has either a legal or
moral right to service of this nature. It is only the poor and distressed that we are
bound to relieve. I do not mean that we should not do all in our power to relieve
the sufferings or otherwise assist any members who may be in distren, rich or poor,
but we are not obliged to dispense charity to the rioh.
Tn answer to a query, the Grand Master said: "There is no reason why a Lodge

Hrn'ALGO.-A communication received from the Grand Lodge Of the State of
Hidalgo, on the sixth day of December last, informs us that, on the seventeenth
day ef October, 1884, a General Assembly of the Lodges of that Atate convened at
the city of Pachuca for the purpose of constituting an Independent Grand Lodge
therefor. Five Lodges appear to have been represented, each by its Master and
Wardens, and, except in one case, by Its Secretary and Treasurer also. The Ven.
Bro. RICARDO PASCOE was the temporary President, and the Ven. Bro. FRANIJISOO
MoEDANO, the provisional Secretary.
After the usual preliminaries the convention proceeded to the election of a
Grand Master which resulted in the choice of the Ven. Bro. RICARDO PASOOE, who
took the oblig~tion, was saluted in the customary manner, and was installed in his
high station. The other Grand Officers were then elected and installed, and the
"Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the Atate of Hidalgo" was de·
clared to be duly constituted. The Constitution of the Grand J,odge of the
Federal District was adopted, with the solii exception that the office of Orator (ma
subordinate Lodge,) was to be retained. It was provided that the ordil1ary Hession•
of the Grand Lodge should take place in January and July of each year, and ex tr.,.
ordinary ones when necessary; and it was ordered that an exchange of Represen~
tives with other Grand Lodges be requested.
Later communications give the information that the publication of an Offioial
Bulletin will soon be commenced, which will be transmitted to us ; and that, on
the twelfth day of January, 1887, the Ven. Bro. RICARDO PABOOE was re-elected
Grand Master, and the Ven. Bro. ROBERTO MORENO, Grand ~ecretary.
Jausoo.-We have continued files of El Libre y Aceptado Mason, a monthly
periodical and the official organ of the Grand Lodge of the State of J alisoo, to and
including September, 1887. From these we learn that on the first day of April,
1887, the Ven.". M. ". FELIX L. MALDONADO was again installed Grand Master, as
was the R. ".Bro. DoNAOIANO P. ZABBE, Grand Secretary. On the twentieth day
of March, next preceding, was held the first Annual Communication of the Gra?d
Lodge, at which these Grand Officers were duly elected. The Grand Maste.r dehV·
ered an eloquent Address, in which he gave his brethren much good advice and

The Proceedings of this Grand Lodge for 1885 and 1886 have been received. As
our last report reviewed. only. the transactio~s of this Grand Body to and including

two years.
At the usual Quarterly Communications little business of general interest appears
to have been transacted. The Annual Oommunication for 1885 was held in the
city of Lima, on the eleventh day of January, the M. •• W," ANTONIO ARENAS
Grand Master, presiding, and the V. '. W. '. J. ARTURO EGO-AGUIRRE being Grand
Secretary. Eleven subordinate Lodges were represented. In an able Address the
Grand Maater recites the principal transactions and events of the previous ;ear
together with his official acts, and clearly sets forth the conditi0n of the Craft i~
that Jurisdiction. The difficulties occasioned hy the persistent invasion thereof
by the Grand Orient of Italy, the Grand Lodges of Hamburg and Scotland and
the Supreme Council of Peru, still existed, with little hope of 11 proper settle~ent.
~he. Grand Lodge of ~ambur~ endeavored to escape the responsibility of its un·
JUst1fi.11bl'; act by alleg1~g that 1t was not 11 Sovereign Body, but was subject to an
org11mzat1on called the 'Grand Diet of the German Grand Lodges." The Supreme
Council o~ Peru, in justification of its acts, assigns patriotic motives; and the
Gr~nd Onent o~ Italy. ur~e~ reasons of convenience, notwithstanding that it claims
for itself exclusive Jur1sd1ct1on over all the peninsula of Italy.
'l'he Grand Master makes appropriate allusion to the deceased brethren of his
own and other Jurisdictions, and pays 11 fraternal tribute to their memory. The
report of the Grand Secretary gives 11 clear and concise account of the transactions
of. his office, and in conclusion he says: "May Divine Providence, which has per~1tted our reunion to-day, be pleased to give us wisdom to understand and appreciate our actual condition and boldly face the constant enemy of our Order; union
to ~nabl~ us to go resolutely to the conflict ; anC!I prudence to dictate practical resolut10ns m favor of persecuted humanity. By accomplishing this1 and faithfully
complying with ~e laws, we may become worthy members of an institutlon the
most self-denying, the most noble, the most holy that the wisdom of man has been
able to create." A vote of thanks was tendered the Grand Secretary for the able
manner in which he had discharged his duties.

~119ter, Deputy Grand Master, and Grand Chaplain, which "were attentively

Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of GEORGE WILLIAMS, who
was expelled by Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21, on the fourth day of July, 1887, have carefully examined the evidence adduced before the Commissioners and can see no
r11ason why the judgment of the Lo~ge should be reversed.
The accused was charged with unmasonic conduct in having embezzled the
funds of a Tribe of Red Men, while acting in the capacity of Secretary thereof, of
which Tribe of Red Men the accuser and sPveral other members of Hawaiian Lodge
1ue members.
There are fifteen specifioations in the charge, naming the various sums received
from different parties and appropriated by the accused to his own use. The grounds
nf appeal are, that if the offense was one punishable by the laws of the country, it
•hould first be tried by the Courts, and then by the Order of Red Men wherein
the offense was committed; and that the Masonic Lodge had no right to receive or
act upon the charge.
The testimony shows that oha.rges w1we entertained in the Tribe of Red Men,
that the Tribe triw them and gave judgment, and that the accused appealed from
1aid judgment to the Great Council of that Order. It is the duty of a Mason to
be honest in every station of life, and he cannot justify a crime in himself, because
It was not committed in our Ord'.lr. The CommiHioners found the accused guilty
upon twelve of the fifteen speoifioations, and unanimously sentenced him to expul·
alon.
Your committee find that the trial was had in proper forin; that the testimony
was suffirient to support the findings ; and that there appear no grounds whereon
to reverse the judgment. They therefore recommend the adoption of the following
rtsolution :Resolvl!d, 'l'hat the appeal of GEORGE WILLIAMS, from the judgment of Hawaiian
Lodge, No. 21, sentenoing him to expulsion from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry, on the fourth day of July, 1887, be dismisRed; and that the sa.id jud(/·
ment be and is hereby affirmed.

have had the record and testimony under consideration, and find that there appears

vember, 1886, be and is hereby affirmed; and that the appeal therefrom be dismissed.

Bro. LEWIS FULLER JoNES, from the Committee on By-Laws of
Lodges, presented the following report :To the M." W." Grand Lodge of Oalijarnia:Your committee, to whom were referred those portions of the Address of the
Grand Master and of the Report of the Grand Secretary which relate to amendments to their by.Jaws proposed by sundry Lodges, and to the by.laws of Lodl!l!ll
under dispensation, have. carefully examined the papers and books submitted to
them, and report as follows :In the seventeen cases of proposed amendments to the by-laws of Lodges approved by the Grand Master, your committee recommend that hie action be
affirmed by the Grand Lodge, except in the one relatin'f to FriU .River Lodge, No.
270. In that case they are unable to find that any propoeed amendment, or copy
thereof, was forwarded to the Grand Secretary, as required by law, nor a.ny suffi·
cient notice that such amendment had been d11ly voted by the Lodge. The only
notice to that officer seems to be a clause in a letter from the Secretary of the
Lodge to the Grand Secretary, without seal, saying, among other thinlfB not relevant to the matter of the amendment of b~·laws, that "the affiliation fee was
stricken out of our by-laws, from five dollars to nothing, by a two-thirds vote.of

1887.]

179

Grand Lofige of Oalifor.nw.

the Lodge." Whether at a stated or special meeting of the Lodire; whether any
previous notice of intention ta move for such acliion of the Lodge had been given ;
or in what Year of Light such action of the Lodge was had, is not intimated.
While your committee do not question the good faith of the Secretary of the
Lodge, they venture to suggest that a proposed amendment to the by-laws of a
Lodge is required to be presented singly, under the 1eal of the Lodge, and with
date of the action of the Lodge and of previous notice of motion for such action, as
well as of the vote by which such action was taken. We therefore recommend
that the sugge1ted amendment to the by-laws of *Fall .River Lodge, No. 270, be
denied by the Grand Lodge until properly presented for approval.
In the cases of the disapproval by the Grand Master of the proposed amendments to the by.Jaws of Lodges Nos. 21, 79, 246, 259, and 271, your committee
also recommend that his action be affirmed by the Grand Lodge ; and they see no
occasion to add any reasons to tho1e of the Grand Master for his disapproval.
Your committee have examined the Books of By-Laws of the eight Lodges
under dispen1atfon, and have compared the same with the Uniform Code of ByLaws for Lodges; and they report that those of the following Lodges, viz.: Oallayomi, South Wut, M<UrJIQd,l, Tyrian, Pa10 .Roble1, Winntdumah, and EWmme, are in
consonance with the Uniform Code, are well-written, and have the full names of the
members of the Lodges ai!l'lled thereto; and it is recommended that they be ap·
proved by the Grand Lodge.
The by-law1 of San Migud r~odge are neatly written and properly signed by
the members thereof, and, with one exception, are in a.ocordance with the Uniform
Code. Article IV, Section 1, of the Uniform Code, prescribes, in the matter of
petitions, that "every such petition shall be referred to a committee of three, whose
duty it shall be t<t report thereon at the next regular meeting, (unless further time
be granted,) when the applicant shall ~ balloUd for, and received or rejected." This
provision for an immediate ballot is imperative, and is based on auch strong grounds
of prudence and reason that it should not be amendtd out of the Uniform Code in
favor of an optional or po1tponed ballot. But the corresponding section of the bylaws of San Migml Lodge, provides that the applicant "may," not "shall," be
balloted for, and adds, "or the ballot may be postponed until the next stated
meeting."
Your committee find no other fault in the by-laws of the Lodge, as presented,
but they consider this one so serious that they are compelled to recommend that
the by-lawe of San Migud Lodge be not approved by the Grand Lodge.
All which ie respectfully submitted by

Your committee have examined the reports of the several Masonic Boards of
Relief, viz.: those of San Francisco, Oakland, Sacramento, Los Angeles, Stockton, and San Jose, and find the usual calls for relief continued, and the accustomed
charity extended.
The Board of Relief of San ]'rancisco has a.gain expended the amount of its
~eceipts, or nearly so, having a balance in its treasury on the 30th September, 1887,
of but $645 78, which was only $61 78 in excess of its bafance on hand at the
beginning of its fiscal year, October let, 1886. Your committee therefore deem it
proper that the Grand Lodge make it the same appropriation as that of last year.
The Board of Relief of Oakland desires five hundred dollars, but, seeing that
its balance on hand September 30th, 1887, was $220 35 In excess of that at the
beginning of the fiscal year, October lat, 1886, and considering its close proximity
to San Francisco, your committee have concluded to decrease the amount appropriated last year by $100, believing that to be doing this Board full justice.
The Board of Relief of Sacramento requests the same appropriation as that of
last year, (though then their request was for $1,000,) and your committee conclude
it but fair to allow it the same as was then appropriated.
The Board of Relief of Los Angeles asks for nine hunolred dollars, in which
amount is included $300 to Msist in paying a Secretary; but, from its favorable
report and the condition of its treasury on the lat October, 1887, there being then
on hand $276 11, although your committee do not deem it necessary to provide
especially for its Secretary, yet, owing to the great increase of population in its
locality and the increased demands upon that Board in consequence, they have
concluded to increase its appropriation 'this year hy $200.
The Board of Relief of Stockton prays the Grand Lodge to be as liberal as possible in its appropriation thereto, and your committee have concluded to increase its
amount by $50.
The Board of Relief of San Jose, having but one Master Mason, (who is nonaffiliated,) his wife, and two children to assist, your committee, thinking it a bad
precedent to encourage the establishing of Boards· of Relief in places having but
one or two Lodges, have concluded that they cannot recommend any appropriation
for that Board this year.

Bro. RoBEB'.r OscaB ORAVENS, from the Committee on Grievanoes,
presented the following report : Tu the M. ·. w.-. Yra~d Lodge of California:-

Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. JosEPH LrP~MAN, in
the case of Bro. CHARLES FREDERICK BROWN, sentenced to reprimand by Mount
Moriah Lodge, No, 44, on the fourth day of May, 1887, have had the satne under

1887.]

Grand Lodge of OaUfornia.

191

consideration, and respectfully report that the Commissioners found the accused
guilty of writing and publishing a defamatory letter, ae set forth in the specifications of a charge of unmasonic conduct; and that Bro. LIPPMAN contends that the
punishment is inadequate and that the accused should be more severely dealt with.
It appears from the transcript of the trial-record that the charge was properly
presented to the Master of the Lodge, and that a Commission was duly elected in
M:Cordance with the Constitution. At the first meeting of the Commiuloners, all
the parties being present, the accused interposed a demurrer to the sufficiency of
the charge and specifications, on the ground that the facts stated therein did not
constitute a Masonic offense. Greatly to their discredit the Cpmmluioners sus·
tained this demurrer, and dismissed the charge without hearing any testimony ; to
which proceeding, strange as it may appear, the Master assented. How it was
possible to find a Master and seven Commissioners, in a Lodge of Masons of Ualifornia, so utterly ignorant of MMonic Law and deaf to the demands of justice, is a
conundrum which your committee is unable to answer.
The fact of this proceeding coming to the knowledge of the Grand Master, he
ordered the Master of Mount Mariah Lodae to reconvene the Commiuion and pro·
ceed to try the case on its merits. In obedienoe to the order of the Grand Master,
the Commission was reconvened and proceeded to hear te.etimony, both the accused
and the accuser being present. No objections were interpoied by either to the
Commissioners or to the legality of the proceedings.
The record of testimony is very voluminous, and some objectio111 to the intro·
duction of certain parts of the testimony are noted, but the rulings upou. the points
raised were not such ae to prejudfoe the rights of the accused in any material
manner. Indeed, it appe11rs that he WRS given unlimited latitude in the introduc·
tion of testimony, and that all the rules of evidence were set at defiance to give him
an opportunity to justify his action and to besmirch the character of the acouser.
Notwithstanding all this, out of his own mouth he convict& himself. He says:
" Having some busineH grievance against Bro. LIPPMAN, I addressed the letter in
evidence to a delegate." The langu111fe of the letter here admitted ie highly defam·
atorv, and, to add to the gravity of the offense, it was anonymous; and It wae only
by companson uf the handwriting that Its authorship was traced to the accused,
wlio, when confronted with the evidence, admitted his guilt, and on the trial
attempted to show justification. Although ample opportunity was given him to
do so, he failed to produce any evidence tending even to reduce the grade of the
offense or to mitigate the punishment which it deserves.
That the letter was defamatory, and not only intended to injure the brother in
his good name, but calculated to brini{ disgrace upon his family, Is clearly shown
by its language, and ths manner of its publication. That it was uttered with
malicious intent is equally clear, the offensive words having been written and sent
out with deliberate premeditation. The utterance of a slander always implies
malice in the author, and the burden of proof that there was no malice re11ts upon
him. The evidence in this case shows actual malice. The accused, becoming
offended with the accuser, nurses his wrath for aeveral month.a, and, like the midnight
asSMsio, lies in wait for l\n opportunity to strike his victim In the dark. The
opportunity came and he utilized it, and we are called upon to pass judgment upon
what appears to be little less than an attempt to shield him from the puni1hment
which he merited.
To permit the offender in such a case as this to escape with a simple reprimand
is an a.ct to which your committee cannot give their assent. It is declared in the
old Constitutions that " If a Mason go amiss or sW,mkr his brother, so as to bring
the Craft to shame, he shall have no furth'2r maintenance among the brethren."

After due consideration your committee are of the op1mon that the inability to
pay a just debt, however annoying it may be to the creditor, is not a Masonic
offense; and that, when no moral turpitude is involved, it should never b~ made the·
basis of a charge of unmasonic conduct. They therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption : . .
Baol,vt;d, That the proceedings and record of the Comm1sS1on convened by Haywanl Lodge, No. 226, by which Bro. CHARLES HENRY DAVI°:' was sente~~d on
the tenth day of December, 1886, to be suspended from all ~he nghta ~nd pnvileg_es
of Masonry, are diaapproved; and that the chai:ge there111 be and is hereby dismissed.

day of March, 1887, have had the same under consideration and report as follows :The accusation of habitual intemperance, set forth in the specifications, is fully
llW!t&ined by the evidence. The intemperate use of intoxicating liquors is & grave
offense against the teachings and principles of Masonry, to which our attention is too
often called without its receiving the notice which its lll'avity demands. Through
a commendable desire to bring about the reformation of an errina' brother, we often
extend the mantle of charity over his acts until forbearance ceases to be a virtue,
and the adoption of extreme measures becomes necessary to protect the Craft from
ehame. The case before your committee appears to be one of this kind. The accused
was frequently drunk, quarrelsome, and abusive, often using the vilest language and
applying the most obscene epithets to his brethren, or others, who attempted to
remonstrate with him for his conduct.
your committee cannot refrain from alluding to the fact that very many of the
cases of unmasonic conduct which have come before them have had their origin in
the too free use of intoxicatinv liquors; and they believe that the time has come
when this Grand Lodge should emphasize its action in such cases by subjecting all
such offenders to the severest penalty of the law. They therefore recommend the
adoption of the following resolution :.
Ruolved, That the action of Nicolam Lodge, No. 129, in supendin&' VIRGIL
WILLIAMSON from ~ the rights and privileges of Masonry on the fourth day of
March, 1887, be and is hereby reversed and set aside ; and that, by the action of
this Grand Lodge, the said VIBGIL WILLIAMSON be and is hereby expelled from all
the rights and privileges of Masonry.

Bro. WILLIAM ABRAHAM DAVIES, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following report:To the M. •. W. •. Grand Lodge of Oalifomia :-

In the matt.er of the proposed amendment ~f Section 2, Article III Part III
of the ?<>nstitution, offered by Bro. J AHll:S BAUNTY STXVBNs, your com.'.nittee find
that ".31~ amendment purposes to add to that section, as it stands, the words "upon
a 1111\Jority vote of the Lodge ;" thus making the 110ction, so far as it provides for
the ~tora~ion o~ ~ Mllllon auspended for non-payment of dues, restrictive hy
l'lqumng, m add1t10n to the payment of his iniebtednees, that the suspended
brother should again snbmit to the ordeal of the ballot.

196

(Oct. 14,

Procudings of the,

This proposition, in various forms of expression, has been several times passed
upon by your committee and by the Grand Lodge. As the law now ~tands and has
stood for nearly thirty years, suspension for non-payment of dues is.a summary
proceeding, without even the fol'lll of a trial. If a member of a Lodge 18 more th~n
six months in arrears for dues, the Secretary sends him a notice of the fact; and if,
at the next stated meeting, his dues be not paid, or sickness or inability be shown
al! a reason for such non-payment, the Master must declare him to be suspended,
unleu the dues be paid or 1emitted, or the time of payment be extended by the
Lodge. The law has met the approval of a decided majority of. the Fraternity,
and your committee-think now, as heretofore, that it would be UDJnst ~place any
impediment in the way of a brother's restoration, other than that provided for by
the payment of all arrearages and such further dues a11 would have accrued had he
continued in good Rtanding,
If any change be made it should be radical, and should provide that, in case of
delinquency in payment of dues, the delinquent should be tried upon ch~rgee of
willful neglect of duty, as for other Masonic offenses; and then, if the ve~dict were
that he was guilty, the judgment of suspension would be final and conclusive. :But,
proceedings for suspension are summary in such cases, the means of
80 long as the
restoration should be equally summary. Your committee recommend that the
proposed amendment be not adopted.
All which is respectfully submitted J;iy

To the M. '. W; •. Grana Lodge of <J<difornia:Your committee, to whom was referred the trial-transcript from the Commission convened by Santa <Jlmra Lodge, No. 34, for the trial of PABKEB BUTTERll'IELD
Hor.iras, charged with unmasonic conduct, who was found guilty and sentenced
to be reprimanded on the sixteenth day of January, 1886, have had the same under
consideration and report as follows :The proceedings are found to have been regular, and the tr4nscript comes in
proper form. The several specifications of the charge comprised slander and the
use of vile language at sundry timee. An extended trial was had, and the accused
was found guilty upon two of the specifications and was sentenced to be reprimanded.
Upon the rendition of the judgment and sentenCll great trouble ensued in the
Loda-e. Some of the principal officers resigned, and the Commissioners endeavored to justify their light sentence by sayini that they were induced to render it
by the promise of the accused that he would withdraw from the Lodge. Time
passed, the brother did not withdraw, great dissatisfaction was caused, and, if your
committee may be permitted to say it in this report, the ~ was nearly broken
up.
After a careful review of the testimony presented, your committee are of the
opinion that the sentence in this caee was an insufficient punishment for the offen~s
of which the accused was found guilty; .and they therefore offer the following reso•
lution and recommend its adoption:Ruolwd, That the action of the Commission convened by Santa <Jlmra Lodge,
No. 34, by which, on the sixteenth day of January, 1886, PABKEB Bti'ITERFIELD

Aid PARKER BL'TTEBl!'IELD HOLMES be and is hereby suspended from all the rights
and privileges of Masonry.
