Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. MARKS FLEISHER
from the action of Huperi,an Lodge, No. 264, on the second day of July, 1887, in
sentencing Bro. SAMUEL EUGENE CBOW to be reprimanded for unmasonic conduct,
have given the same careful consideratio11 and report as follows : The accused is chanted with having used very obscene language in speaking of
the appellant, and also with threatening to cowhide that brother upon the streets.

206

Procet,</,ings of the

[Oct. 15,

From the trial-transcript it appears that, at the first meeting of the Commis.
sioners, the appellant objected to Bro. HmraY C. BAGLEY, a businesa-partner of
the accll8ed, as a member of the CommiBBion, which objection was overruled by
the Master. Immediately thereafter the accused pleaded guilty to the cha.rgee,
eta.ting, as his reason for threatening to cowhide the brother, that he had understood
that Bro. FLEISHER was interfering with his business; and saying that, for the
filthy and obscene language used, he asked the brother's pardon and would try
not to use such language again.
The Commissioners thereupon decided that, the accused having pleaded guilty,
no testimony could be introduced ; and they at once proceeded to assess the penalty.
On the following evening the Mas;er presented the findings of the Commission to
the Lodge, and then and there carried out the Rentence.
'l'he accuser appeals from the sentence of the Commissioners on the ground that
Bro. BAGLEY was disqualified from acting as one of the Commi.esioners; that no
trial was really had, the Commission having refused to accept any evidence for the
reason that the brother had pleaded guilty; and that the sentence was not com·
mensurate with the offense committed.
It is evident to the minds of your committee that the appellant has just ground
for complaint. A business partner of the accused was not competent to act as one
of the Commissioners; and the accuser should have been permitted to introduce
testimony to prove that the attack made upon his good name was without cause or
provocation, as claimed by him. Moreover, aside from the apparent unfairness of
the trial, the offense is one that merits a severer punishment than a simple reprimand in his own Lodge, which reprimand, the appellant asserts, was administered
in a farcical manner. When a Mason so far forgets his duty towards a member of
his own Lodge as to use the most vile and filthy language in speaking of such
brother, and even gqing so far as to threaten personal violence upon him, the sooner
such a diseased limb is lopped off the better it will be for the Masonic body; and
your committee ·t herefore offer the following resolution and recommend jts adoption :Ruol:vm, That the action of the CommiBBioners of Huperin.n Lodge, No. 264, in
sentencing Bro. SAM'CEL EUGENE CROW to be reprimanded only, is hereby disapproved; and that, by the action of the Grand Lodge, the said SAMUEL EUGENIC
CROW be and hereby is suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
The foregoing report was submitted to the Grand Loda-e by your oommittee on
Thursday last, when, after some discussion, it was ordered that it be re-committed
thereto, with instruction to so amend the resolution accompanying it as to affirm
the action of the Commission of Huperin.n Lodge, No. 264. In compliance with
that instruction, your committee now present the following resolution:Ruolwd, That the action of Huperian Lodge, No. 264, on the second day of
July, 1887, in sentencing Bro. SAMU&L EUGENE C&ow to be reprimanded, be and is
hereby affirmed.

and expelled the petitioner.
.

Your committee have given the matter patient attention. The principal eviclence adduced for the prosecution was the affidavit of the accused, wherein he
·1141knowledges that, before the sale, SHAVER agreed to give one J&ssup and himself
five hundred dollars if they would vot.e to purchase the SRAV&R lot, and to give
one HUNTER one hundred dollars also; that aft.er the sale SHA V&B only paid four
hnndred dollars; that be gave JESSUP two hundred dollars; and that JESSUP had
told him that he, J&SBuP, had paid HUNT&R one hundred dollars.
The defence, naturally enough, object.ed to this evidence and tried to throw it
out, on the ground that it was procured under a promise of Masonic secrecy; but
your committee are of the opinion, from the corroborative testimony adduced, that
the facts stat.ed in this affidavit were true, and that it was obtained from the accused
under fear of and with a view to escape criminal prosecution and punishment, accompanied by the thought that, under a proper state of circumstances, it would
form a basis for turning State's evidence. Furthermore, the correspondence submitted by the M. •. W. •. Grand Master shows that SHA\r&R made an affidavit corroborating the stat.ements of the accused.
Your committee are of the opinion that the verdict of the CommiSBion was
erroneous, and they therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:Ruol:vt.d, That the action of Marin Lodge, No. 191, whereby WILLiill L&VI

Bro. Wn.wLUt CALDWELL BELOB'.EB, from the Specia.1 Committee of
Pa.st Grand Masters to which had he~m referred that portion of the
Grand Master's Address relative to the deoease of Pa.st Grand Masters
LEONIDAS E. PRATT and JoNATHAN DoAN HINES, transmitted the following report : To the .V. •• W. '. Grand Lodge of Califm-nW-:y our committee, to whom ws.s referred tha.t sorrowful portion of the Address of
the Grand Ms.ster which speaks of the great loss sustained by our Grand Lodge
during the past year, by the death of two of its honored and beloved members,
Pa..,t Grand Masters LEONIDAS E. PRATT and JONATHAN DOAN HINltS, submit the
following:As to the first of the above named brethren, although his death occurred since the
last Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge and was therefore properly alluded
to by the Grand Master, all that ws.s possible to do to honor his memory ws.s done
at a Special Communication called s1on thereafter to conduct his funera.l. The
proceedings thereat were published with those of the Annual Communication, and
your committee do not see how aught can be added to the beautiful and impressive
eulogy then pronounced by one of its members over the body of our dearly loved
brother, LEONIDAS E. PRATT.
It was a cause for much sorrow that the decease of the second of our lost brethren
occurred under such circumstances s.s to render it impossible for the Grand Lodge
thua also to express its mournful appreciation of the sad calamity which had befallen
it. Bro. HINES' death was the result of an accident. His residence was in the

1887.J

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

215

Ojai Valley, near the village of Nordhoff, some twelve or fifteen miles from San
Buenaventura, the principal town and county-seat of Ventura County. On the
thirtieth day of December last he had driven to that place to attend a meeting of his
Lodge, called for the purpose of insta.lling him, for the sixth time, as its Ms.ster; and
that business being completed, he had departed thence for hi!' home •ome time afte;
dark that evening. From what ws.s afterward discovered it appears that his horses
had ta.ken fright on the way and become unmanageable; that he was thrown from
his spring-wagon when within a.bout three miles of his house, the team proceeding
there ; that he wandered in the darkness, probably in a dazed condition, for a con•iderable distance in a wrong direction ; and that he fell into a baranca some thirty
feet in depth, breaking his neck upon its rocky bottom. As soon as it became
known that he had not reached his home, large numbers of his brethren and neighbors joined in the search for him, but it was not until the second day thereafter that
his body was thus found, about four miles from his house. On the following day
he ws.s buried by his Lodge, San Buenaventura, No. 214; and it was not until that
day that a telegram reached our Grand Secretary, giving information of his death.
Bro. JONATHAN DoAN H!NES was born in the County of Clinton, State of Ohio,
on the first day of January, 1825, and there his childhood and youth appear to have
been spent. He studied law with the Hon. THOMAS CORWIN, and for several years
was engaged in business connected with railroads. At the commencement of the
war of the Rebellion he enlisted as a private in the 12th Ohio Volunteer Infantry,
and when he was mustered out of service at its end, it was with the rank of Colonel
and an excellent record as a brave and efficient soldier. Thereafter he appears to
have made his home in the State of Missouri, where he is said ti> have held variou•
offices of trust, until the year 1872, when he came to California. He remained for
a few months at San Jose, and then removed to Sau Buenaventura, where he
resumed the practice of his profession and soon became one of the leading lawyers
in that portion of the State. In 1879 he was elected to the office of Judge of the
SuPllrior Court of Ventura UOunty, a position. which he occupied with credit during a period of ti ve years ; and at the expiration of that term he removed to his farm
in the beautiful Ojai Valley where he had since resided.
Bro. HINES was made a Master Mason in Tipton Lodge, No. 33, at Loiansport, in
the State of Indiana, on the eighteenth day of February, 1847; was exalted to the
degree of Royal Arch Mason in XenW- Chapter, No. 36, at Xenia, in the State of
Ohio, in October of the same year; and was created a Knight Templar in Mount
Vernon Commandery, No. 1, at Columbua, in the State last named, in November,
'
1847.
Our brother was the second Master of our San Bumw.vmitura Lodge, No. 214,
and aerved five terms in that capacity. Since his first appearance in our Grand
J..odge, at its Annual Communication in 1875, he had been one of its most laborious
and useful members. After much service on important committees, in 1881 he was
elected its Senior Grand Warden; in 1882, its Deputy Grand Master; and in 1883,
its Grand Master, to which great office he was re-elected in the following year.
At the end of his period of service s.s Grand Master of Masons in Celifornia, in
October, 1885, not only the customary resolution of thanks and requeat that he sit
for his portrait were offered him, but it ws.s ordered that a committee of Grand
Officers procure a further and suitable testimonial to "the untiring zeal, assiduity,
and good judgment which had characterized the administration of his high office,"
to be presented to him at the following Annual Commumcat1on. Thl8, consist ing
of a gold watch by one of the most celebrated makers, with corresponding chain
a.nd a jewel of finest workmanship, was accordingly presented in October, 1886, as
related in our Proceedings of that year, but little more than two months before his

216

[Oct. 15,

Proceedings of the

untimely death; and it was found upon hi~ where he had fallen, the watch having
stopped at 2.24, as told by one of the brethren who discovered him.
Our brether was the first High Priest of Ventura Chapter, No. 50, which was
established in 1875, and occupied that office during seven terms. Thenceforth he
was constant in his attendance upon the Grand Chapter and always active in its
labors. He was elected its Grand Scribe in 1881 ; its Grand King in 1882; its
Deputy Grand High Priest in 1883; and reached the highest station in its gi~ in
1884.
:Bro. HINES was also the first Commander of Ventura Commandery, No. 18,
formed in 1881 ; was thus. honored by his companions for four terms thereafter ;
and, but a few days before his aeath, had been again elected Commander of his
Commandery and High Priest of his Chapter.
In all the relations of life, as soldier, judge, citizen, and Mason, our brother was
loyal, intellijrent, and faithful; ready at all times to do that which Lis convictions
led him to believe was right and proper to be done, and fearle88 in combating
wrong and injustice whenever and wherever manifested. Accomplished in social
and domestic virtues ; esteemed and trusted in business circles ; zealoUB and devoted in his duties; genial and love-inspiring in his friendships; how greatlyhow sadly-as we ~ther around our altars, shall we miss the welcome presence
of his familiar face and the hearty pressure of his loyal hand !
All which is respectfully submitted by
WILLIAM CALDWELL BELOBll:B,

find Masonry in its aacendancy; and wherever you may chanC6 to find it dormant
or languishing, you are sure to find it side by side with ~he prostrate form of freedom
or enfeebled intellect, where nationality is lapsing into decay and the race arreated
in its development. Amid all the fierce storms of persecution it stands abreast
the times, and has ever been characterized by energy and intelligence. Masonry
has oo material ceuter. The world is its sphere. Its votaries have many tongues,
but Masonry speaks intelligibly through them all. Ite great pulsating heart-throb
encircles the globe. It.a principles a.re steadfast as time; its life a homogeneous
•
•
whole.
It is said of the great NAPOLEON that, when on the eve of battle upon the m.
fated field of Waterloo, and when the flood-gates of heaven were pouring down
torrents of rain, though ill and well nigh exhausted, he spent the night in the
saddle, &11 ever on the alert for advantage. In the thick darkness of that fearful
night he was still buoyed by that ambition which characterized his life; and when
the vivid lightning flashed athwart the sky, hie countenance was seen to be marked
by the same stem, grim smile, and the words that"escaped his lips were: "We are
agre,ed, " Standing to-day on the record of the remembered past, and peering into
the future of the usefulness, universality, and destiny of Masonry, "we are
fL(J'f'Ud." Upon the undying faith in the broad principles underlying its foundation, its unity of purpose, its purity of intention, its catholic spirit, its unselfish
aim, its unswerving fidelity, and its faith in Gon and immortality, "we are
agre,ed."

Time files apace; the recurring' seasons come and go; man is born into the
world, flourishes, fades, and passes hence ; but Masonry in its heaven-born mission
pursues the even tenor of its way. As individual character becomes dignified and
ennobled by passing uniicathed through the refining fires of calumny and slander,
so Masonry exalteth itself above the bigotry and persecution with which it bas
been assailed: There was a time when political prejudice offered a determined
opposition to the Institution; but soon this anti-Masonic element lost its distinctive character and ceased to exist, To-day the resistance is passive and comes
from religious fanaticism ; but the purpose of Masonry is steadfast and its destiny
assured. As well resist the moming sunbeams, or the moon's soft light, or the
ceaseless buffetini\' of ocean's waves upon the shore. It was conceived in wisdom
-born of justice-the gift of Gon.
It has b'*ln asserted, times without number, that Masonry never designed to
take the place of religion. It simply contents itself with being a co-worker in the
great school of morality and virtue;. teaching man his duty to Gon, loyalty to
government, and the golden rule of life. These are the first lessons of the novitiate;_and when he falters in the precepts he thus receives, he violates his vows and
·betrays a sacred trust. When a man justly receives the proud title of being a good
Mason, it is a guaranty that he will maintain the credit of being a good citizen.
The religionist who condemns Masonry because of the fancied barrier it uresents
to membership and zeal in the church, does so with no assurance that the-churchroll will be increased or the interest in spiritual affairs be heightened. The individ.ual who may be impressed with the responsibilities and duties of a religious life will
not grow apathetic by reason of alliance with Masonry. The few who claim Masonry_as their religion would scarcely, if ever, adopt any other, even though they
might be denied the privilege of the Lorure. The man whose mind is deeply imbued
with a pure spirit of benevolence, and who cherishes the good for the amelioration
of his race, will not prove an idler in either institution. It ia not strange that many
W:ho .are averse to creeds express a prefereece for this great Institution, whose only
aun 18 to promote the peace and happiness of man.

In oompari.son, the chief purposes and objects of each are greatly at variance.
The church stipulates broader obligations and has a wider scope. Its direct aim is
to impart knowledge of Gon aud faith in His revealed will; to inspire the depraved
with a just realization of the duties of the creature to the Creator; to plunge into
heathen darkness and unfold the lightof civilization and the great plan of redemp·
tion ; and to lift from degradation the benighted of the earth. Masonry does not
seek the reformation of men. It seeks to bind good men and true in closer bonds
of fellowship and love, and to perfect the good work already begun. Its object is
not to teach man of the existence of Gon and eter:n,J. lifer for these form the basis
of introduction to its mystic rites, the iWne qua non, without which he can never
become a subject for M asonic consideration. Whatever there is of religion in
Masonry is that "general one of nature and primitive revelation handed down to
us from some ancient and patriarchal priesthood, in which all men may agree and
in which no men can differ. It inculcates the practice of virtue, but it supplies no
scheme of redemption from sin. It points its disciples to the path of righteousness, but it does not claim to be 'the way, the truth, and the life.' In so far,
therefore, it cannot become a substitute for Christianity, but its tendency is thitherward; and, as the hand-maid of religion, it may, and often does, act as the
vestibule that introduces its votaries into the temple of divine truth."
The Masonic year with us has been prosperous, and to me it has been a very
busy one. I have written nearly four hundred letters, and I could not well have
•curtalled the number. Besides these, many scores of circular letters have been
mailed Go matters of a special nature.
Early in the year a circular was issued to ea.ch Inspector, tendering a reappointment and calling attention to the fifteenth · of our General Regulations. A few
changes were made, occasioned by an Inspector not being able or willing again to
serve. The purpose of i•uming the circular letter was to get a reply of acceptance
from each appointee, with the view that the duties of this important office might
•be faithfully performed. As a reason for reappointment, it was presumed that
the fact of having already been deemed worthy of the honor, and the added advantage of experience, would afford a guaranty of fitness for the duties. Previous
to any action the Grand Lecturer was consulted, as his long official connection
with the Grand Lodge gives him a much better idea of the qualification of thoae
who may be chosen, and upon his advice I chiefly relied.
A new District has been formed, embracing Phamiz Lodge, No.178, Pomona
Lodge, No. 246, and Evergrt.en Lodge, No. 259; and FaU Riwr Lodge, No. 270, was
changed from the Fourth to the Third District.
Seven Lodges proposed to amend their by-laws by the reduction of their dues.
In only one instance did this action meet my approval. It was a surprise to me that
some of these Lodiree should propose such reduction, when they had scarcely any
available funds and were dependent entirely ution dues and fees as their only sources
of revenue. In one instance a Lodge, with a membership of twenty, desired a
reduction from $12 to S6 per annum, having lees than $i50 in its treasury and a
mere pittance due from its members. Another wanted the same reduction, with
not much money in its treasury and a membership of hut twenty.-five.
In addition to the authorization of five dispensations to form new Lodges, sundry
others of a special nature have been issued, the purposes for which will he found in
the Report of the Grand Secretary; where also will be seen the recommendations
and appointments of Representatives to and from this and other Grand Lodges.

Two years ago he returned to California, and has continued to contribute to the
Lodge in Maine till the present time. He now wishes to affiliate, and claims that
he is in good standing and should not be compelled to pay the six months' dues
required by our Constitution. Is the brother in good standing?
Answer. No. Sec. 8, Art. V, Part VI, of our Constitution, with its reference,
is very plain upon this subject. Being a non-affiliate, he must comply with our
laws while he resides in our Jurisdiction.
Quite recently Di-ytqum Lodge, No. 174, filed a complaint charging San ])Ugo
Lodge, No. 35, with neglect and ill-treatment of a member of l>rgtmon Lodge,
during his last ilh\ess within the jurisdiction of San Diego Lodge, and with a
refusal to bury him with Masonic honors after his death. As the case was brought
to my attention within the past three weeks, it was deemed best to have it adjudicated by this Grand Body rather than pass through the tedious routine of trial as
laid down by the Constitution. With this view the papers were forwarded to the
Grand Secretary, to be referred to the appropriate committee. I have informed
both of the aforesaid Lodges of the course decided upon.
On the fifth day of November last a Special Communication of the Grand Lodge
was held at San Jose, at which time the corner-stone of the new City Hall thereof
was laid with the usual formalities of the Craft. The occasion was auspicious and
the streets of the beautiful city were literally thronged with people who viewed the
large procesllion;of which the Masonic Fraternity formed a comparatively small
part. The wives and daughters of our brethren there are deserving of mention.
Their busy hands had transformed the Lodge-room into one grand bouquet of the
choicest flowers, the fragrance of which lent a charm to the place during the impressive ceremonies of opening the Grand Lodge. Such profuse, beautiful, and
tasteful floral decorations are seldom witnessed ; and they bore testimony of the
natur..J advantages that have won for San Jose the coveted appellation of the
"Garden City." On this occasion I had the assistance of the V. ·. W. '. NATHAN
EUGENE JULIUS GREGORY, Junior
WESTON SPAULDIJiG, Grand Treasurer; the
Grand Deacon, and the W. '.THOMAS HENRY·LAINE, Grand Orator, who delivered
an eloquent and appropriate address.
On the twenty-second day of December last I accepted an invitation to meet the
brethren of Sacramento as a guest of Washington Lodge, No. 20. Owing to recent
heavy rains the trains were all off tillle, and I was on the road from four o'clock in
the morning till half-past twelve at night. A brother appropriately remarked,
" man proposes and the railroad fails to connect ; " so I was denied the privilege
and pleasure of this most enjoyable meeting. The following dav was spent with
the brethren, atb.ong whom were a number of the officers of the Grand Lodge who
were present by invitation to attend this meeting. I take the occasion to eipress
my thanks to our M. ·. w. ·. Past Grand Master EDMUND CLEMENT ATKINSON, who
devoted almost the entire day to my comfort and entertainment.
On the eleventh day of February I held a meeting in the Thirtieth Masonic
District, at Modesto, and installed the officerB of Stanislaus Lodge, No. 206. There
was a large attendance, and every Lodi;:e in the District was represented. Nearly
the entire membership of Oakdale Lodge, No. 275, came a distance of fifteen miles
by private conveyances to attend this very pleasant meeting. At the close of the
installation, I was called upon to perform a very pleasant duty by presenting, on
behalf of Stanislaw! Lodge, a beautiful Past Master's J ewe! to its retiring Master,
the W. ·. WILLIAM HENRY HATTON, who is Inspector of the District and the present
Grand Sword Bearer of the Grand Louge. The brother was surprised in a genuine
manner, .but soon regained his equilibrium and responded appropriately and feel·
ingly. The meeting closed with a sumptuous repaijt at the Ross House, to which
all were invited.

On the first day of August a circular letter was mailed to the Inspector of
each
of the several Ma.sonic Districts, reminding them of their duties in submittin
g reports to the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer, as required by the fifteenth
of our
General Rejl(ulations. Of the reports which have been received some
are quite
exhaustive , are models in every particular , and reflect great credit upon
their
authors. I much regret that space forbids a proper and extended notice
of them.
It is also with regret that I announce to you that the Inspectors of the
following
Districts have made no report, viz.: the Second, Thirteent h, Sixteenth ,
Twentysecond, and Thirtieth.
On the second day of Nevembe r last I received a communic ation from
the
Grand Secretary of. the Grand Lodge of Arizona, written by authority
of the
Grand Master of that Jurisdictio n, complaininir that our Anaheim Lodge,
No. 'l!Yl,
located at Anaheim, Los Angeles County, had violated the jurisdictio nal
rights of
the Grand Lodge of Arizona, in the immediate jurisdictio n of White Mountain
Lodge, No. 3, located at Globe, Gila County, Arizona. The complaint
set forth
that one JORN H. LUJIDKlll was a resident of and doing business at Pinal
and Silver King, in the County of Pinal, Arizona Territory, for seven years last
past;
that, in November, 1886, the said LUEDD visited Anaheim, California, and
while
there petitioned the Lodge located in that place for the degrees of
Masonry
and was elected to receive them; that, on the fourth day of April, 1887,
be received the first degree therein,; that, after receiving said degree, he returned
to
bis home in Pina.I, where be continued to reside, being engaged. in mercantile
business in that place; and that the Master of Anaheim Lodge informed
White
Mwntain Lodge that ea.id Lmmn: would in due time return to Anaheim and
receive the second and third degrees. The communic ation concluded as follows:This action on the pa.rt of Anaheim Lod~ being a direct violation of the
jurisdictional rights of the Grand Lodge of Arizona, the matter is laid before
you in
that fraternal spirit which has uniformly characteri zed the relations existing
between the respective Grand Lodges. The M. '. W. ·. Grand Master does not
to suggest to you any action in the premises, well knowing that you will presume
give the
matter that attention which the ments of the case demand.
I immediate ly addressed a. letter to the Grand Master of Arizona, ths.nkin11:
him
for calling attention to the matter, expressing my regret that anything should
arise
which would have a tendency to disturb the friendly relations existinit between
the
two Grand Bodies, and assuring him that I would inquire into the merits
of the
case without delay, I at once wrote to Bro. THEODORE REISER, Master of
Anaheim
Lodge, requesting a full and complete statement of the facts, and directing
him to
suspend further action until properly advised. Bro. REl!!ER promptly complied
with
the request, and informed me that he had known the applicant from his
boyhood,
he having been raised in Anaheim, where his family still resided; that he was
twenty·
four years of age and had been residing in Arizona for about eight yea.rs,
and had
been to Anaheim but three times during that period; that, upon.his last
return to
Anaheim, he petitioned that Lodge before he bad been there six months;
that, not
feeling satisfied, he (Bro. REIBER,) questioned the applicant closely as to
his residence, and was informed by him that he not only considered Anaheim
his home
during all this time, but henceforth would remain there permanen tly ; that,
after
being elected and receiTing the first d~ee, the applicant was suddenly summoned
on business to Arizona, promising to return for the other degrees in two
or three

and appomting Inspectors wae a wise provision, and has been of incalculable benefit
to the Craft; bnt it fails to fully accomplish its purpose. There are now thirty-eight
Masonic Districts, with an Inspector for each. I have not the pleasure of a personal
ac_qnu.intanc~ with ~alf of th~se brethren, and of that number I know scarcely anyth10g regard10g their Mu.some qualifications. Doubtless this was the experience of
my predecessors and will be tbe experience of those who are to succeed to the office
of °:rand Master. In some Districts it is next to impossible to find a brother fulfy
quabfied to fill the office of Inspector; and in snch localities the Lodges have been
for years gradually drifting into greater and still greater variance from the ritual
as bngbt by onr Grand Lecturer.
Our Constitution makes it obligatory upon M88ters of Lodges "to confer the de·
greed in strict accordance with tbe ritual which h88 been, or may hereafter be
ordained b:f the Gran_d L~dge.'.' The Inspector of a District, or the Maeter of a Lodge:
may be stnctly consc1ent10us ID tbe desire to t"nlly comply with this requirement of
the Constitution, but it is not always within his reach. He may be quite unable to
spare the time in which to perfect himself' in the work ai the fount or source of Masonic knowl~dge. The means best adequate to the purpose in view would be to
send a brother into the field to labor for a higher standard of Masonic intelligence
and stricter conformity to onr ritual, that the requirements of the Constitution may
·
be complied with.
An appropriation for this purpose would be a timely and judicious expenditure
and could be discontinued BB soon as a higher standard in the work had been attained'.
I would suggest that the office of Grand Lecturer be preserved, as at present, as an
honorary one; making the brother who may hold tbat appointment the custodian of
and responsible for the work. Then clothe the Grand Master with authority to appoint, with the advice of the Grand Lecturer, a Deputy Grand Lecturer, who sLall
receive a salary and dev~te his e~tire time to the work, with the understanding that
the Lodge or Lodges, dnrmg the time of receiving his services, shall defray hie necessary expenses. ~hese suggestions are offered under the firm conviction that it Is
only by the adoption of some such plan that the work can be preserved in uniformity,
and that by such adoption there would be the additional advantage of havin t
whose duty it would be, by frequent comparison, to preserve the work nnchan:ed~o
Du~lng the month of March I received notice that our esteemed Ohairman of the
Oomm1ttee on Correspondence, the W.•. Bro. WILLiill HENBY HILL had so far fail d
In his eyesight as to render it impossible for him to proceed with th~ preparation 0 ; a
report. Bro. JAJ11Es WRIGHT AlmEBBON was appealed to, and, although burdened with
important duties and responsibilities, was, as I have ever found him to be prom t to
express hie willingneBB and readineBB to nudertake any duty whereby the intere:te r
the Craft might b_e snbserved. While I know _that yon freely unite with me in t:e
warmest expressions of sympathy for our affi1cted Bro. Hu.r., yet we are free to

On th~ sec~nd day of April last, information was received that Suisun Lodge, N 0 ,
65, at Suisun, m the County of Solano, had incorporated under the laws of the State
and W88 about to apply to a Court for permission to mortgage certain real estat~
of said Lodge, in the corporate name thereof. An investigation was immediately
instituted. The Master and a number of brethren of the Lodge called upon m ·
this city, and informed me that tbey were not aware that they were violatinge ~:
edict of the Grand Lodge, 88 they were following the precedents of Bllflioia, Naval,

1888.]

Grand Lodge of California.

467

and VacatJille Lodges, all located in the same County of Solano. Thus was developed
a most startling fact; for I had not an idea that another Lodge in this Jurisdiction was
t;ansacting business as a corporate body, in violation of an edict of this Grand
Lodge.
Feeling doubtful as to the possible number of Lodges in the same predicament, I
considered it my first duty to make diligent inquiry with 11 view to the needed in·
formation upon the subject. Through the kind assistance of the Grand Secretary,
8 circular letter was mailed to the Master of each Lodge in the Jurisdiotion, request·
Ing a full investigation and a report of the result. In July, I found it neoe11sary to
issue another circular letter, as seventy-five of the Lodges had failed to respond to
the first. In the early part of September, a third notice was issued, as sixteen Lodges
were yet delinquent in sending me reports. The result of the investigation thus far
reveals the fact that the following Lodges had been regularly incorporated, and no information h88 been received that they have disincorporated: Benicia, No. 5; San
Joaquin, No. 19; Hawaiian , No. 21; Forbestoum, No. 50; Suisun, No. 65; NatJal,
No. 87; Vaca1'ille, No. 134; .Abell, No. 146; Phamiz, No. 178, and .Alturas, No. 248.
The dates of the incorporation of each may be found by reference to the reports on
file in the Grand Secretary's office. The following Lodges have made no reports,
notwithstanding that three several notices were mailed to each, viz.: Enf,eJprise, No.
70; Lerrington, No. 104; Mountain View, No. 194; ~anza Italiana, No. 219, and
Hope, No. 234.
No order has been issued requiring any of the Lodges to disincorporate. I could
not consistently do so in one case, while there was reason to believe that others had
'for an extended period been enjoying immunity from discipline; and the year has
drawn to a olose before asoertaining all the facts. Haste in iBBning such an order
would not have been pmdent or conservative. In two instances I had been informed
that Lodges, 88 corporate bodies, had effected loans on their real property for
the substantial improvement thereof, which could not have been coneommated
through a board of trustees for the alleged reason that the money lender was not
satisfied with the security thus offered. To have issued a peremptory order requiring
them to dieincorporate would have resulted in much discord and the risk of pecuniary
loss to the Lodges, and I did not feel justified in assuming such a responsibility.
There is another feature of this question, to w:tich your attention is invited for
some more decided action. A oommunlcation was received from the W. ·. Bro. THOMAS
Plll'!LINGTON, a member of a special oommittee of Pacifi,o Lodge, No. 136, which had
been appointed to formulate a plan for the investment of the funds of that Lodge.
The plan suggested and aubmitted for approval was the formation of a corporation
by individual members of the Lodge. The proposition did not receive a favorable
consideration, for the reason that it seemed to be an effort to acoomplieh an objeot
indirectly that our subordinates are prohibited from doing directly, and which I
feared would be open to many of the objections that have been urged against the
incorporation of the Lodge itself.
The matter is herewith submitted. A limited time should be allowed for Lodges
to dieincorporate, with the understanding that such fact be repor.ted to the Grand
Master, and that failure to so report shall incur a forfeiture of oharter. The Grand
Lodge should further declare as to the expediency of incorporation upon any plan.
The matter has received such pnblioity that it is not at all probable that any Lodge
will plead ignorance on this subject in the future, and whatever may be your action
will be final.

sentative near that Grand Body, with a brief and instructive report of its proceedings.
The favor was gratefully acknowledged, and I expreBBed to him the hope that Representatives generally might follow his example.

A pamphlet has been received containing the proceedings of the Oentennial of
Frederioki/Jurg Lodge, No. 4, F . ana A. M., under its charter from the urand Lodge
of Virginia. This Lodge, almost from the date of its existence, has bean memorable as
the Masonic .Alma Mater of America's greatest patriot-the immortal WASHINGTON.
Besides much that is of pleasurable interest to the Oraft, the pamphlet contains the
very excellent addresses delivered on that interesting occasion, and has been referred
to the Oommittee on Co~respondence.
Oomplaint was made that a Lodge was renting the lower part of its hall for a
saloon. The complaint set forth that the lease wonld soon expire and that the Lodge
had voted to relet the property for the same purpose for another period, notwithstanding the very earnest entreaty of some of its members to the contTary. The
letter reciting the complaint also contained an appeal for my aid and advice. The
brother while nrglng bis objection to the action of the Lodge, says: "I am confident
that there are •good men and true ' who would have applied for admission, had it
not been for this • deadfall' under the threshold of our Lodge."
I did not do else than to offer what I deemed to be wholesome advice, which was
substantially that I regarded it in bad taste for a Lodge to rent any portion of its hall
for saloon purposes. It is evil in tendency and brings Masonry into disrepnte. There
are, probably, members in every Lodge within our Ju.risdiction who oppose a practice
of this kind on priooiple, and to whom such action is very distasteful. It will e.ver
prove a fruitful source of discord, and will in many cases nentral!ze the influence of
a Lodge.
In almost every instance where I have visited a Lodge and inspected its books, the
Secretaries have been more or less delinquent in writing up the Black-Book. This
book is the great Masonic bugbear of the age. In large and prosperous Lodges
where Secretaries are well compensated for the work it is comparatively a small
matter;· but in very many of our Lodges the pay of the Secretary is nominal, and to
such it becomes a great burden. The neglect of Secretaries in this particular has
ever been a cause for complaint, and, even nuder the most rigid discipline, this provision of the Constitution will continue, in many instances, unenforced. The bimonthly circulars issued by the Grand Secretary could be conveniently filed for reference. If this plan were systematically pursued, it would effectually accomplish the
purpose in view, and I am incJUled to think that the Constitqtion should be amended
and the Black-Book abolished. From the general sentiment expressed, I am led
to believe that if an amendment abolishing that book were at this time submitted,
it would receive the necessary vote to adopt It at this Communication. While our
organic law should not be disturbed for other than the most obvious reasons, in
this Instance the exigencies of the case seem to demand it.
There is one subject that I take this occasion to allude to with a great degree of
pleasure. I mean the absence of stimulants from the table at Masonic banquets. At
the various places where I have been most hospitably entertained by our generous
brethren during the year, only in one instance have I seen wine served at a banquet.
It is indeed gratifying to know that this objectionable custom, which a few years ago
was almost universal, is fast falling into dlsuse.
There are brethren to be found in almost every Lodge, who, upon special occasions, enter into the festivities with a zest and abandon that is truly surprising to
those who, by nature, are more conservative in their habit.H. Among just such
brethren, from a social and benevolent standpoint, we find our best men-great, warmhearted characters, who are always foremost in their efforts for relief to the needy;
who are first at the bedside or the Mick and dying; who linger longest at the grave of
the departed ; and whose very nature rebels at doing anything in a hall-hearted manner. It is not surprising then that these individuals often allow their social proclivities to carry them beyond the bounds of prudence. Is it consistent that a Lodge,

1888.J

GTand Lodge of Oaliforn-ia.

469

whose duty it is to teach morality and rectitude of conduct, should thus tempt its members to violate one of our cardinal virtnoe, temperance?
Brethren, let yonr own hearts answer this qnestion. I do not advise or ask legislation npon this enbject, as is being done in some Masonic Jurisdictions. I have an
abiding faith in the pure motives and better judgment of the California Mason, that,
whatever may be his Idea upon this qnestiou as an Individual, fealty to his Lodge
will prove paramount to every other consideration ; and I trust that the time is near
at hand when all will rejoice to know that this practice has become a thing of the
past.
The Oraft in Caiifomia have ample reason for the satisfaction and pride they feel
in consequence or the noble work that le being done by our Boards of R~llef. Compared with some other Jurisdictions the difference is remarkable. For instance in
the great city of New York, as shown by a late report, the Board of Relief expended
for the year but $96166 for charity, while the report of our Sao Francisco Board shows
an expenditure of $9,026 81 during the. past year, omitting the salary of the Secretary
and other expenses which, when added to the above, makes a total of $ll,004 61.
The Boards of Relief of Los Angeles, Sacramento, Oakland and Stockton ar~ also doing commenclable work, and I urge upon you the importance of giving them such
aid as their necessities may seem to demand and our resources to permit.
Quite recentry I received a copy of the Masonic Manual, a most useful little
volume, compiled by the W.·. JAMBS WBIGHT ANDEBBoN, P. M., the present Ohair·
man of our Committee on Correspondence. As a book of reference it is far superior
to anything of the kind which has been offered to the Masons of C~lifornia. It com·
prises all the decisions of the Grand Lodge of thlR Jnrisdlotlon, from its formation to
the present time. It also contains the Constitution of the Grand Lodge ; the Uniform
Code of By·LRws of Lodges; the Monitor ; the Funeral Ceremony; the Installation
Ceremony ; the Ceremony for Laying "Corner-stones ; the Form for Keeping Records
of Lodges; and the Form for Condncting Trials. It is compact in form and most
admirably indexed, and reflects great credit upon its compiler. The interests of
Masonry would be greatly enhanced If every member of each Lodge in California
• should make frequent reference to this most valuable 11ade meoum.
On the twentieth day of last month, the Grand Secretary forwarded to me a letter
from Jacksonville, Florida, signed by " 0 . W. JOHNSON, Chairman of the Masonic
Relief Committee." The letter called attention to the suffering and terror occasioned
by the ravages of yellow fever at that place, and appealed to the Orart in California
for assistance. I immediately sent a telegraphic dispatch to the Grand Master of
Masone In Florida, inquiring whether he had authorized the call for relief, and if so, to
inform me In whose care aid should be sent. After waiting four days and receiving no
answer, a second message was sent to ascertain whether the first had been delivered.
This likewise failing to bring a response, a letter was addressed to the Grand Master·
or Grand Secretary asking for an immediate response, and offering the assurance
that the Fraternity in California were as ready and willing to respond to calls for
relief from our sister Jnrisdictloos, as they had shown themselves to be in the past.
On the fourth day of the present month, the Grand Secretary forwarded to me a letter from Bro. A. W. KNIGHT, the acting Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Florida
giving information that the Grand Master of ihat Jurisdiction had authorized thei;
Relief Committee to ask for aid. After consultation with the Deputy Grand Master,
?rand Treasurer, and Grand Secretary, it was decided to send the sum of $500, for
immediate needs, and to refer the matter to the Grand Lodge for such further action
as the circumstances might require. I accordingly authorized a warrant upon the
foods of the Grand Lodge for said amount, which was forwarded by the Grand Secretary in a telegraphic draft from the Bank of California, the otD.cers of which, as
heretofore, m11de no charge either for exchange or the cost of transmission. The
lllatter is herewith submitted for your pleasure.

It seems but yesterday since for the first time I sat in the councils of this Grand
Lodge, enraptured with its imposing opening ceremonies, the organ's swelling tones,
and the solemn invocation to the Gon of our fathers to guide its deliberations. What
changes have been wrought in that interval of time! Alas, bow many or the old
familiar faces are missing here to-day I Many or those whom we delighted to honor
have put 00 Immortality; while other~, who have been spared to lead the wa~, bear
the unmistakable impre88 of the swift·fleeling years. The days come and go like the
"countless ripples in the tide of time that regularly roll and break on the eternal
shore," the harbingers of that change that inevitably aw&its WI in the consummation
or ur-10 the ultimatum of worldly triumphs.
To-day we behold the beautiful flower, decked with the radiance of nature's perfect ·band and bearing upon Its petals the sparkling dew-drops of early morning,
ewayed by gentle zephyrs in all its pristine loveliness. A day hence it perishes,
withered by the rays of a noon-day's sun. From the ephemeral flower we learn one
of the sad lessons of man's mortality. How rapidly the ruthless hand of time lays
waste these human tabernacles ! How sad would be the thought but for the principal
tenet of our faith that we shall be reunited in a purer Lodge and a holier life beyond
the tomb!

At the late Annual Commtrnioation of our Graud Lodge there was presented an
appeal from the " STA.RB KING Mon11ment Association" to the people of California,
for fnnds to aid in the ereotion of a memorial monume11t to the distinguished patriot
whose name the Association bears, 11ccompl\n!ed by a communication from the President and Secretar.v thereof, asking the co-operation of our Grand Lodge and its
s11bordinates with "the old-time friends and admirers of THoiuli STABB KrNa in
adopting measures for the erection of a memorial, as a titting testimonial of his p,reeminent services in the preservation of the Union and in the oanse of humanity. '
Those papers were referred to 011r Committee on Finances, the adopted report
from which, after setting forth the services to his country of that illustrio11s brotber,
and regretti11g that 011r regulations prevented a direot appropriation by the Grand
Lodi>;e in aid of the praise-worthy purpose of the appeal, con cl oded with the recommendation " that the clrc11lar of the Association, accompanied by a comm11nic11tlon
from the Grand Secretary, setting forth the facts, be transmitted to the Lodges of the
Jorhdiotlon, req11esting that they give the subject the consideration I& well deserves,
and expressing the hope that their members, each in his Individual capaoity, will be
found willing to contribute genero11sly to this noble and most worthy object."
It seems needless to dilate upo11 the virtues and fame of one whose name wa&
almost, if not quite, as familiarly known to the people of California as was that of
LINCOLN or of GRANT; and in this communication to .Masonic Lodges, ft Is probably
snffioient to say that Bro. THOMAS STARR Knm was the Grand Orator of our Grand
Lodge in 1863; that the Address which be delivered before that Body, at its Annual
Communication in May of that year, was one of the most tbougbtrul and interesting
productions that has ever i>;raced itR proceedings ; that Its effect was such that he
was re-appointed to that office for the succeeding year, but bis notimely death prevented 11 second fulfillment of jts dnties; that be was the Chaplain of Orie11tal
Lodge, No. 14.4, in this city, nntil his decease; that he was a Mason whose pure,
bea11tiful, and useful life exemplified, in the highest dei>;ree, the tenets of the Order
'to which he belonged; and thl\t he was 11 man, beloved by those who had the good
fortnne to possess hi• intimate acquaintance, and respected and esteemed by all who
knew him, inclnding even those who~e proclivities were for a cause against which
bis fervent patriotism had so often sped the shafts of his brilliant eloquence.
.M~sons will honor themselves in honorinp: him, and it is hoped that sub~oriptlons
may be as generous as are the patriotic and Masonio feelings of the brethren of this
Jurisdiction. Not large contrlb11tions, but many, are desired, and they sbo11ld be the
willing gifts of individuals-not appropriations from the treasuries of the Lodges.
Subscriptio11 lists will accompany this communication, and it is req11ested that the
Master, Wardens, and other officers of each Lodge, will endeavor to give every
member thereof, and every other regular Mason within its jurisdiction, an opportunity
to cootrib11te bis mite iu aid of this laudable undertaking ; and that, as soon as practicable, the Master or Secretary will transmit the proceeds of such endeavor to the
undersigned, with the lists of the co11trib11tlons and the amounts contributed. Receipts therefor will of course be immediately transmitted, and, In due season, a fall
report thereof will appear in 011r publications.
ALllANDBB G. ABELL,
Grand. Seoreta.ry.

This pitifully meagre result is undoubtedly the consequence of the construction
givon to our lawi by the Grand Lodge at the last Annual Communication , which
permitted only individoal sobscriptlona and forbade the Lodges to appropriAte
money from their treasories for the purpose indicated. Our laws have certainly not
always here~ofor'e been so contracted in their construction. When an appeal from
the "GARFIELD Monument Association of the Pacific" was presented to the Grand
Lodge In 1881, that Body appropriated from its own treasury the sum of one hundred
dollars to aid the Association in its patriotic elfort, and recommended its circular
to the Lodges of the Jurisdiction. (See Proc's, 1881, page 174..) It is true that in
that recommendation the "hope" was expressed that contributions from the Lodges
would be by members "In their individoal capacity; " but It is almost equally true,
as shown by the round s'ums of many of their subscriptions, (see Proc's, 1882, page
4.73, aud Proc's 11183, page 4.6,) that a large portion thereof, amountiug in all to the
sum of $906 75, was the result of appropriations from their several treasnriea. Is it
altogether certain that the decision forbidding Lodges to appropriate their fuods for
certain purposes, includes or was intended to include a purpose like ei\her of these?
And, If it does, would it not be well to so amend or modify that decision that the
Grand Lodge and it~ subordinates may be at liberty to give assurance, from their
treasuries, of the love, respect, and veneration in whlch they hold the memory of a
citizen so well known and dletingoished, an orator so eloquent and patriotic, an
officer of our Grand Lodge so beloved and revered, as was our departed Brother,

and keep their •'lamps trimmed and burning" in anticipation of the work which
they believe will, ere long, be ready for the working tools of the Craft.

report of the condition of the three Lodges under his charge, which sets forth that
Inyo Lodge, No. 221, and Bodie Lodge, No. 252, have done no work during the year.
Their financial condition is good, but, owing to their widely scattered membership,
the average attendance is small. The officers, however, are well skilled in the work
and the books are neatly and correctly kept. Winned1'mah Lodge, No. 287, is in e.
fiourishing condition and ha.s conferred ten degrees during the year. The brethren

and the average attendance is at leBl!t seventy-five per cent. of the membership. The

thriving e.gricul tural community, it bids fa.ir to have e. steady and permanent growth.

In Angast last, in company with the Grand Master, I visit.ed the First Masonic
District, comprising the counties of Del Norte_and Hamboldt, 11nd containing Oreacent
Lodge, No. 45, Humboldt Lodge, No. 79, .Arcata Lodge, No. 106, Eel River Lodge,
No. 147, and Ferndale Lodge, No. 193. The trip np would have been very pleasant,
as we went by steamer, had it not been for certain inequalities in lhe surface of the
Pacific Ocean, which occupied a larg~ portion of my time. We Rrrived safely, however, and were most kindly and hospitably received by the brethren of Eureka and
its vicinity, who spared no pains to make it pleasant for us. A meeting was held, at
which !loll the Lodges in the District were represented, except Orescent Lodge, No. 45.
The work was exemplified in the several degrees, and we found the officers of the
various Lodges to be, in most· cases, well instructed in the ritual and zealous in the
discharge of their duties. The occasion was a most enjoyable one; and I regrett.ed
that I could not accompany the Grand Master in further visits.
Dnring the year I have, as nsaal, given instruction to such Inspectors and officers
of Lodges as have applied to me for that purpose, and I !)ave no hesitation in saying
that the officers of Lodges in California are as competent, proficient, intelligent, and
zealous as those of any J arisilictlon in the world. Oar system of inspection has now
been in operation for so many years that its good effect is manifest in the large number of competent instructors which have grown ap under it, the uniformity of work
now existing thronghont the Jurisdiction, the systomatic manner in which the books
and records of our Lodges are kept, and the general harmony which prevails among
the Craft. It will be notieed in my report, which embodies a summary of the reports
of thirty-four Inspectors, that not a single grievance is complained of; the white.
winged angel of peace sits enthroned upon all our altars; and the words of the
Psalmist, "Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together
in unity," are thoroughly exemplified.
In conclusion, I would say that, from all the information which has come to hand,
I am constrained to believe that the Lodges of California were never in better condi·
tion than at present.
All which is respectfully submitted by
JOHN WERNER SHAEFFER,

To the M. •• W. ·• Grand Lodge of Oalijornia :The undersigned present the following report of the :Me.sonic Board of Relief of
the City of Los Angeles for the period from October 4th, 1887, to October lat, 1888,
inclusive:As was ste.ted in their le.et report, this Board was organized on January let, 1885,
under a compact which had previously been entered into by the three Lodges of the
City of Los Angeles. By the terms of that compact the Masters and Secretaries of
the severe.I Lodges constituted the Board, and it was agreed that a monthly assess·
ment or donation of ten cents for each and every Master Mason borne upon the r~lls
of those Lodges should be paid into the "Charity Fond" of said Board, the object
for which it was organized being .the relief of members of the Fraternity, and their
families, not affi.lie.ted with the Lodges of this city.
At the stated meetings of the three Lodges, held in January of the present year,
the above compact was so amended e.s to read twelve and one·half cents for eaoh
member, in lieu of ten cents for each, said action being necessitated by reason of
the increased demands made upon the financial resources of the Boe.rd by visiting
brethren coming to Southern California. in search of health, many of whom arrived
here poor, not only in health bot in means, and came, in fact, only to die. In addition to these demands npon its resources, the ce.lls for assistance were so numerous
that it became necessary to adopt the plan of the Board of Relief of the City of 811n
Francisco, and to require the.t the time and services of the Secretary be devoted
exclusively to the business of the Board. To assist us in this purpose Signet Chapter,
No. 57, of Royal Arch Masons, donated twenty dollars per month for eight months,
and Oaw.r de Lum Commandery, No. 9, of Knights Templar, ten dollars per month
for the same period of time; making 11 tote.I of two hundred and forty dollars, which
a.mount appears in the financial statement hereinafter given.
From October 4th, 1887, to January 1st, 1888, the members constituting the Board

Bro. JAMES WRIGHT .ANDERSON, from the special committee to

consideration which Its great merit st> rightfully demands. It le a source of great
pride and satisfaction to the members of your committee, as it must be to yon, to
know that our Grand Master has so ably sustained the credit that has hitherto attached to the utterances of those who have been selected to preside in the Grand
East. It is right that the brethren should take pride in the character or those to
whom they entrust the interests of our great Jurisdiction ; and it Is pleasant to find
those brethren showing full appreciation of so distinguished an honor as la that of
being chosen to fill the high position of Grand Master. The excellence of this paper
indicates that Grand Master Buoua has formed a very proper estimate of the honor
bestowed upon him-one to which his eminent services in this Grand Lodge, and in
behalf of the interests of our whole Fraternity, so justly 'e ntitled him.
In the beautiful sentiments contained in the introductory portion of this Address,
your committee most heartily concnr. Every line is suggestive, offering food for
pleasant and profitable reflection.
The position of Grand Master In the Jurisdiction of Oalifornia le one burdened
with many cares and heavy responsibiliti es; and he who would worthily gain the
honors belonging to· it, must do so ai the expense of much time and greai labor,
Weighed in the balance of duty, our present Grand Master is not found wanting.
Your committee are not a little surprised that he could enlll.ciently spare the time
from hie professional duties to enable him to make such a record'of visitation; but
It has been done, and many Lodges ha.ve been made to rejoice in the personal presence of that high officer, and to feel the beneficent effect resulting from such Grand
Visitations. Yon, and we all, can realize what must have been the feelings of joy
and satisfaction experienced by the good brethren of Humboldt County on receiving
a visit from the Grand Master, especially when he was accom~anied by our good
and genial Bro. JonN WEBNEB SHAEFFBB, the Grand Lecturer, to assist him In ex·
plaining and emphasizing the work,
All Lodges enjoy and fully appreciate the visits of Grand Officers, especially those
of the Grand Master. They look upon these visits as being peculiar marks of respect, and they l\re encouraged and strengthened in consequence of them. Your
committee know, from personal observation a.nd experience, how gladly Lodges
everywhere welcome any Grand Officer, and they think that Bro. Rucx:EB deserves
great commendation for hie faithfulness in this regard; and, wbile congratulatin g
the Grand Lodge upon the earnest a.nd faithful manner in which our present Grand
Master has conserved its every interest; and upon the great measure of success which
has attended his efforts to promote the peace, the harmony, and the prosperity of
the Ora.ft, on your behalf a.nd on behalf of all his brethren, your committee desire to
render unto him the meed of praise a.nd satisfaction which his faithfulness, zeal aud
ability so richly deserves.

excellent Address; and, in order that those matters may all receive from this Grand
Body the consideration which their importance merits, they recommend the following distribution thereof:That so much as relates to the re-appointme nt of Inspectors and the formation ()f
new Masonic District.a, be referred to the special committee on the Report of the
Grand Lecturer:

A brief but very excellent Address was delivered by the Grand Master. We are
pleased to·learn that renewed interests is manifested in disseminating the great truths
or Freemasonry, end that the material interests of this Jurisdiction are in so prosper·
ous a condition. Of the latter the Grand Master thus speaks :We rejoice to see the rapid progress that is being made by our commonwealth in
material prosperity and the development of intellectnal cnltare. Oapitel and labor
are fl.owing in avon us, seeking investment and employment. Onr mountains, hitherto bleak and barren, have become tribntary to oar Increasing wealth. P erhaps
no State, in all this broad land or States, has ever moved onward in a grander and
more rapid march, achieving result e.l'ter result In so short a period, as our beloved
Alabama. The North is teeming with a busy population, pushing and driving every
energy in developing her vast and almost boundless resources. The smoking furnace,
the whistling engine, the crowded city, the bnstling town , the active village, tells a
story that is marvelous and matchless. Capital end enterprise are fast finding their
way to the timber belt in the beautiful pine forests of the South. Last, but bv no
means least, the agricnltnral district stretchlug through the central part of the l:ltate
is rejoicing in the midst of a boantilul harvest, and the hnsbandman wears a cheerful
smile.
Among other decisions rendered we note that, in reference to the qaalifications
of candidates, to the elfect that it is not necessary for them to be able to write their
names, if qualified in other respects. The Grand Lodge of California thinks dilfer·
ently, and prescribes, among the other qualifications for a candidate, that he must
be" capable of reading and writing." It seems to us that, in these latter days of
advanced improvement and intelligence, Masons should stand apon a higher plane,
and that the influence of our Order should be cast in favor of qualifications so uni·
versally recognized as are those of reading and writing.
The Grand Master had during the year visited a large number of Lodges, delivering addresses relating to the principles of Freemasonry. As an evidence of the interest
manifested, the appropriation made by the Grand Lodge for traveling expenses had
remained untouched, the brethren haviug in all cases , with commendable liberality,
borne these themselves.
We concur in the seutiment expreBBed in the following. Masonry is a social insti·
tntion, and its greatest benefits originate In, and are dependent upon, the exercise of
this featnre :It occurs to mti , that the social featare or our Order ought to be more cultivated
and practiced. Beneficial results follow every public Masonic gathering, when prudence and judgment guide and direct. I am assured of the fact that it woald give
Masonry a deeper, stronger and more permanent lodgment In the affections of Its
members, were they to meet in annaal re-nulons. Two or more neighboring Lodges
might agree to assemble on some designated day, install officers, have an address,
inviting the outside world to participate. This would relieve ns of the charge of
selfishness or clannishness, so often but erroneously urged against ne.
The Grand Master thinks that the time has arrived when the Masons of Alabama
should take under advisement and formulate some plan looking to the establ!shment of
a home for the widows and orphans of worthy Master Masons. We do not altogether
coincide In this view. If Grand Lodges, and Lodges and Masons generally, were more
earnest in encouraging a.ad urging worthy Masons to establish homes for themselves,
thus avoiding the necessity for Masonic homes for those left behind, we believe that
Masonry and the interests of widows and orphans would be much better conserved.
In this land, fl.owing with opportunity, prudence would enable every Mason to leave
his fllmily enough to preclude the necessity of homes otherwise constitnted. True
charity would be better exempllll.ed if Masons stood in with one another in aiding by
counsel and otherwise to make our homes ai home what they should be. We do not
disparage good enterprises, but we think that the effort which would enable Masons,
their widows and orphans to be self-sustaining, are far more worthy of consideration
than are the formalating of plans by which they may be supported by others.

To lift man to a higher and still higher plane of moral development should be our
constant study and effort; to be useful we most be virtuous and goc' d ; to guide others
aright we most go right ourselves. A nation's glory, a nation's prosperity, a nation's
freedom depends npon the chivalry, integrity and virtne of its people.
The forcefulness and benefits ot Masonic principles most depend upon the unflinching devotion of its members. To proclaim a truth and act a falsehood
dethrones the very subject sought to be attained. Heroic, unyielding devotion to
moral sentiment and moral troth begets a pric"eless manhood.
The report of the Oommittee on Finance shows a very healthful condition of the
Permanent Trost Fond, there beiilg in it, w~ll invested, the sum of $16, 764 92.
A resolution was adopted dividing the Jurisdiction into four districts, and author·
izing the Grand Master, upon the written recommendation of the Committee on Work,
to appoint a Lecturer for each district,-whose duty it should be t o verify the work
therein. This ls a step in the right direction, bot does not go far enongh. We
prefer the plan adopted in California, which provides for the appointment of a Grand
Lecturer, who is an officer of the Grand Lodge and is the accepted custodian of the
·worlr. The Jurisdiction Is divided Into thirty-eight Districts, for each of which an
officer, termed Inspector, is appointed, whose duty it is to visit each of the Lodges in
his District once a year, and oftener, if desired by any Lodge, to inspect and correct
the work, and to give such instruction to the Lodges as may be deemed necessary.
This plan works well in our State, and has the advantage of enabling the Lodges to be
so distributed that all can have the benefits of Inspection and instruction. Nothing
conduces more to the increase of interest in Lodges than a proper system of supervision, and so we have found it in California.
Past Grand Master PALMER JoB PILLANS presented, as usual, a very Interesting
review of the proceedings of fifty-three Grand Lodges, California being among the
number. Bro. PILLANS Is a Master in the art of reviewing, and hence gives to his
brethren matter not only interesting bot highly instructive. He has opinions of his
own, strongly marked, and does not hesitate to let others have the benefit thereof.
In commenting upon a resolution on the subje,c t of temperance, adopted by the
Grand Lodge of Arkansas, he says that it " Is bot another eO'ort to make Masonry a
part of the temperance movement, which will recoil and eventually prove useless."
From this we take it that he Is not in favor of such action by Grand Lodges. We are
in favor of both preaching and practicing the cardinal virtue of temperance; bot we
agree with our brother in believing that the passing of resolutions upon the subject
is not calculated to be very eO'ective for good,
California is freely and favorably noticed. The opinions of our Past Grand Master
Tn!Nm, on the manner of conducting trials, are quoted with approval, the writer
believing that "e:ood old·fashioned common-sense, under the feeling of honest
charity, is all that is needed in such cases.'' Speaking of our Boards of Relief, Bro.
PILLA!IS says :Perhaps the most notable and admirable portion of this pamphlet are the r eports
of the various " Boards of Relief," under the guidance and control of the Grand
Lodge. Jost such a system established in every Jurisdiction would not onlf r elieve
much distress but greatly diminish the number of frauds and "dead beats.'
Bro. PILLANS very kindly" goes for our scalp" on the matter of the prerogatives
of a Grand Master. He is in error, however, in representing that " none of the opponents to this report have done aught than sneer at the positions taken by the Grand
Lodge of Alabama." We read the report of the committee appointed by the Grand
Lodge of Ale.be.ma to consider that subject, and were profoundly impressed with the
astuteness displayed by them in making so strong an argument on so bad a case.
" Good old-fashioned common sense" Is all the goidanoe that is needed in such
matters, in these latter days, to enable os to arrive at a proper conclusion upon this
question. Enlightened, we no longer permit ourselves to believe that rulers hold by
divine right; but we do believe that when the head of any government is an elective

1888.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

507

officer, the first and fundamental principle of election renders him a.menable to that
power which has invested him with his authority. Grand Masters, from the days
whereof the memory of man ronneth not to the contrary, have been elective officers;
oonseqoently they are but the creatures of the power that coostitoted them Grand
Masters, and possess no preroga.tives other than those delegated to them. They
a.re bot tbe agents of the electors, dependent upon the electors, and responsible to
them. In our day, and in all the days, the Grand Lodge has possessed the highest
delegated authority among Masons. As in our civil government all powers emanate
from the people, so in Masonry all powers emanate from the several subordinate
Lodges; and hence a Grand Lodge is bot a representation of the Craft with the
power of legislation. The Grand Officers are but constituent parts of the Grand
Lodge, and it is as true here as is the axiomatic principle that a pa.rt oannot be
greater than the whole. The Grand Lodge possesses no prerogatives except such as
are confided to it by the strict letter of Its Constitution ; and, if the Grand Lodge
possesses no powers by implication, surely the Grand Master, who is bot a part-the
creature-of it, possesses no such powers. California has had one tronbloos experience
In this matter of prerogative. She has had most convincing proof that Grand Masters after all are but men, endowed with like passions and attributes as are other
men; and hence she has wisely availed herself of the provision contained in the
Ancient Constitutions, and has relegated to the shades a doctrine that savors more
of absolutism than of those that should characterize intelligent beings capable of
eelf-government. Grand Lodges and subordinate Lodges are constituted nowadays
out of a species of material that cannot be subordinated to the dictum of any principle outside the limits of enlightenment. The Oonstitntion of ihe Grand Lodge of
Oalifornia does provide in Subdivision 3, of Sec. 1, Art. I, Part II, that the Grand
Master may grant dispene.e.tions to ballot for and confer the degrees upon candidates,
without reference of their applications to committees of investigation; bot it does not
acknowledge his right to make Masons at sight, or at will, or to do any important act,
the power to do which is not granted in that instrument. Many matters, it is true,
io the exercise of his functions, are left to the discretion of the Grand Master; such
as granting dispensations for the formation of new Lodges, for the holding of elections of officers at. other times than those specified in the Constitution, the arrest or
charters, the suspension or Masters, etc., but these powers are all specially conferred
upon him by our organic law, and each act is subject to review by the Grand Lodge.
His discretion most conform to, or come within the purview of, that law.
With reference to the Solomonic origin of Masonry, and its existence "when the
stars first sang together," we seriously doubt the former, and do not, at all, believe
the latter. We do believe that it,& principles and teachings are "based upon the rock
of eternal troth, and that it has withstood the floods, and the rains and winds of
bigotry, and jealousy and wrong." Bot to agree that its principles are so based, is
by no means a granting of the fact that Masonry has existed since the time when
"the stars first sang together " -whenever that melodious performance may have
occurred. Doring all the years of its existence, It has withstood all attempts to crush
it, because It Is based upon the principles of eternal truth. We think that if we
wonld glory more in the trnths of Masonry and boast less of its great antiquity, we
would appear much less ridiculous and be much better appreciated.
We have seen so many good things in this excellent report that we feel very loth
io leave it; but we are reminded that our Oommittee on Finances may have something to say if we too greatly overstep the limits of moderation. Hence we close,
remarking that, if the brethren everywhere could have opportunity to peruse such .
reports as this is, Masonry would be much the gainer.

Regarding the Masonic burial of non-affiliated Masone, the Committee on Jnrisprndence reported, recommending that h was a matter which should be left to the
discretion of the Lodges. They remark that "there are many Masona who have
contributed to the support of the Fraternity and their needy brethren for years, who
entertain for it a high respect, who are themselves worthy and honorable men,
blessed with many Masonic friends, and are yet for the time being nnaftlliated. At
the deoease of snch, npon proper request, we consider it to be eminently proper that
the Lodge should confer burial." Bnt they consider that a non-affiliate who has lived
without friendship for the institution of Masonry, or whose character had been one
of reproach, should not be the recipient of this honor. In the latter we concur; bnt
as to the former proposition, we think the party should not be entitled to the honor
unless he has kept himself in good standing. Upon this snhject our law is as follows:
It is the dnty of every Master Mason to be a member of some Lodge; and every
non-affiliated Mason who, having resided six months within this State, shall refuse or
neglect to make application for membership to some Lodge therein, shall he deemed
unworthy of Masonic consideration, and shall not be entitled to nor be the recipient
of any of the rights, privileges or cha.rities of the Order.
He must pay a sum equivalent to six months' dnes of the Lodge to which he
applies, and, if rejected, he is deemed to be in good standing for six months following the application. He may again apply at any time and to any Lodge in the State.
To grant this benefit to non-affiliates, who are not in standing, seems to ns a species
of premium on non·affiliation.
' The Committee on Jurisprudence also reported a provision for life-me111bership.
They specifioally stated, however, that they were not desirous of encouraging the
principle, believing that the payment of Lodge dnes should be considered a privilege
rather than a burden. It may be well enough to establish the principle of snch membership ; but we are at a loss to discover how any great benefit can result therefrom
to either the member or the Lodge. Dnes in the Lodges are nsnally so light as not
to form mnch of a burden. Even members of Lodges submit themselves to mnch
greater burdens to gratify some useless habit, the indulgence in which results in
harm. We are not in favor of the principle. If members have regularly paid dues,
and through any canse should become unable to continue doing so, their payment
should be remitted, at least dnring the continuance of the inability. We have not
fonnd Lodges disposed to deal uncharitably with their members, and consider that
there can be no occasion for life-membership unless it be simply the trouble of frequent payments.

The Grand Master begins a very neat Address with the sentence, "Another

•
Relations with all other Grand Lodges were moat fraterna.J. Every subordinate
Lodge in the Jurisdiction had reported, and the abstract made from the returns
exhibits a most healthful condition of the Craft. There had been a net increase in
membership of five hundred anli twelve, or an average of over five per Lodge-a
very flattering addition. Dispensations had been issued for the formation of eight
new Lodges; and five, to which charters had been granted at the last Annual Communication, had been regularly constituted.
The Grand Master reports two decisions, both sound, in our opinion. The first
is to the effect that a Lodge under dispensation has the ri11ht to discipline its members
for uumasonic conduct; the second, that an applicant for the degrees of Masonry,
who has lost a single joint of the index finger of bis right hand, is not physically
disqualified.
The Grand Master had very properly refused to grant dispensations to receive
the petitions of ministers of the Gospel and other gentlemen who had not resided
the required year within the jurisdiction of the Lodge.
We have been not a little surprised that so many dispensations to confer degrees
ont of the usual time are asked for and granted in the various Grand Jurisdictions.
We suggest that the plan adopted in California, whereby proficiency is made.the
basis of qualification for advancement, is much better than requiring a candidate to
wait one month, whether proficient or not. The moral and other qualifications
have already been passed upon, and proficiency in the ritual and lectures is all
that ought to be required.
The Committee on Jurisprudence presented a full report upon two questions
referred to them at the last Annual Communication, viz.: First. " What is Legitimate Masonry?" Second. "What is the status of a non-affiliate?" In answer to
Jibe first question the committee say, in substance, that they know of no Masonry that
the Grand Lodge can or should sanction as legitimate, except the three degrees of
Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft, and Master Mason. The an.ewer to the second
is to the effect that a non-affiliate can visit a Lodge not more than three times ;
that he cannot join in any Masonic procession, nor participate in any festivity of the
Lodge, except by courtesy ; that neither be nor his family can make any claim for
charity upon the funds of the Lodge; that he is bound to respond to the calls of
distress by individual Masons, and that they are in like manner bound to him;
that he has no ri1rht to Masonic burial, though it may be given him by .the Lodge at
its discretion; and that he is subject to all Masonic obligations and amenable to
.the Lodge nearest which he sojourns or resides, for any violation of the moral or
Ma.ionic law. Both answers are sufficiently definite.
