1888.J

Grand Lodge of California.

523

I attribute much of this success to the custom which has been inaugurated by
nearly all the Lodges-that of dispensing substantial refreshment when called from
labor. That which ensures success shon1d be encouraged.
We do not presume to say that the interest engendered by the presence of substantial refreshments originates from any gormandizing disposition of our brethren
of the District of Columbia, as we suppose they could get more and better things
both to eat and to drink at home; but it probably does arise from the increased
friendly intercourse incident .to these pleasant occasions. There ii tr" often a
coldness, a lack of brotherly sympathy in our Lodges, the result of slight acquaintance. Lodges are not constituted for the mere making of Masons, but to give to
Masons, when ma.de, the opportunities for a closer and more brotherly communion
which will tend to cultivate them in all the graces of Masonry and make them bet_
ter men.
The report of the Board of Relief shows that out of seventeen applicants five only
had proved themselves worthy, a fact showing clearly the necessity for such Boards,
not only as a protection to the worthy, but as a defence for the Lodges against parties
who make it a practice to act the part of "dead beats."
The Report on Correspondence was presented by the Grand Secretary. It is a
brief but comprehensive review of the proceedings of some forty-five American Grand
Lodges. Commenting upon a decision of the Grand Master of Arizona, to the effect
that a Lodge cannot surrender its jurisdiction except by unanimous consent, Bro•
SnrGLETON remarks that no such consent is necessary; that the vote of a Lodge to
waive jurisdiction does not elect any one to receive the degrees of Masonry; that his
election must be by the LodgA receiving his petition; and that, for this reason, the
unanimous consent of the Lodge granting the waiver is not necessary. Our Grand
Lodge has no provision for a " waiver of jurisdiction" until the party makes appli.
cation for the degrees to the Lodge within the jurisdiction of which he resides, and
has received one, or two, of the degrees. There is nothing in our Constitution that
authorizes a Lodge to take any action in respeo& to a person, not a Mason, resident
within its territory, until he has made application to it for the degrees. Upon the
presentation of such an application its jurisdiction is called into exercise. It can
then elect or reject him; and, having elected and conferred the first degree upon
him, it can surrender its jurisdiction over him to another Lodge at his or its request.
California receives a reasonable share of notice from Bro. SINGLETON. He quotes
from the Address of Grand Master Tn.-NIN relative to Masonic trials, and thinks that
"the truth in such trials is what we are to arrive at, by any laudable means whatever, and that any attempt to screen a criminal should be discountenanced."
Bro. ABELL'B report is termed the business paper of our Jurisdiction, and is pronounced the very best tha.t he had seen in its arrangement of the subjects contained
therein.
.
Relative to the examination of Masters of Lodges, Bro. SINGLETON holds views that
are fully in accord with those of our Grand Lodge, and thinks that the Masters of
Lodges should be examined as to their knowledge of the government of a Lodge and
or the "General Regulations" of Masonry, as well as to their knowledge of the ritual.
Few of our Masters ever direct that attention to the Constitution and By-Laws that
are framed for their go?ernment, which their importance demands; and, as to the
"General Regulations of Masonry," it is safe to say that very many have no knowledge of them whatever.
Bro. SINGLETON is in fnll accord with us on another important point. He does
not believe in making one a Mason t.oo rapidly. We have often thought that there
le a great deal too much haste in conferring the degrees upon candidates in our
Lodges. If they can repeat the ritual and show that they have gulped down vast
lot of verbiage, it seems a matter of indifference whether they understand what they
have learned or not. Generally our candidates are " crammed " for the occasion.

permits us to epitomize this excellent address. Soflice it to say that, at a meeting
held on the sixteenth day of December, 1786, the Grand Officers of the Provincial
Grand Lodge, then existing under the proviooial regulations of England, resigned
their positions and an independent Grand Lodge was formed. This was chartered in
1796, and cootinned with varying success until 1820, at which time a schism occurred,
owing to the contlicting interests of the upper and the lower portions of State. A Con·
veotioo met in 1826, at Milledgeville, and adopted a oew Constitution. The Grand
Lodge at Savannah refused to recognize the new order of things, and , in 1827, elected
Grand Officers. The Milledgeville Grand Lodge also, in 1827, elected Grand OftlceTst
and pa8sed resolntions declaring null and void the proceedings of the Grand Lodge at
Savannah. Matters continued in bad condition until 1838. Many of the Lodges that
had continued with the Grand Lodge at Savannah closed, never to be opened.
Finally the last named Grand Lodge accepted terms of reconciliation, and, lo 1889,
all diftlcnlties were healed. Since that time to the present the Lodges have increased
from a half-dozen to its present enlarged list, and, as Bro. EBTILL says, " there is no
reason that this prosperity shoald not continue." He further remarks, what every
one will recognize as trne, that "Masonry has more to fear from those who are within

because it is good :Masonry, my brothers, was never designed for the gratification of foolish vanity
or the mere employment of idle hours. She holds out to her votaries no promise of
pecuniary gain, or gratified ambition, or social or political preferment. She has a
more earnest and a higher mission than this. Her aim is to elevate humanity by
awakening in every brother a deeper appreciation of his own dignity as a man, and
a proper reg11rd for the dignity of his brother man. Masonry is not a system of
religion, as some have ignorantly thought. She does not aspire to usnrp the flace
of the church, but she oows to this as the human to the divine. It has been wel said
that" religion is the bond of man to his Gon; Masonry is the bond of man to m11n."
Beyond the great idea of GoD, as revealed in His word, Masonry has no religious
test: and therefore, while the atheist and the deist find no place within her portals,
and while she teaches a profound reverence for Deity and for the divine attributes-temperance, truth, and justice-her toleration is as broad as the grand brotherhood
of human kind. And her mission in this human brotherhood is to purify and to
ennoble.
I know of no humlm institution so well calculated to withstand the shock of time
as is Freemasonry ; but, let her cardinal principles be forgotten, let her children be
untrue to the vows which they have uttered and the lessons they have been taught
in the Lodge, and the preservative powers of the Order will be destroyed and the
temple will bec<!me but a mass of distorted ruins.

ILLINOIS.
On opening the beautiful volume containing the proceedings of the Grand Lodge
of Illinois, the first object that meets our gaze is the likeness of one whose name had
become a household word among the Craft in his own Jurisdiction, and was known
to Masons in every portion of the Masonic world. "A prince has fallen in Israel!"
TimonoBE TUTHILL GURNEY has been gathered to his fathers. His Grand Lodge and
the brethren of Illinois have lost one whom they not only delighted to honor, but
whom they had learned to Jove. His Joss is not that of Illinois alone; it is that of all
the Craft. Wherever Masons are found the loss must be felt. He has left as a legacy
to the Fraternity a fair and untarnished name-an example and teachings that will
prove a perennial source of benefit and blessing.

INDIANA.

The llixty·seventh Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Indiana wu
held in thA city of Indianapolis, commencing on the twenty-second day of May,
1888,-th.e M. ·• W.·. MORTIMER Nn:, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W. ·.
WILLIAM H. SKYTHB being Grand Secretary. Four hundred and sixty.two Lodges
were represented.
The Adrlress of the Grand Master ie a well prepared exposition of bis official
acts during the interim of the eeBBioneof the Grand Lodge. With pleasure becalle
attention to the condition of the Craft in the State, The J uriediction has had an
era of prosperity; the increase in membership in the past year has been four hundred and twenty.four; and the Craft bad been strengthened by the introduction of
good, true, and worthy men. Decent and becoming tribute ie paid to the memory
of those who had been called to the other shore. The charters of two Lodges had
been annulled, those of two bad been arrested, and those of two others surrendered.
The charters of fifty-nine Lodges bad been suspended in consequence of delin·
quency in paying Grand Lodge dues or of failure to repori. All but two of these
fifty-nine had subsequently paid their dues or reported ; and the two still delinquent were represented as practically dead.
Diepeneatione had been granted for the formation of three new Lodges, whilst
in twelve instances diepeneatione had been refused. The experience of the Grand
Master had fully convined him that there were already too many Lodges in the
J uriediction.
The Grand Master ie not a believer in the " prerogatives;" hence he had pereietently refused to set aside any provision of the Constitution, or standing rule or
regulation of the Grand Lodge. Quite right, in our opinion.
Relations with other Grand Lodges were of t he most friendly and fraternal
nature. The Grand Master recommended that commissions as Grand Representatives be limited to three years; but the Committee on Jurisprudence, rightly, we
think, reported adversely thereon, inasmuch as no plan had been yet devised by
which the Grand Representative system, now in vogue, can be utilized.
The Grand Master had encouraged the consolidation of weak Lodge11, especially
in towns of moderate size. Twelve bad in this way been made into eix. Thie we
deem a step in the right direction.
.Another very important step was taken by the Grand Lodge, on recommend&·
tion of the Grand Master-the passage of a resolution forbidding any Lodge to iseue
begging circulars under the guise of charity. Such circulars are an abuse of cbaritv,
not justifiable in any manner, nor at any time. Thie bad practice has been common
of late years in many Jurisdictions, and we sre pleased to see the Grand Lodges
taking such action as will put an effectual atop to it.
The report of the Grand Treasurer shows the handsome balance of $16,642 67
in the Grand Lodge treasury. We make note of such an item, it being one of the
beat indices of general prosperity; There ie no question of the fact that a well filled
treasury forms a very strong bond of union and interest, whether in Grand or Subordinate Lodges; and, without stinting their charities, all Lodges should be encourlpd to husband their means.

Among the r,aaes reperted on by the Committee on Grievances and Appeals,
we notice one in reference to charges of unmwmnic conduct preferred by one brother
against another for failure to pay or secure a debt due a brother. The Lodge found
the accused guilty, and adjudged indefinite suspension as the penalty. The brother
preferring the charges appealed the case on the ground that the penalty was inadequate. The Grand Lodge decided that the failure to pay or secure a debt is not a
Masonic offense, unless the brother is amply able to pay or is in some way tainted
with fraud. Fraud in anv transaction would be good l!l'Ound for charges ; but
Masonic Lodges are not the places for, and should not be prostituted to, any such
purpose as the settlement of business difficulties where no fraud exists. Courts of
law are established for this purpose.
We notice another case in which the accused brother was found guilty of larceny,
and the Lodge adjudged that he should be reprimanded. The Grand Lodge contented itself with setting aside the decision, and remanding the case for new trial.
Expulsion by the Grand Lodge would have been more in accord with Masonic
ethics, and with the usage in California.
The establishment of Orphans' Homes seems to be the order of the day. The
Grand Lodge of Indiana passed a resolution to the effect that it is expedient for it
to have such a Home for the education of the children of Master Masons who were
so unfortunate as to die insolvent. We think that the expediency "depends."
We quote the following from a report presented by the Committee on Foreign
Correspondence, and concurred in by the Grand Lodge :That as far back as 1877 there were two Grand Lodges in the Island of Cuba,
each claiming jurisdiction in Cuba; that in 1885 these two Grand Lodges were consolidated under the name of "The United Grand Lodge of Colon and the Island
of Cuba."
In the opinion of your committee the proceedings of consolidation have bee11
regular, and this new Grand Lodge is entitled to recognition by the Grand Ledge
of Indiana.
·
We recommend that fraternal recognition be extended to the United Grand
Lodge of Colon and the Island of Cuba, and that an interchange of Representatives
be had.
We notice that the name of Past Grand Master JOHN MILLS BROWNE is still
incl~ded in its list as the Representative of the Grand Lodge of Indiana near our
Grand Lodge. We simply remark that that brother has long since ceased to be a
resident of California, though still holding his membership in our Naval Lodge,
No. 87.
Bro. SIMEON S. JOHNSON presented a well prepared Report on Correspondence.
In it California for 1886 and 1887 receives a brief but pleasant notice. Bro. JOHNSON gently raps our Grand Officera, including the Chairman of this Committee, for
their great "abundancy of words." Our brother does not appear to take into consideration the fact that California is a great Jurisdiction, and has a great "abun·
dancy" of matters calling for special mention and attention. He does not seem to
favor the publication of a list of membera of subordinate Lodges, and yet Indiana
complains of impostors. If such lists were printed by all Grand Lodges the oppor·
tunities for imposition would, we opine, be greatly lessened.
·Bro. J OHNBON is a good condenser; but, now that his Grand Lodge has resumed
the holding of Annual Communications, we hope to hear from him in a more
extended report. We agree with him that the "material of a Jurisdiction belongs
to a Jurisdiction." Circumstances of distance or convenience cannot affect any of
its rights, and a citizen should obtain his membership in his own Jurisdiction,
if there a resident.
The power which grants a charter is, in our opinion, the only power that can
annul it. The Grand Master may, in accord with con°stitutional provisions, grant

1888.]

GTand Lod,ge of OaUfornW..

535

dispensations to form new Lodges; but we are not aware that any Grand Lodge,
in these latter days, permits its Grand Master to grant charters. Suspension of a
charter should be the limit of his power in this regard. It seems to us a dangerous
thing to extend it further. Common sense as well as common usage teaches us that
the power which creates a regulation or an instrument is the only power that can
annul or destroy it.
We would be pleased to note many more of the interesting comments of our
brother, but we are admonished that we are violating the rule of "abundancy "
which does not find favor in his eyes.

INDIAN TERRITORY.
The thirteenth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Indian Territory
was held in the town of Eufaula, Muskogee Nation, commencing on the first day of
November, 1887,-the M.·. W.·. FLORIAN HARADEN NASH, Grand Master, presiding,
and the B.·. W.·. JOSEPH BAHUEL MURROW being Grand Secretary. Twenty-one
Lodges were represented.
The Address of the Grand Master is a brief presentation of official acts during the
year. Some discord had occurred, but harmoi:y again prevailed. The Grand Master
attributes most of the dissension that had existed to undue desire to hold office. He
very properly remarks that "it is natural and commendable to desire the respect of
Lodges, but it does not follow that to hold office will command respect; for all are not
competent, and it very often happens that the most competent, on account of their
modesty, are kept in the background." The aphorism, "fools rush in where angels
rear to tread," is about as true in a Masonic Lodge as elsewhere.
The Grand Master also alludes to another practice which ought to be condemned
without stint. Too frequently is it the case that the habit of smoking is permitted in
the Lodge-rooms, to the discomfort of those even who in moderation are addicted to
the use of the weed. A Lodge-room ought to be considered too sacred a place for
such a practice during a session of the Lodge. Masons should be considerate of the
feelings and comfort of each other. We have betimes witnessed in Lodges of our
own Jurisdiction that, as soon as they were called off temporarily, a rush was made
to relight the cigar or the pipe or the cigarette. A little self-sacrifice, if restraint in
this particular lilay be termed such, is quite desirable, and Masters of Lodges should
s_ee to it that members are required to act with due order and propriety during the
time the Lodge remains open. We should consider smoking in the Lodge a violation
·
or the proprieties that usually characterize gentlemen.
The Rev. Bro. A. FRANK Ross, Grand Orator, delivered a very practical and timely
address-brief but pointed. He denounces fraud, gambling, intemperance, profanity
and slander in a very proper manner. Humanity is frail, and hence it is that these
evils are too often found to exist among those who profess to be guided by the
Bilblime moral tenets of Freemasonry.

called upon for information, and in some cases be had been asked for dispensation•
to receive petitions from and confer degrees upon men with but one arm or one leg.
Upon this subject be sent a circular letter to the Lodges conveying his decieions" That all such maims or defects in the physical orgaruzation of the man, whether
it be a natural deformity or the result of accident or other misfortune, in consequence of which he is incapable of conforming to the requirements of all our cere·
lllonies, would render him unsuitable material." He further decided that the right
to Interpret the law is unquestionably vested in the Master and hie Lodge, subject
to discipline for an erroneous interpretation thereof. We endorse these deciRiODB

The wrinkled brow and silvery locks of many of us are but silent monitors to
warn us of the absolute certainty of death, and of the decay of all earthly great-

-.That our own lives have been spared to the present time gives us cause for

thankfulness to the Great Author of our existence, and while we rejoice with each
other in the po1session of life and strength, we must not be unmindful of the fact
that many of our noble Craft have, during the past year, been summoned from
among us.

At the request of the Grand Master, the Gra.nd Secretary ha.d prepared and
presented a moat beautiful and fitting tribute to the memory of those of hie own

brief space of time to thought and singing the praises of the dead."
Bro. PARVIN, the very able Grand Secretary of this Jurisdictiori, presented a
most admirable Report; and why should it not be such, since it is the product of a
pen guided by a brain that has had the opportunities and the experience of half a
century? On the fourteenth of March, 1888, Bro, PARVIN rounded out his fiftieth
year &a o. Mason, during nearly all which time he h&e served in the capacity of
Grand Secretary. His zeal in every good word and work is commensurate with
his ability, and the Grand Lodge of Iowa owes to him much of her present pros·
perity. We quote his closing paragraph. Verily, he deserves the reward, and
could not leave a prouder legacy to his children or his Grand Lodge-aye, to his
brethren everywhere, than the record of such a stewardship :I have the consciousness of the reward arising_from the discharge of my duties
to the Grand Lodge and the Masone of Iowa. No praise from brethren can ever
011.ual this, and no ingratitude can make it less. Such an approval I enjoy, and
hope to transmit to my children as their heritage. It is all I have to leave them.
Like our own Grand Secretary, Bro. PARVIN manifests a most abundant pride
in the euccese of hie Grand Lodge Library. This is in a very flourishing condition, and h&e, during the year, received many additions to its several departments.
The Grand Lodge finances, as shown by the reports of the several accounting
officers, are in excellent condition, the total cash aseets amounting to SIS, 711 85.
P118t Graod Master GRANGER, who had been appointed at the preceding Communication of the Grand Lodge for that purpose, presented a draft for a Code of
Masonic Law for the Jurisdiction. This, after having been variously amended,
was subsequently adopted, and became the law of the Grand Lodge. The new
Constitution was approved and adopted at the last Communication of the Grand
Lodge, and airain at the present Communication. It thus became the orgnnic law
of the Jurisdiction. Iowa is to be congratulated on having thus happily, and

the improvements eugceated by the experiencee of so many years.

The Report of the Grand Treasurer shows the total resources of the Grand Lodge

A. special committee on National Relief Board matters presented a very excellent report thereon, and recommended the adoption of the following resolution :Resolued, That there exists at this time a great neceBBity for united action in protecting Masons and Masonic Lodges from imposition and fraud by itinerant tramps
and beatB; and, as t.his can be accomplished fnlly through the agency of tJte Masonic
Board of Relief, the Grand Lodge heartily recommends and earnestly requests subordi· •
nate Lodges throughout this Grand Jurisdiction to become members of such Board.
The resolution was adopted. If a Board of Relief, such as we have In San Francisco and in other cities or California, can be instrumental in the accomplishment of
so much good in doing away with "the promiscuous frauds and impositions that are
daily practiced upon the Fraternity by worthless tramps and vagabonds," certainly
a National organization devised for such purpose will be a blessing to Masons and
Lodges everywhere, and Lodges nnd their members will save many times the expense
incident to membership for better purposes.
The Grand Lodge of Kentucky does not look with much favor upon "preroga·
tives" of Grand Masters, as is shown by the following :We note the Grand Master's" suggestions" in regard to the prerogatives of Grand
M:aa~rs to permit the conference of degrees out of time. Also, the amendment to
our Constitution permitting them to grant such dispensation where a Lodge shows
good reasons therefor, and upon the payment of a fee to the Grand Secretary of'flve
dollars for snch dispensation. The question of "prerogative of Grand Masters" is
like the q_oestion of "ancient landmarks "-a subject on which there is such a diver·
sity of opmion, and which is so susceptible of construction, as to be made applicable to
any case that might arise. We are continnally hearing of some important discovery of
another " prerogative" or the finding of a "new" "ancient landmark." Our fathers,
no doubt, were troubled in the same way, and in their wisdom framed our Constitution so that there could be no differences of opinion on these subjects. They had
worked under the "ancient landmark" giving Grand Masters an immense amount of
"prerogatives." In fact their authority was supreme. A "Grand Master" could
go ahead and exercise his own jndgment or inclination, and if objection was made,
or criticism offered, he at once took refuge behind the "ancient landmarks" and
llhonted "prerogatives." Not having lived in the olden times when Grand Masters
were autocrats, and when they were not restrained by such things as Grand Lodge
Oonstitntions, we can only imagine the immense power they possessed and the great
influence they could wiel~--possibly at times for good, but more frequently, we fear,
for evil. The amendment suggested proposes to revive· one of those "landmarks"
which we all know never resulted In any good to the Order and many times great
harm has followed. We cannot see how the char~ing of a fee of five dollars for
the Secretary is any improvement on the old plan. If there was any good reason for
the Grand Master giving any such dispensation, it certainly should be given without
any fee being charged. But your committee are of the opinion that we had better go
by our Oonstitntion, and not amend it by giving the "Grand Master" any such
authority. We therefore disapprove the amendment suggested by the Grand Master.
[Adopted.]
So say we. The days of autocracy have passed away; the times have chanJled,
and some Masonic Grand Lodges have changed with them, and are now under the
rule of enlightenment that leads them to disbelieve in the doctrines that "Kings can
do no wrong," that "the Pope is infallible," and that" Hrnnd Masters need not be
circumscribed by Constitutions."
Various attemptB were made during the sessions of the Grand Lodge to provide
for a Grand Lecturer and the proper exemplification of the work ; bot all met with
the fate of the first. If our brethren of Kentucky could see the effects of such ap·
pointment and exemplifications as we in this Jurisdicti&'n have seen them, they wonld
not hesitate long in determining otherwise than they have done.

We, too, are opposed to cheap Masonry, bot we cannot endorse the views of our

excellence in Lodge or society most be built.

The Address of the Grand Master is a long and able one, occupying, together with
its appendices, some forty-five pages of the printed proceedings.
In welcoming hie brethren to their labors and trusts, he represents that Provi·
de nee haa been kind to the people and them eel vee ; that rich harvests had rewarded

the husbandman's toil; that the "hammer and sovll" had rang oat their notes with

The net Indebtedness on the Temple had been reduced to $21,000--a very satls·

The Grand Master believes in the rigid enforcement of the provision of the Con·
stitotioo forbidding the right of visit to any Master Mason who shall live in the
vicinity of a Lodge for the space of one year without tbe payment of does, if able to
pay; rightly holding that any Mason who, having received the beoefl.ts of Masonry,
holds them in light esteem, or who, by public neglect, calls forth derogatory and
depreoiatiog comment, is one of the worst enemies to the prosperity of the Order.
We, in California, by operation of law cot on; not only from the right of visitation
but from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, the non-affiliated Mason who by
neglect or otherwise permits himself to be in arrears for a period of more than six
months.
Joint occupancy of halls, except in extreme cases, meets with the disapproval of
the Grand Master. Joint occupancy In California is not objected to; nor have we
found any inconvenience or harm arising from permitting other Societies to jointly
occupy our halls. Were it not permitted to our Lodges to occupy them jointly
with other Societies, many of them would be either encumbered with debt, or
unable to meet at all.
The Grand Master also opposes life-membership, ~emarkiog that the introduction
of this feature into Lodges has long since been almost universally conceded to be detri·
mental to their prosperity. We can hardly concur in this opinion; we think that It
largely depends upon the manner in which the fees for lite-membership are invested.
If properly invested, the income Is quite as certain, and possibly quite as large, as it
would be from the payment of does. Furthermore, the income from this source
would be continuous, and would not cease on the death of the member. We think
that the principle of life-membership is simply the endowment principle, and that,
if properly managed, it cannot be other than beoefl.cial. If the fee for life-membership ls made what it should be, there can be nothing detrimental in it. While not
encouraged by our Grand Lodge, it is permitted; and when proper roles have been
adopted relative thereto no harm has appeared. Oor Grand Lodge has oo two occasions decided that a contract of life-membership cannot be rescinded or repealed
without the consent of both the contracting parties. This we think is just. We are
not prepared, however, to endorse the law of Louisiana on this subject, to the effect
that "life-members should pay only one-half of all does that may be required of
each member borne upon the rolls or the Lodgf."
Tbe feelings of the Grand Master seem to be divideil on the matter of consolidation of Lodges. We think there can be but one light in which the matter can be
viewed: that is, if a Lodge, through any cause, is unable to sustain itself, it should
unite with some contiguous one ; as by so doing the burdens of both are lightened,
and renewed activity would be the result.
The Grand Master takes about the same ground on the Quebec matter as does
oor own Grand Lodge: namely, that the doctrine of exclusive Grand Lodge jorisdic•
tion does not demand any interference in the quarrel of the three contending parties.
On the matter of work we cannot concur with the Grand Master. He considers
that in all that is not deemed essential and indispensable, but merely explanatory,
directory or mooitorial, the ideal work is "that in which the Master penetrates

It is the custom in this J nrisdictioo to open the Grand Lodge prior to the entrance
of the Grand MMter. On the present occasion, this having been done, the entrance
of the Grand Master was proclaimed, he was received with the Grand Honors, and,
having taken his place in the Grand East, he declared the Grand Lodge open in
Ample Form.
The Address of the Grand Master is a brief paper, containing nothing of very general importance. He had few official acts to report, having been absent during a
greater part or the previous six months, on a visit to Europe. He reporte that the
receipts of the Grand Lodge are the greatest that have ever been received at any
Bemi·Annnal Communication, and that, daring the last two years, the income of the
Grand Lodge had gradually Increased, while the indebtedness had as gradually been
reduced. The membership during the past year had also greatly increased, the exhibit
showing that not only were they-on the high road to financial prosperity, but also to
to a greater degree of interest in the Institution.
The Grand Lectnrer presented a very fall report, from which we learn that great
improvement and mnch inlerest had been noticeable in the several Districts. The
system pursued in this Jurisdiction Is very similar to that adopted in on~ own, and
there, as here, it seems to have worked much good.
We observe that a resolution was introduced and referred to a committee, to be
reported opoo at the May Communication of the Grand Lodge, the intent of which is
to reduce the labor and shor.t en the time occupied lo the election of Grand Officers.
The resolution provides for the appointment by the presiding officer of three scrnti·
neers, and as many collectors of the ballots as may be nece88ary. The Grand Secretary is to furnish the scrutineers with a register of the vote entitled to be cast. The
result of each ballot is to be reported to the presiding officer, who 8hall declare the
same to the Grand Lodge. We consider some action of this character very desirable.
Far too much valuable time is spent in elections in our Grand Lodges that might be
spent to moch better pnrpose.
The Grand Lodge adopted an amendment to the effect that no Lodge shall elect
for its Master any other than a Warden, Past Warden, or Past Master, who has served
one full term. We do not look with any favor opon such a regnlation. It restricts
the selection to such a limited onm ber of persons as might render it impossible to secure
the best officer for this responsible place. There should be given to Lodges the right
to exercise a sound judgment in securing those whose interest, knowled11:e, and
ability will enable them to do the work of the Lodges, and manage the affairs thereof
In such manner as to ensure success. Merit. should be made the criterion by which
we shonld determine oar selection of officers; and often this is found in higher degree
on the floor than in the chairs. We believe In the selection of the fittest-the fittest
morally, socially, intellectnally-the fittest by every attribute that constitutes a
Master in the proper sense of that term. The restriction oontained in this amend·
ment precludes the possibility of doing this. It also removes from the body of the
inembership all stimulus to fit themselves for Masters, and, indeed, for any of the
positions in oar Lodges.
From the report of the Chairman of the Masonic Relief Association we learn that
the General Relief Association of the United States and Canada held 11B second
Annnal Beasioo at Toronto, Canada. A careful calculation, by brethren rep~eeenting
the leadiog Boards of Relief In the two countries, shows that there has been a saving of $10,000 to Boards represented by them since the organization of the General
Aasoclation. There are now represented in the Association thirty· one Grand Lodges.
There can be no doubt as to the benefl.ts to accrue from such an organization, and it
la to be hoped that the time is not for distant when all our Grand Lodges will unite
lo branding Masonic tramps so indelibly that the faithful brethren of our Lodges will
be amply protected from their impositions.

The Grand Lodge of Maryland commenced its two hundred and third Stated
Communication, the Semi-Annual one, on the eighth day of May, 1888,-the
M. •• W.·. THOMAS J. SHRYOCK, Grand Master, presidinl!', and the R. ·. W. ·. JAOOB
H. MEDAIBY being Grand Secretary. Seventy-two Lodges were represented.
The Address of the Grand Master is a brief statement of his official acts, containing little that is of general interest. He CODl!'?atulates his brethren of the
Grand Lodl!'8 on the prosperous condition of Masonry in Maryland. In one case
he had been compelled to arrest the charter of a Lodge for great violation of
Masonic custom and usages. The financial condition oi the subordinate Lodges
had improved beyond all expectations, whilst that of the Grand Lodge is represented as most gratifying and satisfactory. The Grand Master favors dual membership within the Lodges of that Jurisdiction; but no action appears to have
been had by the Grand Lodge on his recommendation to modify the Constitution
so as to permit it, except to refer the proposition to a committee.
The decrease in the amount of the indebtedness of the Grand Lodge is quite
encouraging. The debt yet remainin~ amounts to $113,340 25.
The Baltimore Lodl!'e of Relief continues to do excellent work in the wav of
dispensing charity, in savmg money for the Fraternity, and in detecting impostors.
The report of the Grand Lecturer is a brief record of a vast amount of work.
Lodges of Instruction had been held weekly in Baltimore, and much attention had
been paid on the part of the Grand Inspectors, and brethren throughout the JuriHdiction, to the character of the ·work.
Bro. EDWARD T. SCHULTZ presented a well written Report on Correspondence.
California receives pleasant and fraternal notice, Our brother is in error in stating
that our Inspectors report only to the Grand Lecturer. They report the working
condition of each Lodl!'ll to the Grand Lecturer, and the condition of the books
and the manner of transacting the business with reference to its conformity to our
Constitution and Regulati11ns, to the Grand Master.
Bro. SCHULTZ is also wrong in supposing that our system of Inspectors was intro.
duced into California by Bro. CHARLES GILMAN. The system is the outgrowth of
various changes that were sug11"9sted by Grand Masters of our Jurisdiction, notably
by Grand Master LEONIDAS E. PRATT in 1870, until it arrived at its present state of
perfection. Experience . and the wants of the Lodges gave rise to the present
aystem. The matter of uniformity of work, and the best means ot promulgating
such uniform work, was not the result of the suggestions of any one individual. The
system is the l!'?owth of years and the careful deliberation of the Grand Lod1!'9,
l!'Uided bv the necessities of the times and of the Jurisdiction.
We concur with Bro. SCHULTZ in the opinion that it is the duty of Committees
on Correspondence to discuss "points of Masonic law." It is their duty to inform
themselves upon these points, and upon the proper usages of the Craft, and to pl'e·
sent thereto all the information poBBibly to be obtained. We opine that this would
be in much better keeping with the responsibilities ef their position than is the disposition, too often manifested, to make their work a species of mutual admiration.
To the discussion of points of Masonic law and usage are Masonry and all Masonic
interests greatly indebted. Prevention is better than cure, and, by proper discussion, not only is hasty and inconsiderate action frequently corrected, but ie more
frequently avoided.

MICHIGAN.

The forty-fourth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Michigan was held
in the city of East Saginaw, ·commencing on the twenty-fourth day of January, 1888,
at high ttoewe,-tbe M.·. W.·. RUFUS C. HATHKWAY, Grand M.aster, presiding, and the
.R.·. W.·. WILLIAM POWER lmlEs being Grand Secretary. Three hundred and forty·
llix Lodges were represented.
A cursory glance at the ponderons volume now under review ca~sed us to feel a
seose of weariness. We felt inclined ~o pass it by "until a more convenient season; "
but, upon glancing along as far as the Grand Master's Address, our attention was
arrested and we became interested. The avoirdupois of the volnme is equaled only
by the character of its contents and the excellent work of its printer. There are
not among our Wolverine brethren any " croakers " against long addresses, long
Reports on Oorrespondence, o..mucb printing. The Address of the <irand Master
extends through fifty pages. It opens with an epitome of the history of Masonry in
Kicbigan, running back over a period of one hundred and twenty-four yea!'B. It gives
a brief statement of the attempts made to establish Grand Lodges prior to the present one. In September, 18i4', representatives from the four Lodges then existing
met in Detroit and organized the present Gra.nd Lodge. From the eventful beginning
with its four Lodges in 18", the Grand Lodge bas increased almost a bnndred fold,
We would be pleased to cull many of the pleasant and instructive utterances of the
Grand Master npon the subject of Masonry, but our space forbids.
Bro. HATHEWAY very justly condemns the custom prevailing in many of our new
fraternal societies of crowding themselves to the front at Masonic funerals, expecting
to be allowed to appoint pall bearers and take prominent places in the procession,

holds that it is not the duty of a Grand Master to answer any or all questions propounded to him by officers or other members of Lodges, but that all questions
should be presented to the Masters of the Lodges; that it is for them to consider and decide such questions in the first instance; and that their rulings should
be the law in the case, subject to the right of appeal to the Grand Master. He

His views on the "saloon question" are so eminently proper that we make no
apology for giving them in full:Masnnry inculcates temperance as also other virtues. It has continued to do
so for centuries, and yet its Lodges never were temperance societies according to
the common acceptation of that term at the present day. It re'JOgllizes the moral
accountability of nian. It forbids drunkenness in its members, and will expel from
all its rights and privileges those who habitually violate the inhibition. Is it
necessary that it should go any further? 'fhis subject has of late been agitated in
some of the Grand Lodges, and in turn the Grand Lodges have themselves beliln
agitated. If legislation is neceRsary upon the subject, what shall it be? Shall it
be aimed at him who sells the intoxicant, or against him who 11ses it to excess? Or
shall it be aimed at both? And if aimed at the dealer alone. to what extent shall
it go? Shall it reach the maBufacturer, the jobber, the wholesale dealer and the
druggist, or shall it reach the retailer (saloon-keeper) alone? These questions are
certainly worthy of consideration if there is to be any well considered legislative
action taken. For my part, I have a pretty well settled conviction which I think
is as broad as tlie subject itself. I hold that the man who impairs his faculties and
debases his manhood by the excessive use of intoxicating liquors is, before Gon and
among men, the principal Binner; and that he who furnishes the liquor is only an
llUomplice, an aider and abettor. To hold otherwise is to scatter the doct~ne of
the moral accountability of man to the four winds. Therefore, whenever it shall
be d~med necessary th!'t any action ~hall be taken upon th~ subject by this Grand
Lod~, I only ask that it be not hastily done, but well considered ; and that it be
,done ma true Masonic spirit, and in accordance with trne Masonic principles.
Hasty legislation receives very appropriate attention ; the suggestions of the

suit other Grand Lodges as well as that of Minnesota :I further recommend that hereafte; the Grand Lodge take such time as, by
proper diligence and industry, it shall be enabled to perform its work in a considerate !lDd business-like manner, whether that time shall be one, two or three days.

The Address of the Grand Master is a purely business paper. Much of it is
composed of the correspondence between himself and brethren of various Lodgea
in the J uriadiction on questions arising in the management of their affairs. The
Grand Master regrets his inability to report a general revival of mterest all along
the line, but thinks that no ground h&e been lost during the year.
The matter of joint occupancy of halls seems to be a fruitful source of trouble in
this Jurisdiction. The Grand Master suggests that the law should be so amended
as to prohibit Lodges from renting their halls to political or religious societies, and
as to allow them the exercise of their own judgment in reference to renting them
to other societies.
Several dispensations had been iseued for the formation of new Lodges, and for
"the re vi val of some that were so nearly dead that it took a dispensation to revive
them." The " revival " of a Lodge by dispeneation is something new to us. The
Grand Master recites the case of Tlunruutmlm Lodge, No. 124. It appears that the
charter of this Lodge had been arrested by the Grand Lodge in 1879. Several
members thereof, in April, 1887, petitioned the Grand Master for the restoration
of its charter. The request of the petitioners was granted, and subsequently a
question arose &e to the right of the Lodge to entertain fietitions for affiliation.
The Grand M&eter decided that, as the Lodge had been reviml by dispensation, it
was competent for it to perform the functions of a regular Lodge. The Chairman
of the Law Committee, to whom the Grand Master submitted the matter, expressed
it &e his opinion that the Grand Master " had made too much law in the case of
2'/umuut<n11n ;" and that, as the charter had been arrested by the Grand Lodge, he
had very grave doubts as to thA power of the Grand Master to authorize such
Lodge to resume work at all. Whereupon the Grand Master recalled his authority
to Thomastoum Lodge to receive petitions for affiliation, but took issue as to the
right to authorize the Lodge to resume work at all, and says that he h&e always
believed in the doctrine "that the Grand Master is amenable to no law ; that he is
not only the executor of the law, but is a law unto himself;" and that "there is
but one thing that a Grand Master cannot do in the exercise of his authority over
the Cratt, and that is, to make innovations upon the body of Masonry." The Grand
LodgP., we are pleased to note, expressed the opinion that " raising the dead" is not
one of the powers that belong to a Grand Master.
Here is another case of "prerogative ." The Grand Lecturer had asked the
Grand Master for an expression of his views as to whether the Grand Lecturer is
or is not the Custodian of the Work, and whether he is authorized to change its
language where such change would be a manifest improvement . 'fo this query the
Grand Master replied in the affirmative, The Grand Lodge very properly disapproved this decision, the Committee on Law remarking that the " Grand Lecturer's
duty is to dispense the Work and Lectures &e adopted and authorized by the Grand
Lodge." We remark that such decisions are the natural fruitage of a doctrine so
repugnant to all the usages and sentiments of our age as is that of the "prerogatives." It appears strange to us that, in our times, we should find any advocate of
the doctrine that any one can be invested with greater powers than the power which
made him.
The Grand Master thus expr08868 hi111B6lf relative to a General Masonic Convention, and we incline to think that he is about right : But human nature is so prone to reach out after the grandiloquen t, and the
American's mind so naturally hankers after humbugs, that it would take but one
1/.11 two gatherings of this sort to lay an egg which, if hatched out, would produce a
General Grand Lodge.

Our own effort is praised in very flattering terms. It is encouraging to receive
oommendation from one poaaeeaed of so great experience in this work. Our brother
joins iBBue with us on the qualification of applicants for the mysteries of Masonry.
Our opinions on this subject have been frequently expressed, and we see l\o cause
to alter anything that we may have said. We never did believe, and we do not
now believe, that the Constitutions of Grand Lodges or the Ancient Charges ever
meant thats.candidate should be phyaicelly perfect. The authors of these, we are
fain to believe, knew well that physical perfection is a physical impossibility. We
are not a little surpriRed that our brethren of Mississippi are such sticklers for
physical perfection, whilst at the same time willing to admit to membership those
who are simply able to write their names, and read by spelling out their words. A
miBBing finger, or even a miBBing eye, would not be, in our opinion, half so great a
defect as missing intelligence, or miBBing means for gaining and imparting intelligence. We are not a believer iu cleanliness of the outside of the platter, while the
inside is full of all manner of uncleanness. We do believe in a reasonable approach
to human perfection physically, morally and intellectually; and we think that this
is about what the Constitutions and Charges mean, else they demand impoBSibilities.
We do not believe that the laws of Masonry are, ..r ought to be, like those of the
Medea and Persians; on the contrary, they have changed, and must necessarily
change to suit the wants of an ever-chan11ing humanity. The great truths of
Masonry are unchanging, and should be handed down from generation to generation with all the purity that characterizes truth.
If our brother believes, as we infer he does, that brethren maimed after receiving the first, or the first and second degrees, have the right to advance, his duty is
plain-he himself should exercise the fortitude neceBSary to bring such a matter to
the attention of his Grand JJodge. We deem it to be one of the du~ies and prerogatives of Correspondents to point out what in their opinion may be unjust or
nowise. We propose always to do so, and we profess a profound admiration for
thoee who do, even though we may differ from their views.
We would be greatly pleased to follow our brother further, and reproduce many
of the good things which we find in this excel.lent rep41rt; but our limit has been
reached, and we must pass on.

ant episode :In surrendering the gavel to his successor, the retiring Grand Master, Bro. WoBD,

.-ndidatee for initiation, being of eupreme importance, demands the moet thoroUffh
iJlvestigation ; this is especi1<lly true in large cities, where the candidate is quite
frequently a etranl{er to a majority of the Lodge.
The Grand Master had visited during the year almost one-third of the Lodges of
the State, and properly remarks that the importance of officio.I visitations cannot be
easily overrated. He recommended that the law be so amended as to require a petition for a new Lodge to be signed hy twenty resident Master Masone, instead of eight,
as at present. The Committee on J urieprudence, however, reported adversely, and
the recomme11dation was not adopted. We are of opinion that there is wisdom in
the recommendation of the Grand Master. In most of the Jurisdictions Lodges
multiply too rapidly, and many of these Lodgea jll8t barely exist. A Lodge should
not be instituted in any place without sufficient guarantee that it will have abundant material to draw upon, and a revenue sufficient to meet all demands for charity
and necessary expenses. California requires the signatures of at least twelve Master
Masone, and we think that such number even is perhaps too few.
The Grand Master bestows very just commendation upon the excellent Grand
Secretary, Bro. BowEN, for the faithfulneBS with which he had devoted himself to
the discharge of hie duties. We note that through hie zeal the Lodges are induced
to do as in our own Jurisdiction-l!e nd in their reports in due season. All but one
in Nebraska had been on time, and that one was only n few days behind. Having
attained this standard of promptness, there will not be much likelihood of their
bein~ delinquent in future. The recommendation of the Grand Master that the
salary of the Grand Secretary be increased resulted in an addition of $500, making
hie remuneration for a vast amount of work $1,500-much leBB than it should be.
The Commission on the Nebraska Masonic Home, appointed at the last Annual
Communic,.tion, made an elaborate report, which was adopted by the Grand Lodge.
We give its concluding paragraph:Your Commission would recommend that there be organized a corporation to be
called the Nebraska Masonic Home, the object of which Rhoulrl be to extend aid
and comfort to poor and dietreBBed Masone and their families or their widows and
orphans. Such a corporation to have an authorized capital of $500,000, to be divided
into $5,000 shares of $100 each, but euch co~ration to be perfected only when the
Grand Lodge, the subordinate Lodges, and mdividual Masone had subscribed for
500 shares of the capital stock, or so much thereof as in the judgment of the Commission be necessary. Each shareholder in the corpnration, in all its meetings, to be
entitled to one vote for each fully paid-up share of $100 owned by such shareholder.
Your CommiBBion cannot he.re enter into full details of what might be found necessary and essenti~l in perfecting the organization, and can indicate only in a!eneral
way the plan of organization, which would be that, besides the grounds an buildings suitable for present needs, which your Commission does not doubt would be
furnished by the locality in which it might be located, in addition thereto the fund
derived from &Ubecriptions to the capital stock should be permanently invested,
and its income alone used in aupport of the institution. In tbiR general view your
Commission would recommend the al?pointment of a committee of seven melllbere
to prPpare a plan for an organization m the line herein indicated, to solicit subscriptions to the capital stock of the same fr9m the Lodges and from Masone, to invite
proJ?Ol!ale from the different towns and cities in the State for the location of such
mat1tution, and that this Grand Lodge subscribe to such capital stock the sum of
'6,000, heretofore set apart to that purpose, which shall be kept at interest, and
when the necessary stock for ori1anization shall have been subscribed, that the
ltockholders be convened for the purpose of considering the different propositions
for the location of the institution.
A committee appointed one year aiio to examine as to the proper word to be
used for the congregations of brethren, reported that, having gone back over one
hundred and fifty years, or to the earliest records accessible, they found the word to
be need is "Meetings," as applied to subordinate Lodges, and " Communication s,"
for Grand Lodges.

Not so m California. Election for and reception of the degreea

Bro. WAIT is not a believer in the perfect-man doctrine ; but does believe that
the •pplicant should be able to conform to the requirements of the ritual. We,
individually, think that he is right, though we know that neither hie opinions nor
ours would be approved by the able Chairman of our Committee on Jurisprudence.
Our brother thinks that when one Grand Lodge declines fraternal intercourse
with another, such action affects only the official relations of the two Grand Bodies,
and does not extend to the Masonic status of the membership of their J uriedictions.
We dissent from this view. The whole includes all the parts. When intercourse
between the Grand Bodies ie interdicted, it appears to us that it carries with it the
Interdiction of intercourse between the parts of which the Grand Bodiea are com-

posed.
.
Our Grand'Lodge holds that if a party, on a visit to another Grand Jurisdiction
for temp0rary purposes, receives the degrees of Masonry, he cannot be regarded as
a regularly made Mason until after he has applied for and been elected to membership in the Lodge nearest his place of residence.
Bro. WAIT ie eminently sound on the perpetual jurisdiction question. The following ie good common sense, plainly put :It may very well be that a young man may have fallen for a time into such
habits as not only to justify but to demand hie rejection by the Lodge of his resi.
dence; but having removed to a distant State or country he may, after the lapse of
some years, have acquired such a character as to render him eminently fit for
Masonic affiliation. Not only may this be so, but common experience justifies
the assertion that it often is so in fact. In such a case the rejecting Lodge knows
nothing of the change in the person's character, and is unfit to judge of it; besides,
it will often be the case that the membership of the latter Lod'Ie is so changed at
the time of the second application that no member knows anything of the person
or of the reasons of the rejection, and have no means of judging whether or not
usent to the candidate'd application ought to be given. As applicable to such "
case we cannot think that doctrine which would give to the rejecting Lodge per·
petual jurisdicdiction over the candidate a reasonable one.

proceedingd never seen the light.
In regard to the power of Lodges over their own funds, Bro. WAIT concurs in

use its funds for any purpose to which a majority might see fit to appropriate them,

The further we have advanced in this report the less we feel like leaving it, as it
is one of thA very best that has come under our notice. We often have occasinn to
differ in opinion with our brother. He is decidedly original, uses the scissors but
little, and reasons like one who has hia subject well in hand. We must, however,
part company; but before we do so we will say to him that he is right in suspecting
that there was more in the decision of Grand Master TINNIN relative to the retum
of fee paid on application for afliiliation . than was stated. The six month's dues
alluded to was not the affiliation fee at all, but a contribution paid by a non-affiliate
who was out of standing, for the purpose of putting himself in standing. . In California, if a non-affiliated Mason does not make application to some Lodge for membership within the period of six months, he occupies the ea.me position as one suspended
for non-payment of dues, and must pay the six month's dues to put him in standing.
He pays hie affiliation fee in addition, if one is required. The first-named payment
keeps the brother in standing for six months, and during that period he may apply
to the same Lodge, or to another Lodge, as often as he deems proper, without an
additional payment for such purpose. He may have been a non-affiliate for years,
and yet this payment puts him in standing; so that, instead of being an act of
injustice, it is one of favor to the applicant.

The logic of the above soonds to us somewhat atler this order: Any one who has

llr[asonry and all her interests would be much better comerved.

The fair held under the auspices of the "Ladies' Masonic Fair Association,"
proved a very great success, the sum realized as net proceeds having amounted to
$76,352 37. It was originally intended that this sum should be applied in extinguishment of the debt upon the Masonic Hall; but subsequently it was determined
to place it in the hands of the Grand Master, to be held until the payment of the
debt should be completed, when it is to be paid to the Trustees of the Masonic
Hall and Asylum Fund, to be devoted to the erection of the asylum. It is gratify.
ing to learn that the tremendous indebtedness of the Fraternity in New York for
their great enterprise is now reduced to less than $40, 000, and that there is no
reasonable doubt that the payment of the debt will be completed before the next
meeting of the Grand Lodge. The Grand Master and the good brethren of New
York have great reason for rejoicing in the near approach to that which has been
the goal of the Fraternity for nearly half a century. Brethren everywhere rejoice
in their rejoicing, and in the prospect that, "twelve months from to-day, the tangible and sufficient means to lay the foundation stone of the asylum, to place the
copestone upon its summit, and to complete it and pay for it, to the smallest det,illl,"
will be in possession of the Trustees. All honor to the noble women who conceived
and carried to completion so glorious an enterprise I Mainly through their instrumentality has the asylum in New Y urk for indigent Masons, their widows and
orphans, become an assured fact.

1888, are only $1,356 88, whilst those of the San Francisco Board aggregate the
sum of $11,004 61. Even our Board in Oakland expend more than the great city
of New York I We quote the following relative to the General Relief Association
of the United States:Since the organization of the General Association, there have been published,
with a full description of each, no less than five hundred and one M11:sonic frauds,
plying a profitable trade in Masonic charity'; and this notwithstanding the fact
that the Association is in its infancy, and is in receipt of information from a very
small proportion of the grand army of Masons. It does not require a strong prophetic vision to discern some portion of the incalculable good such an organization
is destined to accomplish, and the vast saving in money alone it will utimately
effect. We fraternally urge all brethren into whose hands this report may fall to
give this Association and its objects the benefit of some iiivestigation and thought,
if only to protect Lodge funds and discourage fraud.

Bro. SIMONS does not believe in Grand Lodge, or Lodge, Incorporation. We
believe with him. Nothing can be gained by incorporation, but independent sover·
eignty may be lost thereby. Title to property can be held quite as well through the
instrumentality of 'l'rustees, anll. the Lodge will be exempt from any liability of
being called to account for its Masonic doings, or the execution of its own rules and
regulations, before Ci vii Court8.
We are not a believer in the doctrine that the Tyler of a Lodge is not present
because, forsooth, he is not actually in the Lodge-room. Bro. SIMONS agrees with
the Grand Master of Illinois, and some other Jurisdictions, in the opinion that seven
Master Masons, ezclvaive of tke Tyler, must be preeent before a Lodge can be opened
in any degree. It appears to us that this is a matter which can be and ought to
be regulated by law. Our Constitution provides that no business, other than that
of charity or the conferring of degrees, can be transacted without the presence of
seven members; and the Tyler is, if a member and present, considered as one of the
seven.
We incline to agree with our brother in reference to a Masonic Convention.. All
points of Masonic law and wiage can be fully discussed and agreements reached in
our Grand Lodges, and by means of the Committees on Correepondence, in quite as
available a manner as would be possible in any General Congress. We are not in
favor of any action that may directly or indirectly lead to the formation of a
National Body.

NORTH CAROLINA~

The one hundred and first Annnal Communication of the Grand Lodge of North
Oarolina was held in the city of Raleigh, commencing on the tenth day of Jannary,
1888,-the ltf.'. W.·, CiIABLES H. ROBINSON, Grand Master,preslding,and the B.·. w;.,

the snbordinate Lodg.es, were represented.
The Address delivered by the Grand Master is brief, and is confined chiefly to
matters of local Interest. He reports a growing interest in the Order; and yet we
are at a loss ~o determine how, out of so many Lodges as are in North Carolina so
few are represented in the Grand Lodge. Four decisions are reported-all in acc~rd
with sound Masonic law and cnstom.
Six Special Communications of the Gra~d Lodge had been held during the year.
all for the pnrpolie of laying corner·stones.
The Grand Master represent8 the Orphan Asylum as "the pride and glory of the
Grand Lodge." It had enjoyed a prosperonsyear ; a greater number of children had
been cared for; and, through the liberality of the good people, the financial condition
was comfortable. The Grand Master recommended that it shonld be made the order
of the Grand Lodge that It should meet at the Asylnm on &r. JonN'B Day, in Jnne,
annually. The Grand Lodge subsequently endorsed the recommendation, and also
appropriated the snm of two thousand dollars for the support of the Asylum for the
year· From the report of the Superintendent we infer that the Oxford Orphan
Asylum belongs to, and is under the control of, the Grand Lodge ; that it receives
any class of orphans; ·and that it is largely snpported by allowance from the State,
the latter having contribnted $10,000 during the year. Two hnndred and Jllnetythree children had been provided for during the year; the total receipts had been
$19,072 91.; and everything indicates thatthe Asylnm is in a very prosperous condition.
From the Report of the Grand Secretary, Bro. BAIN, we learn that the outlook for
the Craft In North Carolina islencouraging. There had been an Increasing demand
for Masonic instruction, and the Grand Lecturers had more to do than nsnal, There
had been a net increase of about one hundred in membership, and many of the
Lodges give evidence of the beneficial eft'ects of the improved financial condition of
affairs throughout the State.
The Grand Master had issned dispensations for the formation of six new Lodges.
Several dormant or extinct Lodges had resumed work, and the Grand Secretary had
made special effort to resuscitate others. He reports that there are at least five
thousand non-affiliated Masons In the State, made so either by the disorganization of
the Lodges or by exclnsion for non· payment of does. We think this is greatly attributable to the fact that the law of North Carolina recognizes non-payment of does as a
mi.nor offense, subjecting the offender to !oss of me.mberBhip or expulsion, without the
P.nvllege of restoration except through action of the Lodge. We believe in 9Uspens1on f?r the non-payment of does from all the rightB and privileges of Masonry; bot
we thmk that the party snap ended should have the right to restore himself at any tim1r
by payment of his arrearages. Our observation leads us to the conclusion that many,
if not most, of the cases of suspension for this cause originates in the incompetency

The thirty-eighth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Oregon was
held in the city of Portland, commencing on the thirteenth day of June, 1888,the M. •• W. •, ANDREW NABBUBG, Grand Master, presiding, and the .R. '. W. '.
FRELON J, BABOOOK being Grand Secretary. Seventy-four Lodges were reprll'
eented.
A Special Communication wae held at Corvallis, on the seventeenth day of
August, 1887, for the purpose of laying the corner-stone of the State Agricultural
College.
Aleo, one at Eugene City, on the twenty-ninth day of February, 1888, for the
purpose of dedicating the Hall of E'U(Jl!fTle Olly Lodge, No. 11.
The Grand Master congratulates hie brethren upon the prosperous condition of
Masonry in the Jurisdiction, and upon the advancement which the State bae made
during the year in all branches of industry. He represents the influx of immigration as bavinir never been, in the history of the State, greater than within the past
twelve months; and eaye that before long all the available land in the northwest
will be occupied. He alludes to the driving of the last spike in the Oregon and
California Railroad as one of the most important events, inasmuch as it furnishes
another competing transcontinental line. Two new Lodges had been constituted,
and dispensations had been granted for the formation of three others.
Several decieione are reported- all of a local character except the laet, to the
effect that a Lodge is at all times in committee of the whole, when convened, and
that therefore it is imposaible to resolve itself into such committee. We are not
quite prepared to assent to this proposition. We are unable to see why a Lodge
of Masone may not temporarily absolve itself from the rigor of rules, in order that
greater latitude or freedom in the consideration of any subject may be bad. It is
true a Lodge may informally diecues a proposition; but this ie practically equiva·
lent to the other form of procedure. We are aware, too, that the Lodge while
convened must be at all times under the direct control of the Master, and that par·
liamentary rules do not always llpply as in deliberative bodies. We reserve our
opinion upon the queetien until we are better informed therean.
The net reeourcee of the Masonic Building Aeeociation are $67,495 60-a good
showing. There are twelve hundred shares of the capital stock; of these the Grand
Lodge owns eight hundred and eleven.
In reference to the matter of the claim of the Ma.sonic Board of Relief of San
Francisco against Lyom Lodge, No. 29, for moneys expended by the former for the
relief of the widow of a member of said Lodge, the Committee on Jurisprudence
expreeeed the opinion that the Grand Lodlfe should take no action. We are of the
opinion, and always have been, that a Lodge should not permit the poor and needy
of its members to become a burden upon other Lodges, or other Masoue, and we
are further of the opinion that a Grand Lodge should not permit this on the part
of any of its subordinates.
A report of the same committee recommending that all Masonic communication
with the members of Hiram Lodge, No. l, of Connecticut, should be interdicted
unless said members produce a certificate of standing as regular Masone, was
adopted.

suit the progress of humanity. Its great teachinp-its truths-will never change.
Truth is unchangeable. Bro. CHADWIOK claims that truths come to men, other
than from human source, as fast as they are capable of receiving them, and frankly
admits that his views on the resurrection were largely influenced by his readings.
.Tust so; his Masonic notions have been framed in the same way. But then, we
think that in Masonic matters he got hold of the wrong readings. We hope to see
him converted from the error of his opinions. "The world moves."
California proceedings qf 1887 receive pleasant notice. The Address of Grand
Master ATKINSON is liberally quoted from. The " veteran Secretary " and our
worthy Chairman of Correspondence receive deserved mention. Of the Jurisdiction Bro. CB!ADWIOK says: " There is but one California Jurisdiction in the
Masonic universe."
Our brother seems to have fallen into error in reference to the decision of Grand
Master TINNIN relative to the retum of the fee for affiliation. If the applicant is
rejected the affiliation fee is always returned; but the six-dollar contribution,
required to place the brother applying in good standing, is not returned. Bro.
TINNIN'S decision related to this latter. This latter fee, or contribution, is required
only from unaffiliated Masons who have permitted themselves to remain for a period
of more than six months unaffiliated. If the applicant is rejected, that fee (not the
affiliation fee) keeps him in standing for a period of six months, during which time
he can apply to the same Lodge or any other Lodge by paying the affiliation tee
alone.
As to objection to advancement, we propose to let Bro. CHADWICK refute himself. We quote from what he has to say under New Hampshire, and also from that
under Texas:All to the objection to advancement, Bro. WAIT agrees with Bro. ANDERSON
that an objection should be made the object of inquiry. We hold that it was a
wise provision that objection to advancement should not be made the sql>ject of
inquiry; that it is presumed that an objection, when made, is so made by a Mason
and on purely Masonic grounds; and that the person making the objection cannot be
accused nor compelled to give his reasons for the objection. There can be no trial
between the objector and the person objected to. That would bring discord that
the rule we state does prevent. If objections are made that are not Masonic, that
cannot be known only by the voluntary statement of the objector. But Masonry
presumes that Masons will be Masons always, in the admission and advancement
of candidates, and this cannot be questioned, unleBB the objector voluntarily makes
his reasons known. This is the safest rule. Never do awav with a right1 because
it may sometime be abused, or supposed to be. We regret that our brotner away
up in the northeast comer, and our brother way down in the southwest corner of
this great country, cannot see as we do on this point. Like the old Granite State,
we are there to stay, waiving no part of our esteem for Bros. ANDERSON and WAIT.
An entered apprentice, who had been elected to receive the Fellow Craft Degree,
was a victim of a railroad accident, resulting in a partial stiffness of the hip, but it
was thought he could be "placed in position." The Grand Master decided that he
conld not be advanced in that condition. Thie seems a very hard decision. If the
brother was entitled to advance when he was elected, the right to advance dates at
the election and not at the time of the accident. We believe the candidate should
advance, and must say that it seems to us groBB injustice to not i;iermit him to do so.
When the Grand Master promulgates a decision "openly and above board," it
is a "very hard 'lieuision; •; but when a brother makes the decision, or urges the
objection, it must not be asked whether he has any reason for such objection or not.
We do not see the conslBtenoy.

The reports of the accounting officers present a very fair condition of Grand

The Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge was held in the city of Philadelphia on the twenty-seventh day of December, 1887,-the M. ·. W. ·. JOSEPH
EIOHBAUH, Grand Master, presiding, and the R. ·. w. ·. MICHAEL NISBET being
Grand Secretary. Sixty Lodges were represented.
The Address of the Grand Master relates to matters of a purely local character,
and is a record of much official work faithfully executed. Pennsylvania is a very
large and flourishing Jurisdiction, and the positions in it, particularly those of
Grand Master and Graed Secretary, are by no means sinecures.
Our well known brother, Past Grand Master RIOHABD VAUX presented a Ion(!',
interesting, and able review of the proceedings of fifty-one sister Jurisdictions.
Bro. VA ux wields the pen of a ready writer ; his utterances are those of one who
knows whereof he affirms; and, although we cannot accept all his opinions as in
accord with those of many others, we cannot but admire the cogency and skill with
which he presents them. He is pertinacious and earnest. He considers the work
of a Correspondent to be a serious duty, and be goes about the discharge of that
duty in a manner altogether worthy of the position. He is devoted, as is his Jurisdiction, to t.he preservation and the perpetuation of the great principles of Freemasonry, and hence is earnest in his "efforts to secure their unaltered, unchanged
form, and the fullness of their eternal spirit;" as thus : The forms of Masonry are instinctively a.live. They contain the traditions of
ages; the concretion of the subjective thought of generations; the learning of cen·
turies; the aspirations of immortal souls; the heart-thrnb.. of the faith of multitudPs of men seeking lighten the darkneBB of cycles of time, when esoteric teachiogs were concealed in forms illumined by the spirit of a revealed knowledge which
only the initiated could under11tandingly be taught. It is thus that Freemasonry
has not perished.
Nature, from the last day of creation, clothed in forms the germs of life. Thus
came the corn, the oil, and the wine, each in its appointed order. So the forms
with which Masonic knowledge was first enveiled are now the depositories of the
gerru of that fruit which are accepted as it• essential verities.
Efforts to preserve these forms from the ruthleBS as•aults of ignorance. and the
cn1de inventions of those who claim to be wiser in their generations than "the
children of light," are demanded of the true Mason. The imperative obligation
rests on those who are capable of discharging it. We owe the past all our knowledgA. We owe the future its possession. We owe ourselves the verdict of virtue
and courage which transmits it.
The eternal years of Gon characterize principles ; forms of expressing these
principles, like a.II other human inventions, must of necessity change. The times
have changed ; all things, except truth, have changed. Principles are emanations
from the eternal sourre of truth. The teachings of Masonry are the same yesterday, to-day, and forever. The vehicles of truth have undel'R'one, and will undergo,
the mutations incident to changed humanity. The forms in which Masonic truth
was first enniled have been, and must of necessity still be, subject to change.
These forms are still the depositories of the sublime teachings of our beloved Order.
Bro. VAUX regards the Grand Lodge of Quebec as being de jure and de facto a
Grand Lodge. He considers that to assert its sovereignty it must affirm its character, and that the only course left it is to dissolve relations with England and to
declare its Lodges clandestine so far as Quebec's authority extends. Of the trouble
in Connectic)lt he thus forcibly and properly speaks :Tampering with error is encouraging its growth. Cowardice, that enfeebles
vigorous and prompt treatment of heresy, false doctrine, and schism, gives strength
to them. It invites the ill-disposed to unite in aggression for the sake of the
notoriety of combataots. This 18 one of the pbasee of hwnan nature that the principles and teachings of Freemasonry should eradicate.

In Freemasonry resistance to, and disobedience of, lawful Masonic authorit7
cannot be tolerated. There can be no sufficient justification for either. It 1s
Impossible in the nature of things in Masonry. Both, or either, may be attempted,
but the Masouic destruction of the agitators is sure. It has been tried heretofore.
What has been the result?
We feel at liberty to agree to the request of Connecticut. The interdict against
this Lodge, Hiram, No. 1, so called, is recommended. . Our fraternal relations with
Connecticut permit no other course. The just conception of the integrity of Grand
Lodge authority and its due preservation demand this action.
Having given bis views relative to a General Convention of Representatives,
such as that which assembled in Illinois, he eays, and we entirely coincide with
him:The corollary from tht>se views, if they are worthy of consideration at all, must
be that all meetings of Masons, outside of the explicit limitations on Masonic action,
is without authority; at variance with sound Maaonic teachings; su~gestive of
doubtful results; inoperative for good; useless except to create antagonisms; liable
to be misunder•tood; likely to be subversive of the authority of Grand Lodge government ; tending to the centralization of infiuenoes over the sovereign rigbts of
Grand Lodges; and fruitful in dissensions.
California for 1886, and the Report of Bro. HILL for 1887, (advance sheets of the
latter having been received,) receive very complimentary notice. He quotes freely
from the Address of Grand Master TINNIN. He endorses Bro. TINNIN's action in
granting a dispensation to confer the degrees of Masonry upon an applicant without reffrence of his petition to a committee, remarking that "this is inclining to
the 'making on sight' principle, but yet entirely proper." California does not
believe in the ·making of Masons at sight, and dispensations for this purpose do
not obtain. The "making on sight" principle invests the Grand Master with
power to make Masons without any action of a Lodge. In California the Grand
Master cannot invest one with the degrees of Masonry without the unanimous consent of the Lodge, expressed in the usual form. He is authorized by law, however,
to grant a dispensation for the conferring of the d!lir0eS without the usual reference
to a Committee of Investigation, when, in bis judgment good reasons exist there·
for, and upon application by the Lodge, made by its unanimous vote.

Bro. VAUX is stronaiy opposed to public installations, and considers them to be
