dignity and importance, we can readily understand how both profanes and Masone
may be favorably .and beneficially impressed. We do not believe in parading broad
phylacteries, that we may be seen of men, any more than does Bro. VAUX; but
we do believe that, if Masons would meet in social intercourse with the families and
the friends of one another more frequently than they do, Masonry and manhood
would both be the gainers. There are some kinds of work which Masonic Lodges
may do in public without being "duly tyled." Installation of officers is merely a
ceremony, as the layin1r of comer-stones or the performing of the funeral service is;
and we confess that we are unable to see how public installation can render any
action of a Lodge void. There is no esoteric work in any of these ceremonies, and
we are of opinion that no harm results from parmitting the public to ~itness any
parts of the exoteric.
We are not a little surprised that one so well versed in the moral teachings of
Masonry as is Bro. VAUX, should give expression to a sentiment like this-'' Profane laws cannot make Masonic crimes." .A brother Mason by false statements
induces another to become surety on his bond, and subsequently fraudulently appropriates to his own use fifteen or twenty thousand dollars of money held by him in
trust for the uses and benefit of others. Bro. VAUX thinks that such brother has
committed no Masonic offense, and that he should be punished by the profane law
which he has violated; and adds that "if he is by law convicted, then the Lodge
might well expel him as unworthy of the membership of a Masonic Lodge." Truth,
honor, honesty, fidelity, probity-all Masonic essentials, as Bro. VAUX admitshave heen found wanting, and yet the·brother has committed no Masonic offense
unless ccmvicted by TMo. What if such a party escapes beyond the reach of the profane law? Shall Masonry tolerate him, and carry his name on her honorable roll ?
There are so many interesting matt.en in this able Report that we feel very loth
to leave it; but time and space forbid furtlier notice.

The thirteenth .Annual Communication of thti Grand Lodge of Prince Edward
Island was held in the city of Charlottetown on the twenty-sixth day of June,
1888,-the M.-. W.·. JOHN YBO, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.· B.

Everything connected with the present Communication is characterized by a
brevity that is refreshing ; the Jurisdiction is brief ; the session was brief ; the
Grand Master's Address is brief, and to the point.
We have said that everything is brief; we are in error. We presume that not
another Grand Lodge on this cont~ent can show as long a term of continuous and
faithful service on the part of a Grand Master as can Prince Edward Island. For
thirteen years Bro. Y BO has presided over the interests of Masonry in this J nrisdiction with such fidelity and ability that he has become so endeared to his brethren
that they will not let him go. He asked the Grand Lodge to relieve him, but they
would not; and he still retains the place which he has held from the organization of
the Grand Lodge to the present. No electioneering for Grand Master troubles the
brethren of Prince .Edward Island; the office sought the man, and, having found
him, it continues to hold him. It is well.
The Report of the Grand Secretary, Bro. HmGe, is also a very brief paper. He
reports a gratifying increase in the membership of the Lodges. There is no Report
on Correspondence; but we may hope to have one next time.

The Grand Lodge adopted a resolution to the effect that it would join the General Masonic Relief Association of the United States and Canada. Perhaps it
would be well that all the Grand Lodges should join an association which appears
to be so well calculated to protect their subordinate Lodges from the impostors and
Masonic tramps that infest the country, robbing the Lodges of means that might
be otherwise appropriated in legitimate charity.
Bro. E. D. T. CHAMBERS presented a very excellent Report on Correspondence.
California comes in for a liberal share in the review, and a very courteous one.
We quote the following from what our brother says relative to our Boards of
Relief:.All honor to the Masonry down by the Golden Gate, say we. The eloquence
with which it speaks is that of men and of angels, and, true to the device at the base
of its seal where faith, hope and charity are symbolically represented, it gives
practical illustration of its faith and hope that "the ~test of these is charity."
Our Grand Lodge is in perfect accord with other Grand Lodges so far as the
doctrine of exclusive jurisdiction is concerned, but is of the opinion th.at Quebec
was bound by the agreement between Canada and England. After mature con.
sideration of this subject, we very frankly admit that we are now inclined to the
same opinion. '"e hope to see the vexed question amicably and properly settled.
The views of Bro. CHAMBERS are good and sound, and he possesses one trait
that rather pleases us-he has opinions of hie own, and expresses them in positive,
yet courteous and fraternal manner. We wish such reports "could be placed in the
hands of all our brethren.

Rhode Island believes in "striking from the roll" for non-payment of dues.
We do not. There should be a sanction connected with every law, and that sanction should be strictly enforced. Treat all members with charity; but when a
member, either by carelessness or willfulness, permits himself to violate the law
relative to the payment of dues, cut him olf from privileges, but let his dues continue as a species of penalty for violation of the law.

Masons or others who consider work festivity. We infer from the record which

On this occasion the Senior Grand Warden delivered a very able address eulogistic of Masonry. Had we the space we would quote several passages; that
lacking, only tbe following beautiful and instructive paragraph is selected:The ceremonies made use of might, to the careless observer, seem trivial and
insignificant; but when considered with a full understanding of their symbolism,
they are well laden with significant meaning, and teach important lessons.
The strine .represents the foundation or corner-stone of human knowledge.
Having all its sides of equal length it forms a square, and is an emblem of morality.
It teaches us that we should endeavor, by diligently observing the precepts of ruorallty and virtue, to so conduct ourselves here that we may become square stones in
that spiritual building-" that house not made with hands." As it is also solid, it
forms a cube as well, which comprehends the whole and symbolizes truth. It is
Wrought from durable and lasting material, and is thus emblematical of eternal
life, to which the paths of morality and truth faithfully pursued will eventually
lead us all. When placed in position it is tried by tho11e builders' instrument&-

The question "How shall we dispose of non-affiliates?" was finally disposed of
by the adoption of the following :Non-affiliates.-Subordinate Lodges will not bury voluntary non-affiliates with
Masonic honors, unless two-thirds of the members present, at a meeting called for
that purpose, shall vote so to do.
Each non-affiliated Master Mason is required to pay, on or before the first day
of December each year, a·contribution fee of two dollars and twenty-five cents to
the ~ecretary of the Lodge within the jurisdiction of which he resides; or should
he live where two or more Lodges have concurrent jurisdiction, he shall pay to the
nearest Secretary. For the collection of this fee the Secretary shall have twentyfi~e cents, and the remainder the Secretary shall forward to the Grand Secretary,
with the annual dues from the Lodge, and the same shall b3 paid over to the Grand
Treasurer, and designat<>d the "Widows' and Orphans' Fund," to be disposed of in
such manner as the Grand Lodge shall from time to time direct, provided it is for the
benefit of the widows and orphans of worthy deceased Master Masons. Those
f~ili!'.lg to pay. said contri~ution fe~ shall be dealt .with by th!? Lodges in tbe juriedict10n of which they reside as said Lodges do with their delinquent members.
This may be all very well, but we prefer the plan adopted in California ; we
consider it better adapted to make these non-affiliates "come to time," or otherwise to be cut off from all rights and privileges.
The Grand Lodge of Tennessee adopted a resolution, or edict, to the effect that
the Committee on J urieprudence should consist of all the Past Grand Masters ;
consequently, this committee for the present year is composed of twenty persons.
It is said that in the multitudA of counselors there is wisdom, hence we may reasonably look to Tennessee for some very luciferous decisions on Masonic law and
usage ; but we rather doubt the expediency of such a oomlllittee.

TEXAS.
The fifty-second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Texas was held
in the city of Houston, commencing on the thirteenth day of December, 1887,-the
M.·. W. ·• A. J. RosE, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W. •. T. W. HUDSON
being Grand Secretary. Two hundred and thirty-nine Lodges were represented.
The first thing that arrests our attention, as we take down the volume containing
tile proceedings of this Grand Lodge, is its very ponderous appearance. Like Texas,
there is a "heap of it." It is so "fat" that we kept on, like King AGRIPPA, putting
off the review of it "until a more convenient season ; " but at last we have determined to gird up our loina and "go for it." We will doubtless find it, like Texas,
sunshiny, pleasant, and interesting.
In his exordium to a long, able, and interesting Address, the Grand Master congratulates his breth.ren upon the general prosperity of the Craft in Texas. It is
pleasing to learn that a large portion of the Lodges own their halls, and that they
are in a good financial condition. The Graqd Master does not predicate his report of
prosperity on a great increase of membership, rightly remarking that such increase
is no positive evidence of prosperity, and that, whilst increase in membership of the
proper material is desirable, the best evidences of prosperity are to be found in the
interest manifested by the officers and members.
The Grand Master reports the appointment of Past Grand Master N. GREENE

California, and that of Past Grand Master THOMAS M. MATTHEWS by the Grand
Master of California, near the Grand Lodge of Texas.
Dispensations had been granted for the formation of four new Lodges. Several
Lodges had applied to the Grand Master for authority to call upon sister Lodges
for aid to build halls ; but this authority he had in all cases declined to grant.

UTAH.

The eeventeenth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Utah was held
in the city of Salt Lake, commencing on the seventeenth day of January, 1888,the M. ', W. '.PARLEY LYCURGUS WILLIA.MB, Grand Master, presiding, and theR. ',
W. ', CHRISTOPHER DI&HL being Grand Secretary. All the Lodges-eight in num~
ber-were represented. There were also present many Past Grand Officers, and
the Representatives of thirty-two Grand Jurisdictions. We note also the presence
of one whose name ie familiar to many of the brethren of California-oar genial
friend and brother, the M. '. W. ·.Grand MB'!ter of Masons in Nevada, .ADOLPHUS
LKIGH FITZGERALD.
The Addrees of the Grand Master forms a very interesting resume of the year's
official acts. In becoming terms Bro. WILLIA.MS pays tribute of respect to the
memory and worth of two prominent brethren who had, during the year, been called
to pass to the silent beyond-Bro. OR&D F. STRICKLAND, the first Grand Master of
the Grand Lodge of Utah, and Bro. JOHN A. HuNT&R who, for several years, had
occupied the position of Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of that Territory.
The controversy between the Grand Lodge of Utah and that of Nevada, in reference to the case of Bro. M. D. FoLEY, still remained unsettled. Efforts had been
made on the part of Utah to have the matter properly adjusted, but without effect;
and at the present Communication a Commiesion of three special Representatives
from the Gra'ld Lodge of Nevada were present in the hope that an amicable adjustment might be made of the unpleasant trouble. We are pleaeed to be able to report
that the Joint Commission reported an amicable settlement; which report was
unanimously adopted, and peace and harmony again reigns between these Grand
Lodges. The finding of the Commission was to the effect that the said FOLEY was
then, and had been for many years, a citizen of Nevada, residing at Eureka ; that
he bad been repeatedly objected to by Eureka Lodge, No. 16, of Nevada; and had
then gone to Salt Lake City and received the degrees in Wasatch Lodge, which
was an invasion of, and trespaBS upon, the Jurisdiction of Nevada. They further
found that Wasatch Lodge, under a misapprehension of the facts, had acted in good
faith, and without any intention of wrong to a neighboring Jurisdiction. They therefore recommended that the Grand I.odge of Utah recognize and respect the edict
of suspension declared by the Grand Lodge of Kevada against Mr. FOLEY, and that
the control of his status and standing as a Mason be left with that Grand Lodge.
Thus ended a very unpleasant matter, and so "all's well that ends well."
The Grand Master was pleased to report that Utah lives in harmony with all
other Grand Lodges throughout the world.
Attention was called by the Grand Master to the matter of Hi.mm Lodge, No.
1, of Connecticut, and a resolution was afterwards adopted, interdicting all Masonic
communication with said Hin-am Lodge, No. 1, or with any member thereof, unless
such member firet produce a certificate from the Grand Secretary of Connecticut,
showing that he is a Master Mason in good standing and loyal to said Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master had been importuned to give opinions on matters so utterly
frivolous as to .be almost ridiculous. We quote what Bro. WILLIA.MB has to say of
such ca.see:In answering the parties soliciting an opinion in these instances, I admoniiihed ·
them that they should desist from writing on such frivolous topics, or attempt to
bring them into prominence, or make them subjects of controversy. I mention this
not so much for my own &S for the benefit of my successors. Some good-meaning
people are so constituted that, with the slightest encouragement, they will insist
upon making mountains out of mole hills, and create an irritation and discord
where there is no real cause for complaint.

The ninety-filth Annnal Communication of the Grand Lodge of Vermont was held
in the city of Burlington, commencing on the thirteenth day of Jone, 1888,-the M. ••
W.·. ALFBED A. HALL, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. LAVANT M. READ
being Grand Secretary. Eighty-six Lodges were represented.
The Address of the Grand .Master is excellent in all respects. He gives pleasant
welcome to his brethren from all parts of the State, in reciprocation of the cordial
and fraternal greetings be himself had received, and in recognition of the loyalty
everywhere shown to the Grand Lodge.
The year had been a prosperous one. Great desire had been shown not only to
excel in ritualistic work, but to become better acquainted with the law and with the
philosophy of .Masonry. The following in this connection is applicable everywhere :My brother, if yonr Lodge has been careless in this respect; If Its membership is
looked upon as of donbtful character; if the beat men in yonr society feel t~at _by
attending your meetings or associating with some of the members they are brmgmg
upon themselves the reproach of the world; it is ti~e tha~ earnest, honest effort _was
exhibited. It is your dnty to reclaim the erring if possible; make your meetn~gs
models of decorum• select the best material presented, and purge It of everythmg
that is unbecoming ~society founded upon the grand principles of Truth and Justice,
Virtue and Morality.
The Grand Master announced the death of Past Grand Master Lucrns C. BUTLBB,
Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Oorrespondence, and paid proper tribute to
his memory and worth.
Fourteen decisions are reported. Most of these are local in character; those that
are general are all, in our opinion, in accordance with Masonic usage and justice,
except the following :After a ballot has been declared and the Lodge closed, the Grand .Master has no
power, upon the application of the party or parties claiming .to have c!Lst the blac!'
ball or balls, to order the ballot op.ened, or grant a dispens.ation allowmg the petitioner to renew his petition without waiting the time pres0r1bed by the by-laws.
We do n~t think it right or just to make a petitioner wait the time prescribed by
the by-laws, when an adverse ballot has been cast and the party casting it makes
allegation of mistake or error in so casting It. Wrong or mistake that causes harm
should be remedied without fail and as speedily as possible.
Grand Master HA.LL very properly considers that a person who can neither read
nor write is not eligible to receive the degrees of Masonry; he regards mental and

We take pleasure in quoting the following paragraphs from the Grand Master's
peroration :When as Masons we study more and li1'B better we shall find that Masonry will be
conceded all that its most enthusiastic admirers claim for it.
Glean in the journey of life from the fields through which you pass, from the waysides and halting places, all that is true and pure, noble and good ; all that adds to
the stature of perfect manhood ; oultivate the virtues and shun the vices; then in
your lives will be exemplified the tenets of .Masonry.
We should count it a privilege to bave part in carrying on this work in an age of
intelligence and usefulness.
Finally, in the beautiful language of another, I exhort yon to "take your place in
the onward march of history. Let the glory of the morning rest upon your lives·
learn and change ; turn and overturn; bot al ways see to it that the sunshine chase~
\he shadows, and that the transition be ever from b&d to good and from good to better."
The Report of the Grand Secretary, Bro. LA.vil"T M. Rlill, informs us that
the institution of Freemasonry was never in a more ftonrisbing condition than at the
present time. He had the pleasnr11.and extreme satisfaction of announcing to the

Lodges. This unprecedented record had been accomplished solely by the exercise
of his " powers of persuasion," or which latter he remarks that he shall have a good
opinion hereafter. We think that be Is entitled to have this good opinion, and we
congratulate the Grand Lodge npon bis success.

From the report of the Trustees of the Masonic Temple Aasociation we infer
that that organization is in a most fl.atteringly healthful condition. The present
estimated value of the property of the Aasociation is $136,289 50. The Board is

The A.ddreBB of the Grand :Master is an excellent paper. He pays to the memory

The Grand Master considers the prerogative claimed by Grand

:Masters to confer
degrees regardless of time to be all wrong, and that it should never be exercised
except in the case of most urgent necessity. Nine decisionsare reported. We quote
the fourth:4. Can a brother be installed into an elected office while charges of onmasonic
oondoct are pending against him? No, he should not, nor any other office. Nor
should he be elected to any office while charges of onmasonic conduct are pending
against him.
·
The CommiUee on Jnrisprodence reported as follows, and their report was

adopted:It seems to yoor committee that the principl~s involved in this decision, if pot in
· operation, would virtually be adjudging a brother guilty and denying him his inher·
ent rights, without due trial and judgment by his peers. The mere faot of a brother
having been charged, does not by any means establish his guilt, nor r.an it under oar
broad and equitable laws operate for one moment as a deprivation of his inherent
rights as a brother Mason; and moreover, if Paragraph 2 of Decision 4 were to be pot
in operation, it would have a tendency to encourage the keeping ootof office the best
men in our Lodges by the unscrupulous. The effect of a mere charge in such a case
being brought against a brother in his Lodge by any other member would render him
at once ineligible to office and he could not be elected, regardless of merit or demerit
as to the natnre of the charges. We therefore recommend that Paragraph 2 of Decls·
ion 4 be not concurred in.

In his review of the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Delaware, Bro. REED pre·
sents the following remarks :The suspension, or arrest, of membershiP rights of a brother, presupposes the
oommission of some crime or moral delinquency, no matter upon what charge or
cause alleged; &D;d while th_e cause may, primarily, be non-p~}'ment of d_ues, still
there is unmasomc conduct mvolved, for no brother can be divested of his sacred
rights in the Lodge except in the forfeiture of those rights by his own willful a~t.
All disciplinary powers of a Lodge must stand equally upon the same basis !Jf
sovereignty in action, nor can they in any case be nullified or destroyed at the will
and pleasure of the subjects of their action.
The offense involved in suspending for non-payment of dnes is on an equal plane
of any other offense committed, except only in the degree '!f moral ~rpitude; !t
consists, not in the thing withheld, but in the act of withholding. In brief, the logic
of the whole subject is simply this: that if a brother suspended for non-payment of
dues can, by the payment of the sum withheld, restore himself to memberahip without action of the Lodge, so also, can any suspended brother restore himself at his
will and J>leasure by removing the primary cause.
We have not been led to believe that the non-payment of dues involves anything
aavoring of crime, and seldom, if ever, anything of moral turpitude. A brother
may be divested of his rights and privileges by a simple neglect, or by a aensitiveness that precludes bis asking for aid, which sensitiveness is unknown to his Lodge.
The delinquent does not nullify or destroy any or the disciplinary powers of the
Lodge by his own willful act; be, in restoring himself by the payment of bis dues,
aim ply avails himself of a privilege which his Lodge has granted~ him. We do not
understand that the non-payment of does is a crime; not all violations of law are
crimes; nor do all violations of law involve moral turpitude. If I do not nay my
taxes in the time prescribed by law, I am punished by having an additional tax imposed upon me. I do not understand that! have committed any orime, or that there

WEST VIRGINIA.
The twenty-third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of West Virginia
was held in the city of Charleston, commencing on the fifteenth day of November,
1887,-the M. •• W. •• HIRAM R. HOWARD, Grand Master, presiding, and the
R. •. W. ·. GEO .. W. ATKINSON being Grand Secretary. Eighty.two Lodges were
npresented.
Six Special Communications of the Grand Lodge had been held during the year
for various purposes-among others, one for the purpose of publicly installing the
officers of a subordinate Lodge.
The Address of the Grand Master is an able exposition of his official acts. He
oongratulates his brethren upon the happy auspices under which they meet. Relations with other Jurisdictions are of the most friendly and fraternal character. One
dispensation had been issued for the formation of a new Lodge; and one Lodge
had been duly constituted.
Several dispensations had been granted for various purposes, and several had
been refused. Among the latter we notice one for a public installation of officers.
Grand Master HowABD, unlike his predecessor, does not believe in public display.
Another, refusing permission to a Lodge to accept the resignation of a Secretary
who would not serve without compensation, he also declined to grant.
The charter of one Lodge had been arrested in consequence of failure to pay its
dues and make proper returns.
Twenty.five decisions are reported. The first is to the effect that a dispensation to hold a public installation is not necessary. This would ~eem to be in confilct with the Grand Master's action in refusing one because he was opposed to a
public display.
The twelfth and thirteenth uphold the doctrine of perpetual jurisdiction. No
matter, then, how upright an applicant may be, any refractory or spiteful member
may keep him out of the Order. The twelfth would seem t& convey the idea. that,
if such rejected party were to move to California, he could not apply here. If such
were the case, West Virginia could legislate for California. This decision, as well
as the others, is probably in accord with the law as it is in West Virginia. It and
many of the others, however, do not accord with the law as it is in California.
The reports of the Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer exhibit a flourishing
condition of the Lodges, and of the Grand Lodge finances.
The Grand Lecturer's report shows him to be "the right man in the right
place." He calls attention to a custom, prevalent in some of the Lodges, of examin·
ing a candidate on a part of the lectures of the degrees, and then ilispensing with
the remainder. Also to a custom that is not entirely confined to West Virginia-that Gf electing brethren to important offices simply as a compliment. He reporte

Bro. ATKINSON is not a believer in the perfect-man doctrine, and in this he has

That a Masonic Lodge Hall cannot be occupied by any other body except Free·

not exist without it; and other organizations that do much good, and are blessings

to their members and their communities, often, also, could not exist without it.
Our brother thinks that an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft may be prevented from advancement by a single member of a Lodge, without giving any
reasons therefor. No single brother has a right to injure any brother. An Entered
Apprentice or a Fellow Craft is a brother ; he bas rights that should be respected ;
and he ought not to be prevented from advancement without good reasons therefor.
"Justice is that standard or boundary of right which enables us to render unto
every one his just due without distinction." To debar one from the privilege of
advancing after he has been adjudged good and true, except for reasons that would
justify the belief that be had been misjudged, is certainly unjust.
We do not agree with Bro. ATKINSON in bis opinions as to the right to visit. The
Master of a Lodge is the proper party to have control of it, and he alone is the
party who should determine whether or not a visitor should or should not be
admitted. This is too sacred a right to be left to the whims, caprice, or prejudice
of irresponsible individuals.
~ain, we cannot concur in the opinion that conferring the degrees in a Lodge
upon a profane does not make him a member of the Lodge-that it simply makes
him a Mason. We think the Grand Master of Kentucky is right. California bolds
to the opinion that when an applicant receives the degrees in a Lodge, iplO fa<rta be
becomes a member of that Lodge; that was his intention, and should have been
the intention of the Lodge and the reason why it received the petition of the party.
If a party has been elected to receive the degrees, and circumstances afterwards
prevent him from taking them all in the Lod1re to which he preferred his petition,
he has the right to ask that Lodge to request some other Lodge to confer the degrees for it, or to grant permission to some other Lodge to confer the degrees. In
California this is the case after the party lias taken the £rst degree. If the degrees
are conferred by request, the party becomes a member of the T..odge requesting; if
by permission, it is equivalent to relinquishment of jurisdiction, and he becon.es a
member of the Lodge receiving the permiSBion. Election constitutes membership
in the case of applicants by affiliation; conferring the degree of Master Mason
constitutes membership in the case of applicants by initiation. Signing the bylaws is but evidence of the membership.
There are many points of interest in this excellent report, but ooth time and
apace forbids us the pleasure of further notice.

The Grand Secretary presented an excellent Report on Correspondence. Bro.
KUYKENDALL expresses himself briefly and to the point. He has opinions and
these a.re expressed in positive yet courteous terms; hence his report is a' very
interesting, instructive, and readable document.
Our brother propounds to us the question: "Is.a waiver of jurisdiction over
rejected m ..terial of one Lod~e in California required before such material can be
elected and received into another Lodge in that Jurisdiction? "
In reply we say that if a party has been rejected by a Lodge, and subsequently
moves into the jurisdiction of another, he can apply to that Lodge for the degrees
after the expiration of one year from the time of rejection by the former, provided
h\has resided for six months within the jurisdiction to which he applies. If he
continues to reside within the jurisdiction of the Lodge which rejected him, he
~nnot apply at any time to any other Lodge, nor can the Lodge which rejected
him surrender its jurisdiction to another Lodge. " The inhibition contained in
Sec. 2, Art. III, Part III, of our Constitution is explicit, and one Lodge cannot
lll?TeDder jurisdiction over a person not a Mason, who resides within the territory
over which its juris•liction is exclusive." There is nothing in our Constitution
which authorizes a Lodge to take any action in respect to a person, not a Mason
residing wit~in its territory, until he has made application to it for the degreea'.
Upon ~he presentation of such an application, its jurisdiction over the person is
called mto exercise, and it can then elect or reject him ; and, having elected him and
oonferred the first degree upon him, it can surrender its jurisdiction over him to
-?o~her Lodg~ at hie r13quest. If it does not elect him, it cannot surrender juriedict1on over him so long as he resides within its jurisdiction. The moment he
moves out of its juriediction the Lodge has no control, but he cannot apply to a

636

Proceedings of th1

[Oct. 10,

Lodge, within the jurisdiction of which he has moved, until the Mpiration of a
year from the date of his rejection, and until he has been six months within the
jurisdiction to which he has moved. We trust we have made ourself understood.
If a party has been rejected in Wyoming, and afterwards moves into California, he
can apply to a Lodge in California after a residence of one year in the State and six
months within the jurisdiction of the Lodge to which he applies. No waiver is
required on the part of the Lodge in Wyoming.
.
Bro. KUYKENDALL is not a belh~ver in the doctrine that an applicant for the
degrees of Masonry should be physically perfect. It will have been seen that we
agree with him. Whilst we consider that sufficient attention should be paid to
physical qualifications, we think that if Masons' would direct more attention to
the moral and intellectual ones, the i11terests of the Order would be much better
conserved.
Neither does our brother believe in Grand Masters' prerogatives. The following
suits us, being a very proper and common sense way of setting forth his views : On this question we believe the Constitution is above the Grand Master and
th!'t no prerog!'tive exists ~hereby he has .any right to set one of its provisions
aside, temporarily or otherwise, and that be is as much bound by it as the humblest
Maso!!. 11! !'D emergency where there is no constitutional provision relating to a
quest10n arismg, we ~old be would be justi.fied in !1cting within the scope of any
well-defined and undisputed landmark havmg special reference to the subject and
!J.is power to deal therew~th. If a Grand Mas~er is supreme a~d can do no wrong,
it seems much valuable time has been wasted m the preparation and ado-ption of
Constitutions. We are glad to know that few, if any, Grand Masters claim that
the~ are a law: unto th_emselves and their brethren. .Masonry is and will be judged
by .its deeds m the light of the present day and time, and not by the antiquity
clai.me4 fo~ it. The latter ,is a Sil}all factor in deti:rmining its present usefulness as
an mstitution, and any claim of mherent powers m the Grand Master claimed to
ha".e. been han~ed do"!'n fro1!1 the dark ages, u1!10'!s supported by indisputable and
legitimate testimony, is detrimental. JI.lo man is above the law. Masonry is based
on common sense, which teaches that the power creating an officer can make laws
· to govern him.
Our brother presenta the following, with the reque&t that brother reviewers Will
answer it for their respective Jurisdictions:Does not each Jurisdiction provide that a profane rejected by one Lodge therein
cannot be accepted by any other Lodge in the State without consent or waiver of
the rejecting Lodge? If so, why make a distinction between local and what may
be termed foreign rejections?
Inferentially we have answered for California. California makes no distinction.
If an applicant is rejected, whether it be in Wyoming, Kansas, California, or elsewhere, he cannot here apply to any Lodge until after the expiration of one year from·
the date of bis rejection. If a rejected party removes from the State, our jurisdiction ceases, and he becomes subject to the laws of the Jurisdiction into which he
has removed. Under our laws there can be no such thing as consent or waiver of
jurisdiction until after the party has applied and has received the first degree.
We regret that we mnRt part company with Bro. KUYKENDALL. We hav•
found his report-the second effort-truly multum in plllNJO. His views are sound
and his expression thereof meets with our hearty approval.

VERA Cauz.-The United Mexican Grand Lodge, in the State of Vera Cruz,
held its third Annual Communication in the city of that name on the twenty-fifth
day of March, 1888, the M. ·• R. •, Bro. FBANOIBOO A. DOMINGUES, Grand Master,
presiding, and the M. •• R. ·.Bro. Jost J. MUNOZ being Grand Secretary.
In a well-prepared address the Grand Maeter sets forth the condition of the
Craft in that Jurisdiction and enumerates his official acts. He says :-"At the
commencement of tbe constitutional period from 1887 to 1888, it became necessary
to withdraw our confidence from certain brethren and varioua Lodges that we found
in difficulties. Your co-operation and the good will manifested by all to respect
the law, was sufficient to overcome the troubles and restore confidence."
Under the bead of "Exterior Relations," be says : "It is with profound eorrow
that I announce to yon the rupture of fraternal relations between this Grand Lodge
and that of the Federal District, caused by the supposition of that Grand Bodt
and the affirmation of its J1iepresentative, that this Grand Lodge was lending pro•
tection and assistance to the Lodge Olm:roa de Hilram, under the jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge of Hamburg, at a time when said Lodge was considering the advisability of recognizing the authority of this Grand Lodge ; which action brou1Jht
that matter to an end. All the antecedents are published, and they are the best
demonstration, not only of the justification of this Grand Lodge, but of its loyal
procedure to the end that Symbolic Masonry might be united in the State in which
it held its seat. In the interest of harmony the United Grand Lodge of Colon and
the Island of Cuba offered its mediation, which was accepted by this Grand Lodge,
and a document wa.~ forwarded in our juatification, in order that the mediating
Grand Body might commence its negotiations. I am sorry that I cannot inform
·
you in regard to the result, as it is not yet known."
We find nothing in the organ of the Grand Lodge of the Federal District
relative to this unfortunate controversy, except the bare mention of the fact of the
suspension of fraternal relations, and a letter from the Grand Maeter of that Grand
Body declining to act further as the Representative of the United Me:xican Grand
Lodge. We baYe received a lengthy manifesto from the latter Grand Body, setting forth its version of the case, but, until we have seen that of the Grand Lodge
of the Federal District, we refrain from the expression of any opinion upon the
merits of the controversy.
The interruption of harmonious relations between these Grand Bodies will, we
fear, have a depressini effect upon the prosperity of Masonry in Me:xico, but we
trust that the good offices of the Grand Lodge of Colon and the Island of Cuba
will result in a speedy settlement of the question, and the reetoration of peace and
good will.
The Grand Master further reports that fraternal relations bad been suspended
between that Grand Lodge and the eo-called Grand Lodge of Oaxaca, for the reason
th~t the Body, now claiming to be the Grand Lodge of Oaxaca, was illegally organ·
ized and bas no right to exercise Masonic jurisdiction over that territory. We gave
an account of the difficulty existing among the Masons of Oaxaca in our last report,
and have received no advices which tend to change the opinion therein expressed.
The Grand Master appears to be well-versed in the law of Masonry, and anxious
to promote the welfare of the Craft over which be so ably presides. His address
certainly exhibits marked ability and we trust that be will contmue bis efforts for
the unification of Masonry in bis own country, and the prosperity of the Fraternity
at large.
The M. •, B. •. Bro. FBANOIBOO A. DOMINGUEZ is Grand Master, and the M. ', V. ••
Bro. JosE J. MuNoz is Grand Secretary.

"The Grand Master of New South Wales," Grand Master TABBANT gave a
of the history of Freemaeonry in the Colony. From it we learn tb11t the first Lodge
of Freemaeons in New South Wales was established in 1820, under the Grand
Lodge of Ireland. The first Lodge under the English Conslitution was established
in 1841 ; and shortly afterwards the Scottish Constitution was established in the
Colony. The present Grand Lodge of New South Wales was established in 1877.
Thirteen Lodges joined in the efforts for this purpose ; there are now fifty Lodges,
representing nearly four thousand Masons. Two years prior to 1887, this Grand
Lodge had been recognized by only twenty-nine Grand Lodges; at present it hae
been rec~ized by fifty. The Grand Master deplores the want of unity which
e~sts among Freemasons in the Colony in consequence of the existence of the Provincial Grand Lodges of England and Scotland. It is to be hoped that the time
may soon come when the cause of discord will be removed by the tecognition of
this Grand Lodge by the Grand Lodges of England and Scotland.
Tabular statements exhibit a very prosperous condition of the several fun-is of
the Grand Lodge.

From the copies of T~ Freemason we have the gratifying intelligence that the

its Special Communication in May of the present year, the Grand Lodge of New
South Wales appointed a committee of five, as requested by the District Grand
Lodge of England, to consult with similar committees from the English and Scottish District Grand Lodges as to the means of careying into effect the Malnic
union, as approved by LoRD CARNARVON, the Pro Grand Master of England; These
committees met in joint assembly on the tenth day of May, 1888, and succeeded in
arranging a basis of union among the various bodies heretofore governing the Fraternity in the Colony. It was declared and agreed that, from and after ST. JOHN'S
Day, the twenty-fourth day of June, 1888, the three Grand Lodges should constitute one Grand Lodge under the style of" The United Grand Lodge of New South
- Wales." A large majority of the Lodges under the English and Scotch Constitutions, and all those under the Grand Lodge <!If New South Wales, nccepted the
basis of union. The representatives of the various Lodges that had accepted the
basis of union assembled in the Great Hall ef the University, in Sydney, on the
fourteenth day of Au1rust, and proceeded to the election of Grand Officers of the
United Grand Lodge. Bro. LoRD CARRINGTON, Governor of the Colony, received
a unanimous vote for Grand Master. Of hie election, and of himself, the editor of
The F1'eema1un says:The election of Bro. LoRD CARRINGTON as the first Grand Master of the United
Grand Lodge was a pofular vote, and wisely and worthily so. He was the ,no~i·
nated Grand Master o the Grand Lodge of New South Wales, as alao the Dl8trict
Grand Master elect of the English Constitution, in this Colony, and being a Past
Grand Warden of the Grand Lodge of England, hie position as a candidate was
irresistible. We congratulate the Craft on hie unanimous election, and feel 11Btisfied that he will prove a wise ruler, and materially aid in cementing the Fraternity
into a harmonious whole. He bas been an earnest advocate for the "Union," and
has unobtrusively worked zealously to bring it about. Hie tact, geniality, high
social position and Masonic experience, backed up by the zeal and earnestness of
his officers, will raise Masonry to a perfection hitherto unattainable, and attract to
the Lodges a large number of unaffiliatee who have drifted away from a practical
connection with the Order. Their return will itself be a great gain.
The Ff'll1111U<m, in its issue of October 1st, 1888, contains a full account of the

in the happy termination of their differences, and congratulate them upon the

Under the Grand Lodge of Scotland there are upwards of three hundred and
fifty Lodges in the Kingdom proper, and about two hundred and thirty in foreign
Districts. The home Lodges constitute some twenty-five Provincial Grand Lodges,
whilst those abroad are under the immediate control of what are known as District
Grand Lodges. From the proceedings we undertook to obtain a clear conception
of the classification of Lodges and Grand Lodges; but finally gave up the endeavor
as fruitleBB.
The social feature of Masonry in this Jurisdiction pleases us. The Scotch are
"jolly good fellows" everywhere, and no less in their Lodges than elsewhere. We
infer that they love Masonry as they do their country, and their love of country is
proverbial.

of the Grand Orient of Spain. The terms of the treaty or argument are in brief as
follow6: Neither Body is to receive into its jurisdiction or obedience any Masonic
Body or Mason belonging to, or which has heretofore belonged to the Jurisdiction of
the other, without written permission or dimit in regular form. Sentences pronounced against Masons by the tribunals of either of the contracting power. shall be
respected and enforced by the other. To carry the foregoinginto effect, the Grand
Secretaries shall furnish each other with the necessary notices, and, when the desire
isexpr08sed therein that the judgment of suspension, expulsion or acquittal be made
public, it shall be inserted in the official or6ans, and also the names of rejected can·
didates, with such matters of general interest as may be deemed convenient.
Guarantees of friendship shall be reciprocally proposed by the contracting .parties.
When either transacts busineBB of common interest, or of a general Masonic character in which uniformity of action is necessary, each Body shall appoint three
:fnapectors General of the 33° who shall meet and agree upon that which they deem
moat opportune. The resolutions adopted by this mixed committee shall have no
force unless unanimously adopted by said committee and approved by each
Sllpreme Council, with the sanction of the respective Grand Commanders.
The foregoing treaty was approved by the contracting parties in extraordinary
1e11sion held on the sixth day of February, 1888, and ordered to be promulgated

Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of the trial-record in the
case of THOMAS W. REEn, who was expelled by Saint Mark's Lodge, No. 85, on
the twenty-eighth "day of January, 1888, report that th~ brother was expelled
solely on the ground that he had subscribed to an oath, before a Justice of the
Peace, that he would not ddnk liquor for a period of one year; but that within
ten days thereafter he did drink and became intoxicated.
In the opinion of your committee the Lodge went beyond its powers in holding
the accused to responsibility simply for the obligation taken to refrain from drinking.
It is well known that such an oath is often taken, and that the one taking it probably
does so with a firm determination to maintain and keep it. In a moment of weakness he yields to temptation, with no thought of committing perjury; and he cannot properly be charged with such offence unless by his act he affects some material
issue. The Lodge erred in trying and expelling the accused on the charge presented; but if there is sufficient reason for trying the accused upon a charge of
habitual drunkenness, it should be substituted and the brother be so held to account. Your committee recommend the adopt10n of the following resolution : Resolved, That the action of Saint Mark's Lodge, No. 85, in expelling Bro.
THOMAS W. RICED from all the rights and privileges of Masonry on the twentyeighth day of January, 1888, be reversed and set aside; and that the Lodge be
directed to retry the case in accordance with the foregoing suggestion.
Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. CHARLES L. TISDALE,
Junior Warden of Oak G'1"0'De Lndge, No. 215, from the action of that Lodge in
acquitting Bro. JosEPH WooD MA.STICK on a charge of unmasonic conduct, BD the
eighth day of December, 1887, have had the same under consideration and report
that, from the testimony adduced, which was of a very trifling character, they see ·
no reason to dissent from the action of the Lodge; an~ they therefore reclimmend
the adoption of the following resolution :Resoli•ed, That the action of Oak Grove Lodge, No. 215, in acquitting Bro.
JObEPH WooD MABTIOK on a charge of unmasonic conduct, on the eighth day of
December, 1887, be and is hereby affirmed; and that the appeal therefrom be dis- •
missed.

privileges of Masonry by Fall River Lod~e, No. 270, on the twenty-fifth day of

Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of a so-called trial-record
in the case of GEORGE CALVIN RALPH, a member of Fre:mo Lodge, No. 247, bea.ring
date of the twenty-ninth April, 1888, report that they are unable to determine,
from an examination of the paper in their possession, what really is the status of
the Lo<lge or of Bro. RALPH. It would appear that the brother waB charged with
unmasonic conduct, and was served with a copy of the charge preferred against
him, together with a summons to appear and answer. He informed the Lodge that

The hour for the special order, as announced this morning, havi~g
arrived, the Grand Orator, the W." Bro. TnolllA.B HENRY LAINE, delivered the Annual Oration before the Grand Lodge, as follows :MosT WORSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER
AND BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LoDGE :Time's pendulum has made another swing_ Our Earth with her precious freight
of nations kindred tongues and peoples, hath made another revolution around
.GoD'S lam~, in the 'heavens swung to give light, health and life to His creatures.
We, too, have taken one more step towards that Lodge "not made with hands, eternal in the heavens," since last we met in solemn conclave here. Through storm and
sunshine, "through shadow and sheen," we have walked for another year. That year
has worked change on every brow and written it upon every heart. T?ese. changes,
however, have for the most part oeen the mellowing changes of npenmg character and increasing knowledge. For, of a truth, the Supreme Grand Master has
not forgotten or forsaken us, but has walked with us all in loving kindness in our
several stations through the year, and has brought us once a.gain tog!lther in peace
and harmony. To Him be honor, adoration and glory'. forever and e~er !

1888.]

Grand Lod,<je of Oalif<nnia.

655

.And now, convened in this sacred place, surrounded by the mystic.symbols and
emblems of our Order, and having constantly before. our eyes the whole insignia of
the Craft, all vocal with lessons of wisdom and beauty, the mind, intoxicated with
their perfume, is loth to wander from Masonry to any other subject.
For Masonry, as a theme, like unto the Holy Writings as a book, is always
new, inspiring and exhauetleas; a fountain forever pouring forth the pure waters
of wiedom, love and truth-the true waters of the river of life that Bows from the
throne of Gon. Our loved Fraternity is hoary with age, yet full of the vigor and
beauty of youth, knowing no decay.
''Revolutions sweep o;er the Earth,

Like troubled visions o"er the breast of dreaming Borrow."
Nati on rises against nation, and system rises against system, in the great work
of change and destruction. The world's arena is strewn with ruins, bones and
blood. But, amidst these mighty scenes of passion, war and ruin, the Lodges of
our Craft have stood as beacons upon the highest hills and lights in the deepest
vales, offering places of shelter and repose. In those sacred precincts there has
been forever taught the lesson of all lessons, that there ·is one Almighty Father,
the Architect of all things seeB and unseen- most holy and loving-in whose eight
all men are brethren, equally under His protection- a LIVING GoD, who " discemeth deep things out of darkness, and bringeth to light the shadow of death,"
and of whom it is said, "Hell is naked before Him, destruction hath no coming_"
Whence came this puissant and venerable Order? What corner of the glebe
can claim to be its birth-place? At what point in the tide of time came it into
being?
Geographically considered, it came not into being in the frozen and sterile
N<Yrlh Land, nor from the parched and burning equatorial rll!l'ione, but in some .
temperate clime where the physical needs and strength of man gave him the desire
and power to use the twenty-four inch ~uge, the common gavel, the setting maul, the
equare, the plumb-line, the compass and the trowel. Not only did it originate in
the temperate regions of the Earth, but at some point north of the Equator. Thie
is apparent to the Ma•onic mind without learned arguments to support it; the situation of the Lodge and the location of its hghts is enough-t he North being the place
of Masonic darkness. To narrow further the limits, we claim that it could not have
been born of atheism, barbarism or ignorance. No! She bears upon her brow and
in her body and spirit the unmistakable evidences of her high birth_ That only
.hearts and minds, pure and GOD-fearing, laid her foundations and wrought upon
her in the beginning, is evident from her landmarks and foundation principles.
Some have inconsiderately contended for an Egyptian origin of our Craft, as
that ancient people had much of learning and art. But such a contention is without foundation. Its grand moral and theocratic system could not have been the
outgrowth of the brute-worshipping Egyptian people. No! Search her monuments, from Monre to dieemboguing Nile; examine every inscription, statue and
1tructurt, whether it be sphinx, temple, to'l!b or mighty pyramid; and nowhere ia
there to be found the slightest trace of Israel's GoD, who in the beginning create.I
the Heavem and the Earth. Search other lands, their records and monuments, and
nowhere will you find & civilization from which such an order could spring or find
nourishment in infancy, except in that land in which was erected that wondrous
temple on Mount Moriah, within whose walls no graven image, no statue of man,
bird or beast is found; but only the altar from whose brazen top there ascended
the sweet-smelling odors of sacrifice to the invisible GoD, and where, day and
night, blazed the mystic Shekinah-that fire fed by no human hand or earthly fuel.

That holy temple has fallen; over its ruins long since were heard the screams
of the godless Roman's eagles. Yet neither the tread of armies, the shock of
battle, the breath of pestilence, or the tooth of all-devouring time, have been able
to remove from those ruins the evidences tbat it was the work of Masons-of a
civilized, GOO-fearing people. The foe and tbe elements have dug down on its foundation, lasting as the eternal hill of which it forms no inconsiderable part, and found
the sure evidences of Ma.Jonie work that every well-in~tructed Mason knows how
to read.
We have thus fixed the place and time of Masonry's birth. It is a Royal Order,
brethren. HIBAH of Tyre and SoLOMON of Israel exalted the Widow's Son, whose
royalty was labor, wisdom and fidelity.
The Craft itself has been as well built and enduring as this mighty foundation
was, The ruthless hand of man, with blast, pick, crow and shovel, may remove
Mount Moriah, or cast Mount Zion into the sea; it may pull up by the roots the
cedars of Lebanon; but the Gon-planted institution of Masonry is beyond his
powers. Its roots are too deep and stron~ to be dug out or pulled up; ~ey are
beneath every land and clime, and the nations rest in the shade ~f their great;
tree.
•
But Masonry, like all sublunary thing11, has had and still has its enemiea.
Those enemies, in the times now past, were powerful and often cruel. But I carf
not to open these barbarous record• of the past, either to arraign our enemies or to
vindicate our sublime Craa. Suffice it to say that Masonry, in the ages that are
paet, with charity for all and persecution for none, bas borne with becoming fortitude its trials and perils, biding its time with patience; and that, when her secrets
w~re demanded by the base or the powerful, she has answered with tbe firmness
and devotion of the Widow's Son, and the secrets remained sacred-the would-be
destroyer getting nothing but dust and ashes. When her principles were assailed
or challenged, she answered her accusers with the royal dignity and wisdom of
HIRAM of Tyre and SoLOMON of Israel, and the world listel\ed. When her devoted
leaders were placeu on the burning pile, they fearlessly summoned their persecutors to meet them before the throne of the Eternal Father. When her sons, as "
last insult were denied burial in consecrated ground, she proudly answered that
any ground is holy and consecrated in which is planted by Masonic hands the sprig
of acacia, and on which rests the eye of Goo.
But, despite the war upon her, she now stands forth Sovereign of the ascendant, clothed in royal purple. For she bas this day in her ranks more presidents,
kings, princes, governors, rulers, bishops, statesmen, generals, judge&, law-givers,
and great ones, than any other body of men upon the earth ; and none dare lay
in anger their finger "upon the hem of her garment." She has enemies yet-but who are they! They may be set forth in two classes. First, that class of
men contined to no olime, and called and best described by the word "crank."
This class proudly numbers in its fold the criminal, the fool, iAnd the idler-an unsavory trinity of political cranks, social cranks, and religious crapks-a.body of
men who never begin or advance any good work, but are always trying to pull
down something erected by others. As their cranky disposition renders them
incapable of organi'1ing for any good work, it makes them doubt the capacity of
others; so also it renders them almost powerleaa as enemies. True, they are ~or·
ever jabbering about the perniciousness and uselessness of secret societies, ever
contending that all good things should be made public to everybody. But we,
remembering the wise and ancient injunction, "Give not thou that which is holy
unt.8 the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine," regard them as the .idle

wind and pass on with our work. The second class is composed of peeudo religionists from all creeds-Catholic, Greek, Protestant, Hebrew, Mohammedan,
Buddhist, Mormon and Spritualist-those who are more righteoue than their
brothers in the several denominations of the Earth, a zealous, fuming, frothing
lot, that would light again the torch and the fagot, bring for~h again the rack, the
wheel, and the instruments of torture; but the wise and good of every creed stand
with us against the whole motley herd of self .righteous fanatics, and we laugh at
their fury. Then" All hall thou Masonry divine I

The Grand Master req nested the Deputy Grand Master, Bro. MoBRIB
MA.ROH EsTEE, to make the presentation of the testimonial, which he
did, as follows :PAST GRAND MASTER ATKINSON:-

Before the earliest mysteries of Masonry bad been exemplified, in the darkest
period of human history, when physical force was the recognized law and victory
upon the field of battle the only reward for manly effort, those who did the most
injuri6s to their fellowmen, who destroyed the most lives, desolated the most coun·
try, and caused the most human suffering, were the heroes. Even down to the
golden ages of Grecian and Roman history, conquerors returned with their victims
chained to their chariot wheels, and made a holiday of· their massacre.
But time wrought changes ; the human heart expanded as the world became
older; mankind grew better; and one of the great influences tending to this change
in the human heart, outiiide of the religious sentiments of those early times, was
the teachings of Masonry.
There is a beautiful legend brought to us through the unrecorded and shadowy
past, the sublime lessons of which may have given the ea.rl~est inspi~ation to
Masonry. This legend was the beacon of a new and better hght. It is related
that, in olden times, a city was beleagured by a neighboring enemy. The inhabitants made a desperate defense, but were finally compelled to surrender. The
garrison and the women and children occupying the city were about to be put to
death, or led away into captivity, when suddenly a beautiful Goddess appeared,
clothed in white and wearing a crown of silver. In a voice heard by all, she
said-stay the hand of cruelty ; that he alone was the conqueror and was entitled
to wear the crown, who did the most good to his fellow-men; and that man should
benefit, not destroy, his fellow beings. Tben, as the Goddess swept across the sky
and disappeared, the victorious chieftain said to his followers that the prisoners of
an hour before were their brothers ; that no harm should befall them ; and that
they should be permitted to go ,free.
This beautiful senti'ment has been the guiding star of your life; the love you
bear to your fellow-men has given inspiration to all your acts; and so you have
won a crown of silver, typified by these beautiful specimens before you; and I may
be pardoned for reminding you that it is the first principle of the great Order, of
which you have been the illustrious Head, to do good to our fellow-men.
In the performance of this high inju,nction, you have done that duty well. You
have endeared yourself to every Mason in the Jurisdiction, and to every good man
and woman therein who has been fortunate enough to know you. You have won
the crown ; it is yours ; wear it. It bears no stain of blood nor mark of dishonor
on its shining front. It is as resplendent in its purity as the first sheen of the
morning sunlight that flames across the snowy peaks of the mountains lying to the
East. Take these gifts, dear brother, not aa a reward for duty performed, but
rather as a token of our love. Bear them to your wife and children, and let your
children's children inherit them; and, as they look upon them in the future, they
may remember that their father was worthy of the gifts. Bid them to hold them
in treasured memory as tokens of the love your brethren bear for you.

Past Grand Master ATKINSON made the following response :M. ". W. ·. GRAND MASTER, R. ". W. ". DEPUTY GRAND MASTER,
AND BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA:-

It is not meet for me to expre~s surprise. on this occasion. I listened attentively,
and with deep interest, to ·the reading of the resolution adopted by this Grand
Lodge at its last Annual Communication. I have read that resolution in the Pro·
oee(lings, as recorded by our Grand Secretary, and I do not deny that, in the year
that has passed, my mind has oftentimes essayed to forecast this scene ; but I must
as freely admit that there are surprises which anticipation cannot unfold, for I have
come to feel and to )l:now that the heart may swell with emotions which the tongue
cannot express-that there are thoughts which can never float into speech. Were
I prepared with the most elaborate response, it would be impossible for me properly to express the sentiments which I entertain, for the thoughts that are now
1pringing from the deep"'fountains of feeling would be but poorly clad in words
which memory could recall. I therefore stand before you to say, in a few broken
1entences, how muc\ I appreciate this most magnificent gift; and if my tongue
fail to serve me, I ask that you accept the assurance that my heart beats with love
and gratitude to my brethren for this expression of their confidence and esteem.
It is exceedingly gratifying to me to know that my endeavors to faithfully perfor111 my duties as Grand Master have met with your favor and approbation ; and
I desire to assure you in return, that I received such cheerful support and co-opera·
tion from my brethren as to render the performance of my duty but a labor of love.
Wherever I went throughout this great Jurisdiction, from its northern to its southern boundary, from the mountain sides to the islands of the sea, I was received
with such manifestations of kindness as rendered every duty a pleasure, and taught
me that "Brotherly Love " is not a ineaningless term.
For this beautiful present I thank you from the depths of a grateful heart. I
thank you, not only for the magnificence of the gift, but also for the generosity
and thoughtful kindness that prompted it, and especially for its most appropriate
Je].ection. It is something for the home. Every true Mason loves his home and
delights to bring around it everything which makes life happy and enjoyable, for
he holds it to be the dearest spot of earth. To my home I shall bear this beautiful gift with mingled feelings of joy and pride, of brotherly love and paternal
affection.
Brother Deputy Grand Master, you have kindly spoken of those who are near
and dear to me, and you have antic:ipated their appreciation. I thank you most
iincerely. In the tender years of childhood and youth those dear ones will look
upon this gift only with feelings of wonder an i admiration; but there will come a time
when it will present to them a deeper and more lasting signification. That time
will be when my work is finhhed a'ld my days are done ; when this stammering
tongue shall be silent, and the vital spark which now animates this wasting form
aball have been transferred to the great Valhalla cloisters of the ever living years.
Then, in the riper years of manhood, 'they wiU reverently lift the lid of this treasureaaeket, and, viewing these beautiful tokens, will say, "These were my father's-a
gift of the Grand Lodl(e of Masons of California." On their behalf I again tender
you my thanks.
Brethren, I shall never address you as Grand Master again, but I hope that I
may still be able, in some way, to render service to the Grand Lodge of California.
Be that as it may, I will try throughout the remaining years of my life to live as a
inst and upright Mason. So far as within me lies, and with all the strength that
GoD shall give me to rise above the imperfections of human nature, I will strive

Bro. JAMES BAUNTY STEVENS, from the Committee on By-La.ws of
Lodges, presented the following report :To tM M. ·. W. ·• Grand Lodge of California.:Your committee, to whom were referred those portions of the Address of the
Grand Master and of the Report of the Gran.d Secretary which relate to amendments to their by-laws proposed by sundry Lodges, and to the by-laws of Lodges
under dispensation, have carefully examined the papers and books submitted to
them and report as follows : ·
In the eleven cases of proposed amendments to the by-laws of Lodges which
have been approved by the Grand Master, your committee recommend that his
action be affirmed by the Grand Lodge.
In the seven cases of proposed amendments to the by-laws of Lodges which
were disapproved by the Grand Master, viz.: those of Nos. 8, 85, 149, 208, 220, 271.
and 284, your committee also recommend that hii action be affirmed by the Grand
Lodge, except in the one relating to Rw Vilita Lodge, No. 208. In that case they
are of the opinion, after a careful investigation of the papers, and from statements
made to 'them by the Master of the Lodge and by Bro. CHARLES DALY, the
Inspector of the District in which the Lodge is located, that the adoption of the
proposed amendment would be for the best interests of the Lodge. They therefore l'llCOmmend that the proposed amendment to the by-laws of Bw Vista Lodge,
No. 208, be approved.
Your committee have examined the Books of By-Laws of the seven Jiodgea
existing under dispensation, and, having compared them with the Uniform Code
of By-Laws for Lodges, find them to be in consonance therewith. They are well
written, and, with the exception of Oronge Grow Lodge, have the full names of the
members of the Lodges signed thereto. That deficiency in the book should be
1'8111edied, and it is recommended that all the By-Laws be approved.
All which is respectfully submitted by

To the M. •• W. '. <hand Lodge of CaJ,ifarnia :-

your committee, to whom were referred those portions of the Grand Secretary'&
Report which relate to the L0dges now existin!I' under dispensation, have care.
fully examined the books and papers which have been 1ubmitted to them, and
report as follows :The records of Los Gatos Lodge, U. D., at Los Gatos, in Santa Clara County,
are in proper form, are neatly kept, and reflect much credit on its Secretary,
Although its first meeting was held on August 10th, 1888, it bas conferred three
degrees; has recei 'fed seven petitions therefor, not yet reported on for want of
time ; is free from debt; and has twenty-nine members.
The records of Sunset Lodge, U. D., at East Los Angeles, in Los Angeles County,
are in proper form and neatly kept. Since its first meeting, on June 23d, 1888, it
bas conferred ten degrees. At its last stated meeting, two petitioners were elected
to receive the degrees and one was elected to membership; and one petition for
degrees remains to be acted upon. The Lodge bas twenty-two members, and is
free from debt.
The records of Santa Paula Lodge, U. D., at Santa Paula, in Ventura County,
are in good shape and well kept. Its first meeting was held on July 19th, 1888,
and since then it bas conferred three degrees. It has twenty-four members and is
free from debt.
The records of ElsinOTe Lodge, U. D., at Elsinore, in San Diego County, are
neatly kept and in proper form. Since its organization it has conferred six degrees
and admitted five applicants for affiliation. It bas twenty-two members, is free
from debt, and has a balance of $91 10 in its treasury.
The records of Mamwell Lodge, U. D., at Maxwell, in Colusa County, are in
proper form, are very neatly kept, and are a great credit to its Secretary. At the
last Communication of the Grand Lodge this Lodge was continued under dispen.
saticn, and since that time it has oonferred eighteen degrees, and three members
have been admitted by affiliation. The Lodge now has thisty-two members, and
the recm:ds show that it is free from debt and bas $573 75 in its treasury.
A protest against the issue of a charter to this Lodge, from Tuscan Lodge, No.
261, at Williams, in Colusa.County, has been received and had under consideration.t
but, in view of the fact that the matters therein contained were duly considered
and pas~ upon by Grand Master ATKINSON, during his official term, before be
granted a dispensation to Maxwell Lodge, your committee do not deem it advisable
. to reopen the matter; and, in view of the report of the Inspector of the District in
which Maxwell Lodge is located, that its work is first class and highly creditable to
its members, they believe that the good of the Fraternity will be beet subserved by
granting it a charter.
The records of Traver Lodge, U. D., at Traver, in Tulare County, are in proper
form and are fairly kept, but a portion of ttiem is without mar~l reference&.
Its first meeting was held on June 23d, 1888. Since then eight degrees have been
conferred, and it now bas fifteen members upon its roll. The records show that
the Lodge is free from debt, but, as it does not petition for a charter, your commit.
tee recommend that it be continued under dispensation.
OTange Grove Lodge, U. D., is located at Orange, in Los Angeles County, and
its first meeting was held on April 3d, 1888. Since then four members have been
admitted by affiliation. No petitions for degrees have been received, and, as a
matter of course, no degrees have been conferred.
The Lodge-records consist of certain entries in an improper (so-called) Record
Book, and are very imperfect. So far as can be gleaned therefrom it appears tha~

there are sixteen members of the Lodge, and that only $24 has been paid 11.8 dues, for

past proceedings, properly corrected and 'in the form prescribed by law.

Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the Report of the Grand
Secretary concerning the surrender of the charters of Brotherhood Lodge, No. 251,
at Duncan's Mills, in Sonoma County, and Westport Lodge, No. 276, at Westport,
in Mendocino County, have carefully examined all the papers relative thereto, and
report that there was evidently sufficient reason for the surrender in both those cases.
The affairs of Brotherhood Lodge appear to have been wound up in a satisfactory
manner by its late Master, Bro. DONALD McKENZIE, to whom the Grand Secretary
had given authority for that purpose, and all the requirements of our law relating
to such matters appear to have been complied with .
The closing up of the affairs of Westport Lodge by its late Secretary, Bro.
WILLIAM H. RoACH, to whom the Grand Secretary had given them in charge, does
not seem to ha'fe been quite so successful, as appears from sundry letters of the
last named officer requiring information which he bas thus far failed to obtain;
yet his well-known perseverance will doubtless soon make it complete.
Your committee therefore offer the following resolution and recommend that it
be adopted :.Besolved, That the •urrender of the charters of Brotherhood Lodge, No. 251, at
Duncan's Mills, in Sonoma County, and Westport Lodge, No. 276, at Westport, in
Mendocino County, be accepted, and that said Lodges be and are hereby declared
to be extinct.

Bro. CHARLES RAY GRITMAN, from the Committee on Finances, presented the following reports :To the M. ·. W. •• G-rand. Lodge of OaJifornia :Your committee have examined the petition of Bro. JOHN G. JONES, of Grat!ei
Range Lodge, No. 59, !it Camptonville, Yuba County, together with several letters
from the Master of said Lodge and others, setting forth that said Bro. JONES is
sick and destitute, and ha.a been for a long time travAling from place to place in
search of health, at an expenditure of some $2,fiOO by said Gravel, Range Lodire,
and appealing to this Grand Lodge for assistance.
Your committee fully appreciate the position of. Gravel Range Lodge, No. 59,
and are in full sympathy with the sick brother, but cannot see their way clearly to
do anything in the p/emiees. Such a precedent would open wide the door of the
Grand Lorlge to all sick and destitute brethren, thus depleting its treasury and
taking upon itself the duties of subordinate Lod~s and Boards of Relief. They
therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption : R&olved, That it is not in the province of the Grand Lodge to care for the
individual members of the subordinate Lodges, and that it must therefore dismiss
the petition, leaving the matter entirely with the brethren of Gravel, Range Lodge,
No. 59.
Your committee have examined the statement and vouchers of Bro. GEORGB
.BRAY, Acting Master of the late Santa C'lara Lodge, No. 34, (now extinct,) relative
to the settlement of its affairs, to which reference is made in the report of the
Grand Secretary. They find that the brother performed that service in a correct
and complete manner, in full accord with our Constitution and to the benefit of this
Grand Lodge; and they therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:R&ol.ve.d, That the Grand Lodge fully approves and acknowledges the services
of Bro. GEORGE BRAY in the settlement of the affairs of the late Santa C'lara Lodge,
No. 34, and tender him a vote of thanks therefor.
All which is respectfully submitted by
CHARLES RAY GRITMAN, }

Bro. W:rLLI.UI CALDWELL BELomm, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports :To the M. ·• W. ·• Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :Your committee, to whom wae referred that portion of the Address of the Grand
Master which relates to hie decieione, report that· during the year that officer be.e
decided, in &newer to l!Dodry queetione proposed to him, in elfect as follow~:- .
1. That when the Grand Lodge hae expelled a Mason who wae at the time a hfemember of a Lodge, and bas eubeequently restored him, ench restoration wae only
to the rights and privileges of Masonry, and not to membership in his Lodge; and
that, if he should thereafter become a member of that or any other Lodge, he would
be subject to the payment of dues.
