2. That when the charter of a Lodge has been arrested, and a portion of its members specially exempted from the suspension involved in the order of arrest, in case
the charter is restored by the Grand Lodge, the LodMe, unless there be dissension,
(which your committee understand as meaning a lack of unanimity,) may determine
whether the members so exempted shall pay dues during the time of the arrest; bot
that, if there be dissension, (i.e. if the Lodge be not unanimone,) the payment of does
must be exacted and must be made to the Lodge. And· also that, in case the charter
be not restored, the members so exempted may, if their dnes be paid, receive dimits
from the Grand Lodge as of the date of the arrest.
3. That a newly elected Master of a Lodge is not required to receive the so-called
degree of Past Master before entering upon the duties of bis office and presiding in
hie Lodge.
'· That the degrees of Masonry should not be conferred upon a person snbject
to epileptic fits.
6. ' That the Master of a Lodge, at an election for officers thereof, is not entitled
to a casting vote, in addition to his proper vote, in case of a tie vote in bis Lodge.
6. That the word ballot in our Constitution means a secret vote by the nee of
balls, cnbes, or slips of paper.
7. That no Lodge can confer the degrees of Masonry gratuitously, it being con·
trary to oar Conetitntfon.
8. That when an Entered Apprentice is refused advancement, be is entitled to a
return of that portion of the fee paid by him which is charged for the two remaining
degrees.
9. That when objection is made to the admission of a visitor, the Master should
require the member objecting to state to him the reasons for the objection, that be
may judge of their sufficiency.
10. That a non-affiliated Mason, residing in this State, cannot keep himself in good
standing by contributions to a Lodge in any other State.
Yonr committee fully agree with all these decisions, except that relative to the
rights of a life-member of a Lodge, (numbered 1 in this report,) those in relation to
dues of members exempted from suspension in case of the arrest of the charter of a
Lodge, (collectively numbered 2 herein,) and that (numbered 3) relative to the so.
called degree of Past Master.
With respect to the first of these, (1,) they agree with the Grand Master that the
contract of life-membership is with the particular Lodge of which the party was a
member at the date of the contract; that the contract was only that, for a coneidera.
tion deemed by th"e Lodge snfficient, be would thereafter be exempt from does in that
Lodge ; and that, if for auy reason his connection with that Lodge should be severed
and he ehonld become a member of another Lodge, be would be subject to the pay.
ment of dnes in that Lodge. But if, as in the case presented in the question, having
been expelled and subsequently restored, he should be. again elected to membership
in the particular Lodge of which he had been a member, your commHtee think that he
ebonld be deemed to he restored to all the rights pertaining to hie· life-membership,
as well as to others. Hie contract was that in that Lodge be should be forever exempt
from the payment of does, and common justice would require the observance of that
contract on the part of the Lodge. It is true that when hie connection was once
severed by expulsion or withdrawal it would be for the Lodge to say whether it
would receive him again, but if it 8hould receive him, it should restore him to hie
former standing in all respects, and should be ready to perform all Its obligations to
him.
As to the decisions in relation to the dnes of Masone who, by the order arresting
the charter of a Lodge, are exempted from suspension, (2,) your committee think
that the r~e should be abeolnte that members so exempted should pay dues during

1888.J

Grand Lori{/e of Oal,ijornia.

615

the period of arrest-to the Lodge if the charter be restored, and to the Grand
Lodge if it be revoked and the Lodge be declared extinct. Of course either of these
bodies could remit such dues, bnt tiulese remitted they should be paid. In case the
charter be revoked, they should be paid np to the date of issuing the certiOoate by
the Grand Secretary, which entitles its holder to all the rights which would have
been hie bad he received a certificate of withdrawal (dimit) from hie Lodge. At the
date of the declaration by the Grand Lodge that a Lodge has become extluot, whether
by the revocation of its charter or by the acceptance of the enrrender thereof, all Its
members, theretofore in good standing, become non-affiliated Masons, and, as snob,
are to be deemed snbject to the provisions of Section 1, Article IT, Part V, and Section 8, Article V, Part VI, of our Constitution. The rule in this matter should be
fixed, and never left to the discretion of the Lodge, because the exercise of eoah discretion would he very likely to produce the dissension which is spoken of In the
decision.
Aud as to the decision relative to the so-called degree of Paet Master, (3,) your
committee suggest that the Grand Master has probably overlooked the let of the
General Regulations of our Grand Lodge, which reads BB follows :·1. Thie Grand Lodge recognizes no degree of Past Master conferred by any
authority not holden under a legitimate Grand Lodge-acknowledging only the Order
of that name BB it exists in the ceremonies attending the inetallaiion of the Master
elect of a chartered Lodge; which Order shall be conferred only by a convocation
of Masters or Past Masters, not less than three lo number, who have thnt1 regularly
received it.
'
While the real reason for the adoption of this Regulation was, doubtless, t hat
Past Masters of Chapter creation often claimed the right, at an early period of our
history, to participate in the pror,eedinge of such a convocation as is therein named,
it is evident that the Grand Lodge not only recognized the Order or Degree-whichever it may be called-as an existing part of the ceremonies attending the inetalla·
tion of the Master elect of a chartered Lodge, bnt, inferentially at least, concurred
in the propriety of observing that ancient usage by presorihing the manner in which
the Order should be conferred. It appears in most, if not all, of the many Masonic
H11noale, Monitors, Trestle Boards, etc., which have from time to time been published,
as being conferred at the time of the lnetalfation, but in this Jurisdiction it is cos·
tomary to confer it previously thereto, to avoid an interruption of the ceremonies.
The Regulation has never been rescinded, and yonr committee therefore consider it
to be a still existing law.
Yonr committee, to whom was also referred that portion of the Address of the
Grand Master which relates to a certain complaint from the Grand Lodge of Arizona,
report as follows:Complaint was made to the Grand Master that our .Anaheim Lodge, No. 207, bad
Tiolated the jurisdictional rights of the Grand Lodge of Arizona by conferring the
degree of Entered Apprentice upon a party then, and for a long time prior, residing
in that Territory. The question involved was one of residence, in which the party
claimed to be a resident or California, although be was then and had for several
years been doing business in the Territory of Arizona.
The facts were that JOHN H. Lmw.u, the party in regard to whom the complaint
was made, was the eon of a widow lady who had for many years resided at Anaheim, In Loe Angeles County, California. In 1879, being then seventeen years of
age, he went to Arizona, and, engaging in mercantile business, remained there, bot
.had never voted or been registered as a voter there, and had never exercised any of
the rights of a citizen of that Territory other than that of doing business therein.
In November, 1886, be retnrned to Anaheim and remained there until April, 1887,
and during that time, probably in February or March, 1887, presented hie petition

676

Proceedings of the

(Oct. 11,

for the degrees to Anaheim Lodge. His own statement, made to the Master thereof
dnring the time his petition was before the Lodge for consideration, was that he
had considered Anaheim his home during all the time of his absence, and that he
then intended to remain there permanently.
His petition was received, and he was elected to receiv~ the three degrees of
Masonry; but, after receiving the degree of Entered Apprentice on the ~e.venth ~ay
of April, 1887, he was suddenly summoned to Arizona on business requmng his ~m­
mediate attention, and returned there with the promise and purpose o~ return~ng
again to Anaheim as soon as the business complications which required his attention
could be adjusted.
.
·. ·
. .
.
.
The intent of a party is always an important factor in d_etermmmg his res1?ence,
and his acts and declarations may show his intention. In this case, the legal residence
of the young man was at the home of his widowed niother during his minority. As
soon as he attained majority, he had a right to determine for himself whether he
would still retain and maintain his legal residence there, or transfer it to his then
place of business. He declared for himself that his intention was to r~tain it.at the
home of his mother, and the statement before us shows no act upon his part mcon_sistent with that declaration.
Your com111 ittee do not think it a reasonable conclusion that" on the day he arrived
at the age of twenty-one years he gained a residence in Arizona and lost the one
with his widowed mother." Jt does not matter what may have been his reasons for
desiring to mafotain his legal residence at his Califor~ia h~me, the o~ly qu?stion
being-did he choose to maintain it there, and did he avoid domg any act mcons1stent
with such choice? From the statement of facts before them, they think that the young
man at the time of presenting his petition to Anaheim Lodge, was, and during all
the tfme of his absence in Arizona had been, a resident of this State and within the
jurisdiction of that Lodge. If he had returned to Anaheim on the day of his majority,
and had on the next day presented his petition to Ar.aheim Lodge, there could h~ve
been 00 more doubt of his right to petition, nor of the right of the Lodge to receive
and act upon his petition, then there would have been of his right to be registered
as an elector and of his right to vote at a general election if one had been held on
that day; an'd it seems to your committee equally clear that, at the time his petition
was presented, he was entitled to all the rights of a citizen of this State, and that
he might truthfully say that he then was, and for the last twelve months had been, a
resident of the State and within the jurisdiction of Anaheim Lodge.
If a citizen ofthe State of New York should, for purposes of health, pleasure or
business, come to San Francisco, with the intention of returning to New York and
keeping his legal residence there, and should remain here for two or three or more
years there could be no doubt that he would not thereby acquire such a residence
as w;uld give to any Lodge of this city a right to receive his petition. He would still
be a resident of New York.
In this case the matter has been adjusted, so "that no action is at this time required
by the Grand Lodge. Still, as your committee think that upon the question of residence the views expressed by the Grand Master are incorrect, they have iudic.i.ted
their views, perhaps more fully than was necessary.
Your committee, to whom was also referred that portion of the Address of the
Grand Master which relates to a complaint from the Grand Lodge of Oregon, report
as follows:Complaint was made by the Grand Lodge of Oregon that_i~s jurisdicti?nal rights
had been infringed by our FidelUy Lodge, No. 120, by recemng and aotmg on the
petition of one HENRY BLAClUIAN, and conterring upon him the three degrees of
Masonry.

1888.J

Grand I 10dge of Oalifornia.

677

The case presented shoirs that BLACKMAN had moved to the town of Heppner,
in Oregon, and engaged in business there as early as 1880; that he not only acqllired,
but exercised, the rights ofa citizen of that State by voting at general elections and by
being himself elected to the office of Mayor of the town in which he lived, but that
he had three times presented his petition for the degrees of Masonry to Heppner
Lodge, No. 69, located in the town of Heppner, and had been three times rejected
by that Lodge before making his application to our Fidelity Lodge; that during the
time of his residence in Oregon he had been interested in a business house in San
Francisco, and had made several visits here, never, however, remaining more than
a month or two at a time; that during one of these visits, made in 1887, he presented his petition to Fidelity Lodge, was elected, and received the degrees; and
that, immediately upon receiving the last of these, he returned to Oregon and there
claimed rights as a Mason. The Grand Master directed that charges should be preferred against BLACKMAN by the Junior Warden of F'i.delity Lodge, for having in his
petition to that Lodge made false statements in regard to his residence, and that he be
tried upon such charges. Re was so tried and was deservedly expelled.
The action of the Grand Master was clearly right in this matter, and the only
doubt of your oomruittee is whether he should not have inquired more particularly
whether ·Fidelity Lodge did not, before acting on BLACKMAN'S petition) or at least
before conferring the degrees upon him, know the facts in regard to his residence,
or have such facts before it as should have put it upon inquiry.
The committee of investigation, to whom the petition was referred, ought to have
Informed themselves as to his residence as well as to his character, and were guilty
of a serious neglect of duty if they reported favorably on his petition without reliable information as to all the matters upon which the Lodge required advice. The
fl.rat matter upon which it needed advice and information was whether the residence
of the petitioner had been such as would give the Lodge jurisdiction to act at all. If
that question were answered in the negative, there could be no need of further
lnqriiry on the part of the Lodge. It is true that BLACKMAN stated to the Master that
San Francisco was his place of residence, and that it was his intention to make it his
permanent residence, but his acts were altogether inconsistent with his words.
Your committee, to whom was also referred that portion of the Grand Master's
Address which relates to the subject of life-membership, report as follows:l!J.ecelsior Lodge, No. 166, adopted a standing resolution to the elfect that any one
of its members, who had paid his dues to the Lodge and had maintained good standing therein for the period of twenty-five years, should thereafter be exempt from the
payment of dues. This resolution was in direct conflict with a by-law of that Lodge
Which declares that "The dues of each member of the Lodge shall be one dollar per
month, payable quarterly in advance." The Grand Master very properly declared
this resolution void, as it is clear that no Lodge can amend, repeal, or nullify one of
Its by-laws by a standing resolution.
Your committee join with him in his disapproval of the plan proposed by that
h1ol11tion, even were it lawful, and in his suggestion that the better plan, if there be
any good plan at &II in regard to life-membership, would be to grant such exemption
only npon the payment of a sum of money which the Lodge shall judge to be at least
a fair equivalent for its monthly dues; and that the money so received should in all
caaes be securely invested as a distinct fond, of which only the income should be need
for current or even extraordinary expenses. That fund should stand in the place of
*he member himself for the payment of due11. If extraordinary expense is at any time
tliourred, it should be met by an increase of the dues of the members of the Lodge,
and 11 life-member should no more be exempt from such an increase than one who
had maintained his standing by the monthly payment of his does,

To the M. •. W. •. Grnnd Lodge of Oalifornia :your committee have examined the reports of the several Masonic Boards of .
Relief, viz.: those of San Francisco, Oakland, Sacramento, Los Angeles, Stockton, and San Jose, and find the usual calls for relief continued and the accustomed
charity extended. They are all doing a noble work, and the remarks of the Grand
Master with reference to said Boards, in his Address, are fully appreciated.
The Board of Relief of San Francisco has expended a small amount in excess
:>f its receipts, having a balance in its treasury, September 30th, 1888, of only
$130 97, while its balance on hand at the beginning of its fiscal year, October 1st,
1887, was $645 73. Your committee therefore, though having fully considered its
request for an appropriation of $1,000 more than that of last vear have concluded
in view of tbe many and increasing demands upon tbe finance; of ~he Grand Lodge:
that they are not warranted in granting the request this year, but make the appropriation the same as for the fiscal year 1887-1888.
The Board of Relief of Oakland had a balance of $.'>54 02 on hand on the third
of September, 1887, and at the tind of the year on September 30th, 1888, a balance
of $400 45. being a decrease of $154 43; but, considering its close proximity to
San Francisco and its balance on hand at the beginning of this fiscal year, and not
desiring to encour!Ul"e the Boards of Relief in carrying over large balancea at the
expense of the Grand Lodire, your committee have concluded to reduce the appropriation of last year by $100, believing that to be doing this Board ample justice
and that it will be satisfactory thereto.
The Board of Relief of Sacramento requests a larger appropriation than that of
laet year, but mentions no amount. In view of its balance on hand at the beginning
of this fiscal year, October let, 1888, it being $179 11, and in excess of that at the
beginning of the last fiscal year, October lat, 1887, it being $142, your committee
conclude to make the same appropriation as then allowed.
The Board of Relief of Los Angeles asks for $1,000, and, in consideration of the
increased immigration and the rapid growth of the City of Los Angeles, which
enlarges the demands upon that Board, and in further consideration of the loss by
fire of the halls of its constituent Lodges, and of the fact that it is in debt to the
amount of $354 87, your committee have concluded to allow the appropriation
requested.
The Board of Relief of Stockton shows its receipts and disbursements to be
about equal, with a balance on hand at the beginning of thiR fiscal year, October
lat, 1888, of $115. Your committee therefore conclude to make the appropriation
.
the same as that of last year.
The Masonic Board of Relief of San Jose shows 11 balance on hand, October
lat, 1888, of $34 65, which is $25 25 less than their balance on hand on Oct~ber lat
1887, and it is seemingly in 11 healthful and prosperous condition. Your committee:
however, must refer that Board to their report of last year, in which it was stated
·that it was thought a bad precedent to encourage the establishment of Boards of
Relief in places having but one or two Lodges. Such is still the opinion of your
committee, and they have therefore concluded that they cannot recommend any

appropriation for that Board.

report that, while they think it would be an unfortunate precedent should the
Grand Lodge undertake to reimburse the Lod~es for expenditures incurred in caring for an indigent brother when his own Lodge, as appears to be alleged in this
cue, fails to come to his assistance, t.bey believe that the particular aid asked for
by the Lodge -the remission of its dues-may well be given. They therefore offer
the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Ruolved, That the dues of Selma Lodge, No. 277, for the year ending July 31st,
1888, already paid, be remitted and refunded to said Lodge.
All which is respectfully submitted by

reeolution:Whereas, Our worshipful brother, J AMliB WRIGHT ANDERSON, with great labor
and much research bas compiled and published a Masonic Manual comprising all
the decisions of this Grand Lodge ; as also, the Constitution of the Grand Lodge,
the Uniform Code of By-Laws, the Monitor, the Funeral Ceremony, the Installa.
tion Ceremony, the Ceremony for laying Comer Stones, the Form for keeping
Lodge-Records, and the Form for conducting trials; thus ma.king almost an
encyclopedia of that which forms a complete manual:

bas been prepared, makes it invaluable as a book of reference and entitles it to
the recol(llition of the Grand Lodge; therefore be it

the Ha.me being adopted by this Grand Lodge as authority upon the subjects therein
contained; that said committee be directed to report at the next Annual Communication ; aud that · any action which may be taken with reference to the

Bro. SHAEFFER was a pioneer merchant, being the oldest cigar manufacturer
and tobacconist in San Francisco. His honorable course as a business man and
his acknowledged integrity, had won the confidence and esteem of his r:nowmerchants and of all with whom he was brought in contact. When a lad he was

be

apprenticed to the LoRILLARDB of New York, learning all the intricacies of t~e
trade which he subsequently followed . He was identified with and devoted his
time and energy to the interests of the white laboring man, and for years employed
no Chinese in his factory. Many of his old friends termed his enthusiasm in this
respect as "Bro. SHAEFFER'S hobby, " but tho~ who knew ~im_ best were aw~re
that the employment of white labor was with him a sacred pnnc1ple. In carrying
out this principle he had expended .. moderate fortune, and was but beginning to
realize the benefit of his determined persistence in establishing the claim for preference, in all the channels of labor, of those whose children fill our schools and upon
whom, in the next generation, will devol' e the responsibilities of American citizens,
when he was called hence and his work was left for others to continue.
It may be well to anticipate the question, so many timlll! to be repeated as the
news of our brother's sudden taking off shall spread among the Masons of the
Pacific Coast, and state here that in the month of September last Bro. SHAEFFER
experienced a shock while,.. passenger on I\ railroad train stoppin~fo~ a few minu~
at Roseville Junction, in Placer County, while on the way to this city. The tram
on which he was a pa11senger was run into by another coming from a different direc·
tion, but join~g the main road at this point. The rear platforms were crushed,
and, te those wh9 could not see the danger, the collision gave (among others Bro.
SHAE.FHR) a terrible shock, the effect& of which caused his frienda some uneasine~s;
but our light-hearted brother laughed away their fears and, although temporanly
confined to his house, was in a few days about.his business, requiring only the assistance of a cane. Yet this was undoubtedly the primary cause of Bro. SBAEFFER's
death.
My bret.hren, the fullest and truest tribute to our brother's memory would be
incomplete withaut reference to his Masonic standing in the Fraternity. JOH~
WKBNER SHAEFFER was made a Mason in Mount MOf"i.ah Lodge, No. 44. of this
city, in the vear 1862. He was the Master of that Lodge in the several years 186.'\,
1866, and 1868. He received the Chapter degrees and was made a Royal Arch
Mason in California Chapter, No. 5, in 1868. In the year 1870 ?e was created a
Knight Templar in California Commandery, No. 1. He also received the degrees
of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, and in 1883 was created Honorary
Inspector General of the thirty-third and last degree of that R~te. But of al_l ~is
Masonic promotions nona so fully Ratisfied his tastes and desires as the pos1t1on
which he filled so ably and so accepts bly through the long term of eighteen yearsthe important office of Grand Lecturer of this Jurisdiction. As such we shall
remember him. As such we know that he would desire .to be remembered.
Bro. JOHN WERNER SHARFFER was born at Ca88el, Germany, on the fourth day
of October 1832 and was brought by his parents, while an infant, to the city of
New y or~ whi~h place was his home until he came to C~lifomia in 18112. On his
arrival here like the great majority, he set out for the nunes, but after the usual
viciBBitudes,he returned to the city and engaged in tbe busineBS for which he had
been prepared, and which he has pursued here for many yearb.. Hi~ widow and a
son and daughter survive him. By this death a happy family circle has been
broken. We commend the care of these loved ones to the protection of our Father
in Heaven, invoking His blessing upon those who have thus been deprived of their
earthly stay.
